objectives: To investigate the risk perception of professionals regarding prefabricated buildings when adopting the EPC (Engineering-Procurement-Construction) mode in China; to identify major risks, establish a comprehensive risk-assessment system, construct a grey-fuzzy evaluation method, and apply it to a real case project.
problem_statement: Existing studies on prefabricated buildings in China rarely link risks to the EPC mode, professional understanding of EPC risk perception is insufficient, and there are limited assessment methods for prefabricated buildings using EPC, despite EPC being promoted by national policy as an integrated delivery approach to solve fragmentation problems in prefabricated construction.
methodology: Mixed-methods triangulated study: literature review to derive an initial list of 30 risk indicators; questionnaire survey of 137 valid respondents (AEC practitioners in the Yangtze Delta) analyzed via descriptive statistics and Cronbach's alpha to refine indicators to 27 (7 first-level, 27 second-level); development of a combination weighting method (AHP for subjective weights + Entropy Weight Method for objective weights); construction of a grey-fuzzy comprehensive evaluation model; application of the model to a real EPC prefabricated concrete school project in Nanjing, China, using expert scoring from 12 managers/engineers (two groups) via interviews.
key_background_studies: Jiang et al. [1,2] - SWOT analysis and interviews identifying barriers to prefabricated building adoption in China (codes/standards, policy gaps)
Razkenari et al. [30] - SWOT framework analyzing offsite construction industry in the United States
Nadim and Goulding [31] - argued European reluctance to adopt assembly methods due to past failures
Rahimian et al. [33] - examined offsite construction risks in Nigeria (perceptions, resistance, technical capacity)
Gan et al. [3,4] - identified stakeholder collaboration as key risk in prefabricated building development
Xue et al. [6] - explored relationship between stakeholder cooperative management and cost performance of prefabricated buildings
Pal et al. [47] - investigated subcontractor relationships and their effect on EPC project performance (trust, cooperation)
Gao and Wang [48] - determined main risks faced by EPC general contractors across bidding, design, procurement, construction stages
Yang et al. [43] - path analysis showing interface management and partnering improve EPC project performance and risk management
Hong et al. [20] - noted prefabricated building development in China still in infancy
findings: A risk-assessment system with 7 first-level (management, design, procurement, construction, economic, policy, natural) and 27 second-level risk indicators was established for prefabricated buildings under EPC. Applying the AHP-EWM combined weighting and grey-fuzzy evaluation to a Nanjing case project yielded an overall risk evaluation value of 3.3203 (medium risk level). Construction risk (weight 0.4814) and design risk (weight 0.2298) were the dominant risk categories, followed by procurement, management, nature, and policy. Within construction risk, temporary support system stability was the largest sub-risk; within design risk, insufficiently in-depth design dominated; within procurement, quality defects of precast components were most significant. The study concludes that general contractors under EPC bear most project risk and must strengthen supply chain integration, in-depth design coordination, supplier quality control, and construction-stage safety management.

ideas.idea: EPC transfers nearly all project risk (design, procurement, construction) onto the general contractor, unlike traditional modes where owners provide design.
ideas.quote: the general contractor under the EPC mode undertakes almost all the responsibilities, from the design and procurement to the construction

ideas.idea: EPC is promoted as a solution to fragmentation and coordination problems across the multi-stage prefabrication supply chain (design, production, transport, hoisting).
ideas.quote: the adoption of the EPC mode is a targeted way to solve the obstacles in the development process of prefabricated buildings... the manufacturing and assembly processes can be systematically considered from the design stage.

ideas.idea: Under EPC, the general contractor takes on a leading design role and coordinates manufacture and assembly to avoid split/fragmented construction.
ideas.quote: The general contractor takes on the leading role in the design and comprehensively coordinates the manufacture and assembly as it pertains to the overall objective of the project [29], which can avoid the split construction of prefabricated buildings.

ideas.idea: Design risk in prefabricated EPC projects centers on insufficiently in-depth design, which causes errors and omissions in precast components without close cross-professional coordination.
ideas.quote: the design risk mainly lay in the in-depth design, which had a weight of 0.3420... errors and omissions of precast components can only be avoided by close cooperation between various professionals and participants.

ideas.idea: Procurement under EPC allows design and procurement to intersect since materials needed are determined at the design stage, requiring collaboration between purchasing staff, designers and engineers.
ideas.quote: design and procurement in EPC can intersect reasonably, since the materials required for the whole process of a construction project are also determined in the design stage.

ideas.idea: Quality defects and transport damage of precast components are major procurement-stage risks due to variety, size, and inadequate protective measures during transport.
ideas.quote: the procurement risk focused on the quality defects and transportation damage of prefabricated buildings... if they are not placed in the transport vehicle correctly, and the protection measures... are insufficient, component damage is likely to occur.

ideas.idea: Construction risk, driven by temporary support system instability and machinery selection during hoisting, is the most significant risk category in EPC prefabricated projects.
ideas.quote: construction risk occupied the largest weight, which means that it was the biggest obstacle to the smooth implementation of the project... U46 (temporary support system with poor stability) held the largest proportion of weight (0.4956)

ideas.idea: Economic risk under EPC is amplified because contractors, not developers, bear cost overrun risk, including developer payment delays and price-forcing behavior, despite the higher baseline cost of prefabrication versus cast-in-place construction.
ideas.quote: in the EPC mode some developers may deliberately delay payment for completed engineering tasks or force contractors to bring money into the contract and drive the price down excessively.

ideas.idea: Policy risk impact varies regionally; well-developed local policy environments (demonstration provinces) reduce this risk relative to less-supported regions, suggesting contractual/regulatory context matters for risk allocation.
ideas.quote: policy had the least impact on the final determination of the risk level... Jiangsu has more beneficial policies, in terms of both technology and management, which provide a guarantee for the advancement of prefabricated buildings.

ideas.idea: Management risk within EPC is tied to the general contractor's integration and coordination capability across design, production, procurement, and hoisting, which goes beyond simple superposition of these functions.
ideas.quote: EPC general contracting management is not simply the superposition of design, production, procurement, and hoisting. It goes beyond the project to the level of business operation and development strategy.

ideas.idea: Interface management is identified as a key strategy to manage the complexity and multi-party coordination risks inherent in EPC projects.
ideas.quote: interface management (IM) has appeared as an effective strategy that can promote communication and coordination between diverse parties in EPC projects

objectives: To develop a comprehensive typology of the causes of disputes in construction projects through a systematic literature review, to identify significant causes (with particular focus on payment delays), and to build a conceptual framework showing the interrelationships (antecedent and descendant causes) among dispute causes.
problem_statement: Despite extensive prior research on construction dispute causes and avoidance mechanisms, disputes continue to occur and cause severe cost, time and quality repercussions; existing classifications of dispute causes are fragmented, inconsistent, and lack a systematic framework showing how causes interrelate (antecedent/descendant relationships), leaving a gap in understanding the underlying structure of dispute causation.
methodology: A systematic literature review following the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram, searching Scopus and Web of Science databases (2,816 initial records, narrowed through duplicate removal, title/abstract screening, retrieval and full-text screening to 43 journal articles published 2013-2023). Causes were extracted, duplicates/singly-cited causes removed, similar causes grouped into 12 primary dispute categories (136 causes total), frequency counts used to identify significant causes, and a conceptual framework was developed using process modeling technique, informed by contract theory, systems theory and behavioral economic theory, with detailed analysis of payment delays as antecedent/descendant causes.
key_background_studies: Alrasheed et al. (2023) - classified disputes into four categories (abnormal conditions, financial situation, project delays, project management) and analyzed Kuwaiti court litigation data on payment and delay disputes.
El-Sayegh et al. (2020) - identified UAE dispute causes including contract ambiguity, poor design time, and owner-related, contractor-related and contract-related classifications.
Titus et al. (2023) - categorized disputes into contract incompleteness and opportunism, analyzed Nigerian construction contracts.
Cheung and Pang (2012) - explained contract incompleteness and opportunism theory, categorized causes by risk/uncertainty, collaborative conflict, contract incompleteness.
Francis et al. (2022) - identified payment delay, scope changes, and client administration issues as critical dispute causes in Sri Lankan building projects.
Mahamid (2016) - classified dispute causes into direct and indirect causes.
Rahnamayiezekavat et al. (2022) - found contract incompleteness and payment-related disputes frequent in Australian construction projects.
Wang et al. (2023b) - classified causes into delay-related, communication, contractual, site condition and design problems; used across US/China contexts.
Cakmak (2022) - identified ambiguous/complex contract provisions as a primary source of disputes in Turkish construction contracts.
Barman and Charoenngam (2017) - discussed how ambiguous contractual provisions and opportunistic behavior lead to disputes.
Ahmed and El-adaway (2023) - analyzed US legal causes of bidding-stage disputes including inaccurate cost estimates and improper tender documentation.
Abdul Nabi and El-adaway (2021) - examined modular construction disputes in the US related to scope changes and bid-related issues.
findings: The review identified 136 causes of disputes grouped into 12 primary categories (payment/financial, delay, design/scope, contract, bidding, project management, client administration, quality, risk, claim/dispute management, behavioral/professional, external factors). Payment delays by the client emerged as the most critical and frequently cited cause (28/43 studies), followed by scope changes (owner-initiated), contractual ambiguities, poor quality of work, and contractor progress delays. Disputes occur in both developed and developing countries, though specific causes vary by country. A conceptual framework was developed linking payment delay's antecedent causes (e.g., contractor's progress delay, project exceeding budget, funding issues, client cash-flow difficulties) and descendant causes (e.g., contractor bankruptcy, work suspension, poor quality), showing that some causes function as both antecedent and descendant factors, illustrating the interconnected nature of dispute causation.

ideas.idea: Poorly drafted or incomplete contracts (ambiguous, deficient, inconsistent, or defective terms) are a leading cause of disputes because they create differing interpretations of parties' rights and obligations.
ideas.quote: a poorly drafted contract causes disputes between the parties, as the project is based on an inadequate agreement, leading to miscommunication between the parties

ideas.idea: Unfair or unclear risk allocation, particularly where owners transfer risk to contractors, is a recurring contract-related cause of disputes.
ideas.quote: D-03 Unfair risk allocation, owner transfer risk to contractor 14

ideas.idea: Owner-initiated scope changes and variations are a major and highly frequent trigger of disputes, especially when project requirements are not clearly defined at the outset.
ideas.quote: Abdul Nabi and El-adaway (2021) indicated that many changes in the scope of work are witnessed in modular construction in the United States. These lead to excessive design changes and thus delays in completing drawings and plans.

ideas.idea: Design errors and incomplete design documentation, particularly in complex projects, are a critical driver of disputes and are often attributed to consultants.
ideas.quote: Francis et al. (2022) suggested that design error is one of the critical factors leading toward disputes in the construction industry. Consultants are primarily responsible for such design errors.

ideas.idea: Payment delays by the client are the single most significant cause of construction disputes, cascading into cash-flow problems, reduced quality, and even contractor bankruptcy.
ideas.quote: payment delays are not only prevalent in developing countries but also serve as a major cause of disputes in developed countries

ideas.idea: Bidding-stage problems such as inaccurate cost estimates, unbalanced bidding, and low-bid selection criteria (rather than quality/performance) generate disputes later in the project.
ideas.quote: UAE clients typically prioritize the lowest bids over performance, quality, or value when choosing contractors, leading to increased project issues including delays, claims, and disputes.

ideas.idea: Contract incompleteness enables opportunistic behavior by parties seeking to maximize their own benefit, which in turn fuels disputes.
ideas.quote: incomplete contracts allow for opportunism to flourish and define opportunism at work as a circumstance in which a person tries to maximize his interest in any situation in which he stands to benefit in some way

ideas.idea: Differing site conditions and unforeseen ground conditions frequently lead contractors to claim additional compensation, which often becomes disputed.
ideas.quote: The contractors encountered several instances of differing site conditions, prompting them to seek extra compensation from project owners. These requests subsequently turn into disputes

ideas.idea: Lack of clear dispute resolution methods/strategies and unattended or poorly substantiated claims allow conflicts to escalate into formal disputes.
ideas.quote: Lack of dispute resolution methods and strategies directly impacts the ability of project stakeholders to effectively manage and resolve disputes. Without established dispute resolution methods and strategies, conflicts may escalate, leading to prolonged disputes.

ideas.idea: Causes of disputes are interrelated as antecedent and descendant factors rather than isolated events, meaning a single trigger (like payment delay) can both result from and cause other issues (e.g., poor quality, delays).
ideas.quote: progress delay by contractor [B01] and poor quality/ standard of work [H01] are found to be antecedent as well as descendant causes

objectives: To develop a fundamental understanding of modular and prefabricated construction systems and to suggest an appropriate construction procurement method, based on project type, that addresses the administrative and coordination shortcomings of modular construction in order to achieve sustainable modular construction.
problem_statement: While modular/prefabricated construction offers benefits such as faster delivery, cost reduction, and better quality control, design professionals often neglect the intensive administrative and coordination work (procurement, scheduling, interface management) required, and the appropriate procurement method to manage these tasks is often not selected, undermining project success.
methodology: A literature-based conceptual study using a hypothetical case: the authors define a hypothetical twenty-story urban office building project, identify potential modular design options (precast concrete structural and architectural components, service modules) based mainly on three key sources (Gibb, Torre, Schoenborn), and evaluate procurement and project delivery implications for this hypothetical project to draw conclusions about appropriate procurement strategies for modular construction.
key_background_studies: de la Torre, M.L. (1994) - Thesis reviewing advantages/disadvantages and industry practices of modular construction, forming the basis for the study's discussion of cost, quality, schedule and coordination implications.

Gibb, A.G.F. (1999) - Off-site fabrication textbook providing case studies, applications, and procurement/design implications (strategic partnering, two-stage tendering, nominated suppliers) central to the study's literature review.

Schoenborn, J.M. (2012) - Thesis identifying constraints and barriers to design innovation in modular construction based on industry interviews, used to provide a modernized perspective on procurement and technology.
Precast/Prestressed Concrete Institute brochure - Industry publication promoting total precast concrete construction, used to support cost/time savings claims for precast structural systems.
findings: The study concludes that for a hypothetical high-rise urban office building, total precast concrete structural systems combined with precast architectural cladding and prefabricated MEP service modules offer significant time and cost advantages, but require early and continuous coordination among owner, architect, manufacturer, and contractor. Traditional design-bid-build delivery is poorly suited to modular/precast projects because it precludes early manufacturer/contractor involvement; design-negotiate-build is a slight improvement; and integrated project delivery (IPD) is identified as the best procurement/delivery method because it allows design, fabrication, and construction activities to proceed concurrently, maximizing the time and cost benefits of modularization. Success depends on selecting experienced, competent contractors/suppliers and delegating administrative burden to construction management professionals.

ideas.idea: Selecting an inappropriate procurement method can undermine the benefits of modular construction because administrative and coordination tasks may be neglected while design professionals focus on the modular design itself.
ideas.quote: Because the design professionals need to concentrate on perfecting the modular design, the intensive administrative work may be neglected.

ideas.idea: Design-bid-build delivery is unsuitable for modular/precast projects because it does not allow early involvement of the manufacturer and installation contractor before a general contractor is selected.
ideas.quote: A design-bid-build process is undesirable because early involvement with the precast manufacturer and the installation contractor is necessary.

ideas.idea: Integrated project delivery is identified as the best method for total precast concrete construction because it allows designers and contractors to be selected before the final design concept is complete, enabling concurrent processes.
ideas.quote: The best solution for a total precast concrete construction project is to implement integrated project delivery. Under this method, the designers and contractors are determined before the final concept of the project is realized.

ideas.idea: Modular/prefabricated construction increases certain construction management responsibilities such as planning, scheduling, and design coordination compared to conventional construction.
ideas.quote: Another problem with prefabrication is an increase in some construction management responsibilities. Planning and scheduling will be more complex due to the extensive amount of fabrication, transportation, and intensive erection procedures.

ideas.idea: Procurement of modular components is inherently more difficult because specialty suppliers and subcontractors must be involved heavily and early in the project.
ideas.quote: Trustworthy procurement of modular components is much more difficult to achieve because specialty suppliers and subcontractors must be heavily involved early in the project.

ideas.idea: An overlap of design and procurement activities is highly desirable in modular construction, putting traditionally delivered projects (where the contractor is excluded from design) at a disadvantage.
ideas.quote: An important point raised by Torre is that an overlap of design and procurement activities is highly desirable in modular construction. This may put traditionally delivered projects at a disadvantage because the contractor cannot be involved in the design phase.

ideas.idea: Strategic procurement approaches such as strategic partnering, two-stage tendering, and nominated suppliers help facilitate faster project delivery for off-site fabrication by improving planning and procurement.
ideas.quote: Strategic partnering refers to an owner working repeatedly with reliable suppliers and contractors. Two-stage tendering refers to these suppliers and contractors submitting initial offers early in the project... All three of these concepts facilitate faster project delivery using off-site fabrication because they improve planning and procurement.

ideas.idea: Construction management or design-build delivery methods are recommended over traditional methods due to the technical complexities associated with prefabrication.
ideas.quote: The last suggestion is to choose construction management or design-build as a project delivery method due to the technicalities involved with prefabrication.

ideas.idea: Modular construction requires intense coordination between multiple trades and parties, and inaccuracies or changes in design can severely disrupt the interrelated fabrication, transportation and installation processes.
ideas.quote: Intense coordination is necessary to ensure that fabrication, transportation, and erection occur in sequence with minimal delays. Additionally, original modular assembly design must be accurate because changes can devastate the interrelated processes involved.

ideas.idea: Delegating the intensive administrative work of modular projects (procurement, scheduling, project engineering) to a construction management firm rather than architects can better manage the complexity of prefabricated construction.
ideas.quote: Because the design firm needs to concentrate on perfecting the modular design, the intensive administrative work should be delegated to a construction management firm.

ideas.idea: Unfamiliarity of contracting parties with modular procedures raises the potential for project problems, underscoring the importance of experience among all parties involved.
ideas.quote: Because the parties to the contract may be unfamiliar with the procedure, there is a high potential for problems to arise.

ideas.idea: Owners can reduce risk in modular projects by forming separate contracts directly with suppliers and specialty contractors for prefabricated work, rather than relying solely on a general contractor's subcontracting choices.
ideas.quote: One way for the owner to eliminate the potential for problems between companies is to form separate contracts with a supplier and specialty contractor to perform the precast concrete work.

objectives: To develop a dynamic compensation mechanism and associated optimisation models that enable general contractors and off-site component factories to jointly manage component delivery date changes so as to achieve just-in-time delivery and reduce component delivery waste.
problem_statement: Off-site construction supply chains are fragmented between factory production and site assembly, and production deviations on either side make original component delivery schedules non-optimal. Existing static compensation mechanisms only require factories to absorb demand fluctuations, giving general contractors no incentive to control schedule deviations, resulting in unmanaged inventory, double handling, and other waste.
methodology: Conceptual and mathematical modelling study: a dynamic compensation mechanism (an 'inverse Kanban' of surcharges/incentives released by the factory) is proposed, followed by two genetic-algorithm-based optimisation models (Scenario 1: minimise general contractor's total cost when assembly is delayed; Scenario 2: maximise incentive revenue by trading schedule flexibility) solved using MATLAB's GA solver with illustrative numerical examples built from data composed via consultation with industry experts, plus sensitivity analyses on inventory capacity and surcharge/incentive levels.
key_background_studies: Ohno (seminal, on TPS/lean waste identification, foundational to just-in-time and inventory waste concepts)
Koskela (1992, lean construction - defines waste as non-value-adding activities in construction production)
Luo et al. (on OSC supply chain communication/coordination waste)
Pheng and Chuan (on just-in-time practicality in construction and compensation for flexible delivery)
Khalfan et al. (supplier-Kanban case study for just-in-time procurement in UK public sector)
Gosling et al. / Gosling and Naim (on engineer-to-order uncertainty and information management)
National and AIA California Council (2007, defines integrated project delivery IPD as collaborative approach)
Ju et al. (on redistributing responsibilities between upstream/downstream to reduce conflict cost)
Viana et al. (reports high proportion of components stored long before assembly, evidencing on-site inventory waste)
findings: The dynamic compensation mechanism, implemented via an inverse Kanban sharing surcharges/incentives, allows general contractors to make cost-optimal decisions when assembly schedules deviate. The Scenario 1 GA model reduced total cost by about 98% compared with delivering as scheduled in the example, and cost/reduction sensitivity depends heavily on on-site inventory capacity and surcharge/incentive levels when inventory capacity is low. The Scenario 2 GA model demonstrates general contractors can trade schedule flexibility for incentive revenue (e.g., $1,800 maximum revenue in the example), subject to precedence and fixed-activity delay tolerance constraints. Both models help reduce component delivery waste and support inter-organisational coordination without requiring centralised optimisation, though the framework assumes simplified one-to-one contractor-factory relationships and does not model transportation, labour, or equipment constraints.

ideas.idea: Off-site construction supply chains are fragmented between factory and site, creating coordination and information-sharing difficulties between general contractors and factories.
ideas.quote: The fragmentation of prefabrication and assembly, however, makes the supply chain difficult to manage.

ideas.idea: General contractors and subcontractors/factories often have mistrustful, conflicting relationships due to differing goals and value systems, undermining collaboration.
ideas.quote: The general contractors and the subcontractors usually have a mistrustful and conflicting relationship.

ideas.idea: Production and schedule deviations are inevitable and cause either additional inventory waste for contractors or overtime/rework waste for factories when components are delivered on non-optimal dates.
ideas.quote: There are two types of possible waste when the components are delivered on nonoptimal dates: (1) general contractor's additional inventory cost, transportation, and double handling when the assembly is delayed and (2) factory's possible overtime work to meet the due date for the components, the assembly of which is to be delayed.

ideas.idea: Existing static compensation mechanisms place all responsibility for managing demand fluctuation on the factory/supplier, without incentivising the general contractor to control its own schedule changes.
ideas.quote: The suppliers assume all the responsibility of handling demand fluctuation. Such compensation systems cannot correctly reflect the dynamic cost of the date change, and general contractors do not have the motivation to control their schedule fluctuation.

ideas.idea: Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) and multiparty incentive pools are strategic, project-level win-win mechanisms, but they are not well suited to quantifying and resolving operational-level component delivery date changes.
ideas.quote: The IPD approach is essentially a strategic win-win technique... as a contracting method to encourage parties to collaborate as a team. Component delivery, however, is an operational-level activity.

ideas.idea: A dynamic, quantitative compensation approach—using surcharges for unfavourable date changes and incentives for favourable ones—can more directly balance interests between contractor and factory than fixed reimbursement schemes.
ideas.quote: An explicit, quantitative compensation would more efficiently encourage parties to coordinate to achieve just-in-time directly with balanced interest allocation.

ideas.idea: General contractors should bear more responsibility for implementing just-in-time production in off-site construction, rather than leaving this entirely to suppliers/factories.
ideas.quote: Pheng and Chuan [47] also revealed that general contractors should take more responsibility to implement just-in-time production in OSC.

ideas.idea: Because factories and general contractors are independent, for-profit organisations with differing interests, just-in-time delivery cannot occur naturally without financial incentives or compensation.
ideas.quote: Because factories and general contractors are independent for-profit organizations, just-in-time delivery cannot be achieved naturally.

ideas.idea: Limited on-site inventory capacity forces general contractors to use third-party warehousing, which increases the cost impact of delivery/assembly schedule mismatches.
ideas.quote: Due to the limited capacity of on-site warehouses, general contractors have to lease nearby land [47] or use the logistics providers' warehouse to store excessive components [48, 49].

ideas.idea: Optimising component delivery within a single organisation without shared data across stakeholders tends to produce only local optima, while full centralised optimisation is impractical given the financially independent nature of OSC participants.
ideas.quote: optimising within a single phase without shared data from other stakeholders makes it difficult to achieve global optimisation from the perspective of the entire project... it is not practical to directly optimise inter-organizational activities.

ideas.idea: An information-sharing platform enabling dynamic release of surcharge/incentive data (an inverse Kanban) can support many-to-many contractor-factory relationships while each specific transaction remains governed by a one-to-one contract.
ideas.quote: one general contractor interacts with one factory over a specific contract through the information platform.

objectives: To develop an adaptive smart contract mechanism that encodes construction production constraints and quantifies their interactive relationships to mediate production bottlenecks and enable fair reward/penalty payment rules for a prefabricated (modular) construction project.
problem_statement: Smart contracts in construction are not inherently 'intelligent' enough to handle dynamic, uncertain constraints ex-ante, and there is a research gap in converting intangible process-level constraints (e.g., material, equipment, labor, external conditions) into tangible, quantifiable consensus that smart contracts can manage automatically, especially considering their interrelated effects on cost and schedule.
methodology: Case study data were collected from a high-rise residential building project in Singapore using modular construction (Prefabricated Bathroom Units, PBU installation, 120 units). Four constraints (external conditions/weather, material/PBU availability, equipment/crane availability, labor/worker availability) were identified with three reliability levels each, producing 81 simulation scenarios. A discrete-event simulation model quantified project duration, wait times, and costs; the Shapley value cooperative game-theory algorithm was used to calculate fair reward/penalty payments for each of the three parties (PBU fabricator, crane operator, installation workers). These payment rules were then encoded into smart contracts written in Solidity, deployed and tested on a private Ethereum blockchain (Ganache) via Remix-Ethereum IDE, with validation scenarios run to test correctness of automated payment execution.
key_background_studies: Koskela (1999) - identified seven types of constraints (materials, equipment, labor, prerequisite work, design/methods, space, external conditions) that must be removed during construction planning, forming the theoretical basis for constraint identification in this study
Koskela (2000) - developed the transformation-flow-value (TFV) production theory underpinning flow reliability and waste elimination concepts used in this research

Hamledari & Fischer (2021a,b) - showed smart contracts improve information-sharing accuracy and can automate progress payments, but noted heavy reliance on human-designed consensus and risk of financial loss from poor design
Hunhevicz et al. (2021) - argued complicated construction environments create uncertainties for smart contract execution, motivating the need for flexible/adaptive smart contract design

Lu et al. (2021) - proposed turning construction resources into 'smart construction objects' with awareness/autonomy to serve as a 'Check' mechanism in decentralized smart contracts, informing this study's constraint-based consensus approach

Wu et al. (2021) - proposed formal ontology for representing constraints in construction quality regulations to support auto-generation of smart contracts, cited as related but insufficiently addressing interactive constraint uncertainty
X. Li et al. (2022) - highlighted challenges in developing adaptive smart contracts addressing constraints, risks and uncertainties without causing blockchain redundancy/latency

Chen, Liu, Zhang, et al. (2023) - conducted simulation of prerequisite work readiness as a constraint enforcing critical path workflow reliability via smart contracts, directly related prior work by overlapping authors

Hamzeh et al. (2015, 2016) and Liu et al. (2011) - established links between constraint removal during make-ready/lookahead planning and workflow reliability/project duration, foundational for the constraint management framing
Szabo (1994) - coined the term 'smart contract' as a computerized transaction protocol executing contract terms, foundational definition used throughout the paper
findings: The simulation showed that adverse weather significantly increases project duration and crane idle time while reducing installation worker wait time, indicating installation workers become the production bottleneck under poor weather conditions. Without weather considerations, PBU delivery reliability dominated project outcome contributions, but as weather worsened, installation labor availability became the dominant constraint, underscoring the need to prioritize sufficient installation worker assignment during extreme conditions. The Shapley value method successfully produced fair, quantifiable reward/penalty payments for each participant (PBU fabricator, crane, workers) across 81 scenarios, and these were successfully encoded and validated within Solidity-based smart contracts deployed on a private Ethereum blockchain, demonstrating accurate automated payment execution based on detected constraint reliability levels.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automate fair payment allocation among project participants (fabricator, crane, workers) based on quantified marginal contributions to project performance, functioning as a contractual mechanism for incentivizing reliable production.
ideas.quote: Smart contracts can assist construction managers to motivate reliable production and minimize waste caused by bottlenecks in the system.

ideas.idea: A key challenge for using smart contracts contractually in construction is their inability to handle unexpected events and complex uncertainties automatically, since their 'intelligence' depends entirely on how humans design the underlying consensus rules.
ideas.quote: the inability of smart contracts to handle unexpected events under complicated environments posited challenges in realizing it automatically.

ideas.idea: Poorly designed smart contracts embedded in construction agreements pose real financial risk, since automated execution based on flawed consensus can cause irreversible losses.
ideas.quote: Poorly designed smart contracts may lead to irreversible financial loss (Hamledari & Fischer, 2021a).

ideas.idea: Off-site prefabrication (modular construction) introduces distinct contractual/coordination risks such as out-of-sequence or batch-driven delivery by the fabricator, which can create bottlenecks that interact with on-site equipment and labor constraints.
ideas.quote: The major constraints included uncertain and out-of-sequence PBU arrival due to the fabricator's preference for producing PBUs in a large batch, crane unavailability due to fully scheduled lifting activities, and a minimal number of workers assigned for installation to maximize profitability.

ideas.idea: Responsibility for different production risks in modular projects is split among distinct parties (fabricator for material supply, crane operator for equipment, installation crew for labor), each of whom can be assigned differentiated smart-contract-based payments/penalties reflecting their contribution to delays or bottlenecks.
ideas.quote: Table 4 presents the rewards and penalties under 81 scenarios for PBU fabricators, crane operators, and installation workers responsible for MA, EA, and LA under different weather conditions.

ideas.idea: External conditions such as weather are a significant, quantifiable contractual risk factor in modular/prefabricated construction that shifts which party's performance becomes the critical bottleneck, suggesting contracts should adapt risk allocation dynamically rather than statically.
ideas.quote: With weather considerations and as weather conditions got worse, the installation workers dominated the project contributions.

ideas.idea: Encoding cooperative game-theory-based fair division (Shapley value) into smart contracts represents a novel mechanism for allocating contractual risk/reward among multiple parties based on their marginal impact on project outcomes rather than fixed contractual terms.
ideas.quote: a simulation model was established to quantify the impacts of different constraints and determine the fair payment rules... different constraint-bundled scenarios and execution policies were developed and encoded in the smart contracts for automated executions.

ideas.idea: The proposed smart contract framework focuses on proactive 'make-ready' constraint removal before tasks are released into production, shifting contractual enforcement from reactive dispute resolution to anticipatory risk management.
ideas.quote: the smart contract focuses on the make-ready process, proactively avoiding situations where crews wait for conditions to mature instead of reactively resolving them with centralized control intervention.

ideas.idea: Current smart contract research and design in construction has not yet incorporated the full range of recognized production constraints (only 4 of Koskela's 7), highlighting a gap in comprehensive contractual risk modeling for MMC/prefabricated projects.
ideas.quote: this research only considered the four major constraints that impacted the projects in smart contracts, whereas Koskela (1999) suggested that at least seven types of constraints should be removed during construction planning.

objectives: To provide a comprehensive, up-to-date mixed (scientometric and systematic) review of 172 journal articles on construction cash flow management, identify key contributing scholars, classify research topics and methods, identify literature gaps, propose future research directions, and develop a conceptual blockchain-based smart contract framework for automated payments in modular construction projects.
problem_statement: Despite numerous studies on construction cash flow, the literature lacks a comprehensive review focused specifically on cash flow as the main topic; existing reviews focus broadly on financial attributes (cost estimation, financing) rather than cash flow itself, lack quantitative scientometric analysis, and rarely examine methods/technologies (e.g., blockchain) used to address cash flow issues, particularly in modular/offsite construction contexts characterized by complex supply chains and payment challenges.
methodology: Mixed review methodology combining scientometric (quantitative, using VOSviewer for co-authorship and keyword co-occurrence analysis) and systematic (qualitative) review approaches. Data extracted from Scopus database using cash flow and construction-related keywords, yielding 1575 documents, filtered via inclusion/exclusion criteria to 366, then PRISMA screening and backward/forward snowballing resulted in 172 included journal articles. Articles were classified into five categories (cash flow factors, cash flow-based schedule, cash flow-based capital structure, cash flow-based project type, cash flow and digitalization/blockchain) and mapped against research methods to identify gaps and future directions. A conceptual blockchain/smart contract payment framework for modular integrated construction (MiC) was then developed based on identified gaps.
key_background_studies: Elazouni and Gab-Allah (year not given) - initiated 'finance-based scheduling' integrating scheduling with cash flow
Kaka and Price [52,97] - investigated contractors' financial budgeting practices and S-curve profiles for different project types
Zayed and Liu [42] - identified 43 factors impacting contractor cash flow in USA and China using Monte Carlo simulation
Ikediashi and Okolie [61] - assessed 31 factors impacting cash flow in Nigerian construction industry via survey
Elghaish et al. [56,86,93] - integrated BIM/blockchain with cash flow and smart contracts for automated payments under IPD and other delivery systems
Ahmadisheykhsarmast and Sonmez [91] - developed smart contract to improve progress payment security and reduce conflicts
Sigalov et al. [94] and Sonmez et al. [87] - combined BIM with smart contracts/blockchain for automating progress payments
Le et al. [62] - grouped multiple factors (financial risk, retention, receivables, etc.) affecting cash flow
Al-Joburi et al. [63] - assessed impacts of negative cash flow on Dubai construction firms
Edwards et al. [64] - identified factors causing financial distress in infrastructure projects
findings: Cash flow research has grown steadily, especially in the last two decades, peaking in 2020. Kaka A.P. and Elazouni A. are top contributing researchers. Keyword analysis yielded five clusters: (1) financial risk/uncertainty, (2) finance-based scheduling, (3) cost/budget-related decision-making, (4) technology integration (BIM, blockchain), and (5) contractor-client relationships/late payments. Systematic review classified articles into five categories, with cash flow-based scheduling being most frequent, followed by capital structure, factors, project type, and blockchain/digitalization. Optimization is the predominant method overall. Significant gaps exist regarding offsite/modular construction (OSC/MiC) cash flow analysis, multi-project and supply chain considerations, procurement approach effects on cash flow, and fully automated payment systems. The study proposes a three-stage (preparation, initialization, execution) blockchain-based smart contract framework for automating progress payments in MiC projects to address fragmented supply chains, payment delays, and lack of trust, eliminating need for third-party intermediaries.

ideas.idea: Modular/offsite construction (MiC) projects face distinct cash flow challenges due to high initial capital costs and complex, fragmented supply chains not addressed by conventional cash flow systems.
ideas.quote: Conventional cash flow systems are argued to be incompatible with the fragmented and complex nature of modular construction projects [113,114].

ideas.idea: There is a research gap regarding cash flow analysis specifically for offsite construction and modular integrated construction, despite these project types facing unique financial barriers.
ideas.quote: There is an absence in addressing cash flow analysis for offsite construction (OSC) projects, especially modular integrated construction (MiC) projects characterized by the highest level of industrialization and prefabrication among OSC types.

ideas.idea: The choice of procurement/delivery approach significantly affects contractual cash flow relationships, and this is understudied particularly for nonconventional projects like OSC.
ideas.quote: There is an absence found in the literature on the association between project procurement approaches and cash flow analysis... appropriate procurement systems are ambiguous and differ from conventional construction projects due to the vast difference in processes and, therefore, affect their construction cash flow [112].

ideas.idea: Blockchain and smart contracts can automate payment processes, reduce contractual conflicts, and enhance project financial health by removing reliance on third parties like administrators and lawyers.
ideas.quote: Through the association between blockchain technology and smart contracts, an endorsement policy, compliant with the contract's terms, is enforced for all participants without the need for the involvement of third parties, reducing the chances of potential conflicts and enhancing the project's financial health [86].

ideas.idea: Delay in payments by owners/clients is consistently identified as the most significant factor negatively affecting contractor cash flow across multiple studies and contexts.
ideas.quote: payment delays by clients was the most frequent and highest-ranked factor that could affect contractors' cash flow [61,62,64,115–117].

ideas.idea: A proposed conceptual framework structures smart contract-based payments in MiC into three stages—preparation (contract and delivery system agreement), initialization (billing plan coding), and execution (progress verification and automated payment release)—to secure and accelerate payments among fragmented stakeholders.
ideas.quote: Figure 12 comprises three stages to adopt smart contracts in MiC: the preparation stage, the initialization stage, and the execution stage.

ideas.idea: Existing BIM-blockchain payment systems remain only partially automated, requiring manual updates of schedule and cost data, and fail to address potential disputes or accommodate flexible/rigid contract terms.
ideas.quote: the developed payment systems by the association between BIM and blockchain technologies were partially automated, where the user needs to update the schedule and cost data manually on the system; (3) the developed systems did not consider the possible disputes among participants when developing the smart contracts.

ideas.idea: Existing blockchain/smart contract payment solutions have typically only been developed and tested for a single specific project delivery system (e.g., IPD), limiting generalizability across different contractual arrangements.
ideas.quote: However, their system only considered a single project delivery system (IPD).

ideas.idea: The developed automated payment framework relies on an initial paper-based contract defining contractual relationships before stakeholders register on a blockchain platform, illustrating that traditional contracts remain foundational even when integrating new technology.
ideas.quote: The project participants initially include a paper-based contract to define the reciprocal contractual relationships. The related project stakeholders should then register to the Blockchain platform and create a digital identity.

objectives: To investigate the application of just-in-time (JIT) delivery principles in prefabricated/off-site construction and to propose a conceptual model that enables dynamic coordination and compensation between manufacturers and contractors to reduce delivery-related waste.
problem_statement: When component delivery deviates from schedule due to unexpected events, contractors and manufacturers tend to rigidly comply with existing contracts rather than coordinate, resulting in inventory waste, overproduction, or overburden (muri), and non-optimal outcomes for both parties. Existing JIT and incentive solutions in construction are static and fail to reflect real-time costs of delivery changes, and no dynamic, information-shared coordination mechanism exists between financially independent manufacturers and contractors in off-site construction (OSC).
methodology: Conceptual/theoretical paper: a literature review of lean construction, Toyota Production System, pull systems, Kanban, and JIT applications in construction and manufacturing, synthesised to develop a conceptual model. The model design draws on supply-chain and information-sharing concepts (dynamic resource management systems, optimisation systems, and an information exchange platform) rather than empirical data collection; no case study or validation was performed (proposed as future work).
key_background_studies: Ohno (1988) – foundational description of Toyota Production System, JIT, waste (muda) and overproduction as central concepts underpinning the paper's waste framework
Koskela (2000) – Transformation-Flow-Value theory and definition of waste in construction, central to lean construction framing
Pheng and Chuan (2001) – empirical study on JIT and inventory issues in construction, informing incentive/compensation discussion
Khalfan et al. (2008) – supplier Kanban and quality-price selection mechanism for JIT delivery in UK public project
Wu and Low (2012, 2014) – case studies on high inventory levels and non-value-adding activities in OSC
Bortolini et al. (2019) – on engineer-to-order (ETO) nature of prefabricated components limiting flexibility
Vrijhoef and Koskela (2000) – on waste stemming from supply chain stages, supporting conclusion on upstream waste causes
findings: The paper concludes that current contractual practices in OSC force manufacturers and contractors to comply with fixed schedules rather than coordinate, generating waste (excess inventory, overproduction, muri). It proposes a conceptual model with an information-sharing platform, a dynamic resource management system for manufacturers (issuing surcharges/incentives for delivery changes), and an optimisation system for contractors (automated rescheduling decisions). This model is expected to enable dynamic, real-time compensation that better reflects actual costs than static contractual payments, encouraging coordination and reducing waste, while acknowledging that contracts remain binding if coordination fails. Validation via case study is left for future research.

ideas.idea: Standard contractual arrangements push both contractors and manufacturers to rigidly follow schedules rather than coordinate when disruptions occur, causing suboptimal outcomes.
ideas.quote: out of respect for the contract, neither contractors nor manufacturers can coordinate for optimal. The contract originally is a method to pull components from factories; however, it turns into a push to force both sides to stick to the contracts when variations occur.

ideas.idea: The engineer-to-order nature of prefabricated components makes rescheduling costly and inflexible compared with standard materials, exacerbating contractual risk.
ideas.quote: The most components in the OSC are produced as engineer-toorder (ETO), which means if the construction schedule deviates, the customised components cannot be redirected to other customers as are raw materials (Bortolini et al. 2019).

ideas.idea: Existing incentive/compensation solutions in contracts are static and do not reflect real-time costs of delivery changes, limiting their effectiveness.
ideas.quote: Some static incentive solutions in the extant literature cannot perfectly reflect the actual cost caused by the change of delivery dates.

ideas.idea: Contractors bear more responsibility than manufacturers for implementing JIT and managing schedule changes, according to prior research and this paper's proposed model.
ideas.quote: contractors should take more responsibility to implement just-in-time production in OSC (Pheng and Chuan 2001).

ideas.idea: A dynamic, information-sharing based compensation mechanism (rather than fixed contractual payment terms) could better balance the interests of manufacturers and contractors when delivery schedules change.
ideas.quote: Unlike static compensation such as additional payment according to contracts’ prices and non-lowest tender, the surcharges defined in this research is determined by the real-time cost of the resource consumed at that moment, which can significantly eliminate manufacturers’ risk.

ideas.idea: Even with a coordination model, existing contracts remain the fallback binding mechanism if parties cannot reach a mutually beneficial agreement, highlighting the contract's continued central role.
ideas.quote: However, contracts are still binding if both sides fail to reach win-win.

ideas.idea: Poorly managed delivery interfaces between contractors and manufacturers can erode or cancel out the productivity and cost benefits of off-site construction.
ideas.quote: The advantage of off-site construction will be eroded, even cancelled out by increased cost and time if the delivery interface between contractors and manufacturers is not properly managed.

objectives: To harmonize the fragmented literature on Modular integrated Construction (MiC) by quantitatively and qualitatively analyzing bibliometric parameters, identifying research themes and trends, uncovering gaps, and proposing future research directions.
problem_statement: MiC literature has grown rapidly but remains fragmented; existing reviews either focus narrowly on specific aspects (sustainability, success factors, risks, barriers) or treat MiC collectively with other off-site construction methods without differentiating its unique research themes, leaving gaps such as lack of cost analysis, lack of quantitative benefit assessment, and lack of analysis of appropriate project delivery methods and contractual relationships in MiC projects.
methodology: A three-stage multi-stage critical literature review: (1) bibliometric search using Scopus with iteratively refined keyword strings covering MiC, prefabrication, and offsite construction terms, yielding 237-238 documents; (2) quantitative/scientometric analysis using VOSviewer and Gephi to examine countries, sources, co-authors, top cited articles, and keyword co-occurrence; (3) qualitative/systematic thematic analysis of 107 selected papers (2003-2020) categorized into six main themes (sustainability, construction operations, building design, management aspects, information technology management, others) with sub-categories.
key_background_studies: Gibb and Isack (2003) - top cited conceptual paper on pre-assembly and client expectations, foundational for off-site adoption discourse
Richard (2005) - discussed levels of construction manufacturing evolution (prefabrication to reproduction/automation/robotics)
Kamali and Hewage (2016) - critical review of life cycle sustainability performance of modular buildings, highly influential normalized citation
Wuni and Shen (2019, 2020a, 2020b, 2020c) - series of studies on critical success factors, barriers, and stakeholder management benchmarking in MiC/PPVC
Jin et al. (2018) - prior review combining MiC with other OSC methods, motivating need for a dedicated MiC review
O'Connor et al. (2014) - identified critical success factors and enablers for industrial modularization
Molavi and Barral (2016) and Dakhli et al. (2015) - discussed project delivery methods (CM/DB vs DBB) for MiC projects
Li et al. (2013) and Wuni et al. (2019) - identified and ranked risk factors in MiC projects using fuzzy AHP and literature review
findings: USA, Canada, Australia, and UK produce ~50% of MiC literature, with USA leading in publications and citations. Automation in Construction and Journal of Cleaner Production are top publishing sources. Keyword co-occurrence mapping reveals seven clusters (construction/productivity, sustainability, modularization/building systems, prefabrication/preassembly, structural/seismic design, BIM/construction management, and location-specific PPVC/Singapore) but notably lacks keywords such as risk, supply chain, contractual relationship, and disputes—indicating literature gaps. Qualitative analysis of 107 papers shows building design and management aspects dominate (~50% combined), followed by construction operations, information technology management, and sustainability. Key gaps identified include: no studies on contractual relationships between MiC project participants, no analysis of optimal project delivery method, lack of cost-benefit comparisons between MiC and conventional/other OSC methods, absence of risk allocation studies tied to contract conditions, and no assessment of standard forms of contract (FIDIC, NEC) suitability for MiC. Future directions proposed include studying contractual relationships and lessons from disputes, developing standards/codes, comparing project delivery methods, and creating readiness/sustainability indices.

ideas.idea: The literature notably lacks research keywords and studies on contractual relationships between project participants in MiC projects, representing a significant knowledge gap relevant to standard form contracts.
ideas.quote: a potential knowledge gap is identified as none of the consulted literature has addressed the contractual relationship between various project participants in MiC projects.

ideas.idea: Standard forms of contract such as FIDIC and NEC, which are built on risk-sharing principles, have not been assessed for their suitability in application to MiC projects.
ideas.quote: Standard forms of contract (FIDIC, NEC, etc.) are formed based on risk sharing. However, the literature is yet to assess the suitability of applying these forms in MiC projects.

ideas.idea: The project delivery method chosen affects how and when the contractor is reimbursed under contract conditions, raising questions about advance payments and variation order procedures that remain unanswered in the literature.
ideas.quote: The project delivery method also affects the reimbursement of the contractor for his work at each stage of the project, as contained in the contract conditions... will the advance payment for the contractor be adjusted due to the increased initial amount of money required for materials?

ideas.idea: There is no literature addressing how contractors' responsibility for care of the works, particularly during module transportation, should be handled contractually, including additional insurance considerations.
ideas.quote: How the contractor's care for the works will be addressed during the transportation of modules? Will there be an additional insurance policy for modules transportation in the contract?

ideas.idea: Despite likely occurrence of disputes in real MiC projects, no studies have examined dispute resolution or lessons learned from conflicts between stakeholders in MiC projects.
ideas.quote: the literature has not covered cases of disputes between project stakeholders, even though it is hardly believable that all MiC projects around the world were completed without conflicts.

ideas.idea: Although risks in MiC projects have been studied, no research has clearly addressed how these risks should be allocated among parties, which is normally embedded in contract conditions.
ideas.quote: risks in MiC projects have been adequately addressed in the literature (Li et al., 2013; Wuni et al., 2019). Nevertheless, no risk allocation to has been clearly discussed, which is expected to be included in the contract conditions.

ideas.idea: Early contractor involvement is essential in MiC projects, but the literature has not determined the best project delivery method to facilitate this, despite its critical importance for design coordination and cost.
ideas.quote: Early contractor involvement is key in MiC projects. However, this could be achieved through multiple project delivery methods such as DB, integrated project delivery, EPC, BOT, and so on. However, existing literature failed to present the best project delivery method.

ideas.idea: The design stage in MiC requires special coordination and collaboration, with the contractor or supplier needing to be involved early and share design liability, but this is understudied and highly influenced by the chosen project delivery method.
ideas.quote: The contractor or supplier should be involved from the beginning and accordingly, shall share in the design liability... This point is highly affected by the project delivery method which has only been discussed two studies (Dakhli et al., 2015; Molavi and Barral, 2016).

ideas.idea: Comparative cost-benefit analysis between MiC and other construction/off-site methods remains underdeveloped, limiting the industry's ability to make informed decisions on contractual and financial terms.
ideas.quote: In addition, clear comparison between MiC and other OSC methods in terms of cost effectiveness needs to be established to enhance decision making.

ideas.idea: The owner's role in partnering early with suppliers or contractors is emphasized as a way to improve coordination, communication and planning in MiC project delivery.
ideas.quote: the owner should take advantage of his superior position and partner with suppliers or contractors to enhance coordination, communication, and planning. Furthermore, construction management (CM) or design-build (DB) project delivery method was recommended due to complexity of the project.

objectives: To conduct a comprehensive critical review of existing NLP frameworks developed for addressing legal issues in construction, examine their limitations, and identify future research directions to expand the adoption of NLP for processing legal texts in construction.
problem_statement: Legal issues such as disputes, claims, and litigation are common in construction projects, often stemming from ambiguous, biased, or incomplete natural language in contracts and noncompliance with laws/regulations. Traditional manual methods of drafting, reviewing, and compliance checking are error-prone and time-consuming. While NLP offers promise for automating these tasks, the body of knowledge lacks a holistic understanding of existing NLP frameworks and their gaps.
methodology: A state-of-the-art literature review using a modified four-step methodology (Arksey and O'Malley 2005): (1) identifying research questions and scope, (2) keyword-based search across databases (Google Scholar, ASCE Library, Engineering Village, Web of Science, Scopus, etc.) using terms like 'construction', 'legal issues', 'disputes', 'litigation', 'contracts', 'NLP', (3) screening abstracts/conclusions to select relevant articles, (4) in-depth critical review. Initially 45 articles were collected, narrowed to 28 (19 journal, 9 conference) for detailed analysis.
key_background_studies: Lee et al. (2019) - developed rule-based NLP to detect poisonous FIDIC clauses biased toward owners, achieving 81.8% F-score
Chakrabarti et al. (2019) - developed ML-based 'risk-o-meter' outperforming rule-based methods for risk clause detection (92% accuracy)
Caldas et al. (2002) and Caldas and Soibelman (2003) - pioneered ML-based classification of contract documents into categories for ease of review
Hassan et al. (2020) and Hassan and Le (2021) - developed ML models for extracting subcontract scope from design-build contracts
Zhang and El-Gohary (2016a, 2016b, 2017) - developed rule-based information extraction and compliance checking frameworks linking regulatory text to BIM/IFC schemas
Salama and El-Gohary (2013) - ML-based classification of regulatory provisions into compliance categories
Jallan et al. (2019) - used LDA topic modeling to analyze historical construction defect litigation cases
Fan and Li (2013) and Zou et al. (2017) - developed semantic similarity-based case retrieval systems for legal case databases
Curtotti and McCreath (2011) - used corpus profiling to identify distinctive linguistic characteristics of contract language for ambiguity detection
findings: NLP research addressing construction legal issues can be categorized into three themes: contract review (ambiguity/poisonous clause detection, requirement structuring), compliance checking with laws/regulations (classification, rule extraction, BIM integration), and analysis of historical legal cases (defect analysis, case retrieval). Machine learning approaches, particularly SVM, generally outperform rule-based methods but require larger datasets. Most existing methods are proof-of-concept, validated on small, researcher-labeled datasets rather than real-world scenarios. Key limitations include lack of domain-specific datasets, insufficient integration of domain knowledge (ontologies/taxonomies), and lack of real-world validation. Future research should address contract drafting assistance, automated contract review (especially owner obligations), text simplification, requirement change impact tracing, early-stage compliance checking, construction safety violation assessment, and court outcome prediction.

ideas.idea: Contracts often contain biased or 'poisonous' clauses deliberately inserted by owners to shift risk onto contractors and other parties.
ideas.quote: The client often maliciously modifies the contractual terms and specifications to shift risks to the contractors (Lee et al. 2019).

ideas.idea: Ambiguity and vagueness in contract language, including lexical and syntactic ambiguities, is a major source of misinterpretation and disputes.
ideas.quote: Such misinterpretations of contractual terminologies are caused by lexical ambiguities (i.e., polysemes) (Berry et al. 2003) or syntactic ambiguities (i.e., sentence structure) (Zait and Zarour 2019).

ideas.idea: Incomplete contractual requirements often lead to design changes, disputes, and quality problems, particularly in subcontracts.
ideas.quote: Mitkus and Mitkus (2014) found that contracts with incomplete requirements often lead to design changes and associated disputes... incomplete project requirements in a subcontract often lead to disagreements among the contracting parties (Sun and Meng 2009).

ideas.idea: Most subcontract-related NLP research has focused on classifying and extracting scope from design-build contracts, but existing models are limited to few disciplines and project types, indicating a gap for broader automated subcontract separation tools.
ideas.quote: a more comprehensive model that can extract scope associated with any subcontracted task (such as plumbing, electrical, etc.) in any project type (industrial, commercial, etc.) is still required.

ideas.idea: Automated contract review research has largely focused on contractor obligations, while owner obligations (payments, permits, approvals) remain understudied despite being a significant source of disputes when unmet.
ideas.quote: most previous studies on contract administration were orientated towards contractor obligations... However, owners also have several obligations in a project, such as making payments, providing site information, assistance with permits, work inspection, and reviewing and approving submittals.

ideas.idea: Standard form contracts (e.g., AIA, FIDIC, ConsensusDOCS) differ in how they define owner obligations, and NLP could be used to compare these differences across standard forms.
ideas.quote: FIDIC contracts demand that the owner provide assistance in document preparation only in obtaining approvals, whereas ConsensusDOCS contracts require the owner to pay as well to obtain approvals and permits.

ideas.idea: Legal/contractual language is difficult for engineers to comprehend, motivating research into text simplification techniques to improve contract readability.
ideas.quote: legal contract provisions should be written in such a way that it can be easier for engineers to comprehend (Saseendran et al. 2020).

ideas.idea: Tracing the impact of changes to one contractual requirement on other dependent requirements is an unaddressed but important problem for maintaining contract consistency.
ideas.quote: Assessing the impact of the changes made for a specific requirement on other requirements in the contract is essential to maintain the consistency and correctness of requirements... no study was found that assist construction engineer in tracing the dependencies between requirements.

ideas.idea: Compliance checking research has focused on the design phase using complete BIM models, but early-stage identification of applicable code provisions before detailed design would reduce costly late-stage errors.
ideas.quote: Existing NLP models for compliance checking assumed that a set of requirements applicable to the project is given. Thus, they are only applicable to the later design phase when a complete BIM model has been developed. Any errors found at this stage will be costly to fix.

ideas.idea: Violation of regulatory codes and standards during design is a major source of legal disputes due to engineers' unfamiliarity with current codes and inefficient manual compliance checking.
ideas.quote: One major cause of design errors was found to be the unfamiliarity with relevant and up-to-date design codes, construction laws, and regulations among engineers (Yap et al. 2018).

ideas.idea: Predicting litigation outcomes or claim quality before costly court proceedings could help contracting parties negotiate more effectively and avoid disputes.
ideas.quote: The loss of time and money can be prevented if the contracting parties can evaluate and understand the worth of their claims before taking it to the costly litigation process (Iyer et al. 2008).

ideas.idea: Existing NLP models for legal/contractual analysis are largely proof-of-concept, tested on small or researcher-labeled datasets rather than real industry data, limiting practical applicability and generalizability to different standard contracts.
ideas.quote: none of the current methods was tested in a real-world context and many studies reported a low validation accuracy... the method is less scalable due to the reliance on manual development of rules, which seems tedious and may not perform well on other standards contracts such as the American Institute of Architects (AIA).

objectives: To explore how specialist construction consultancy firms operating in a fragmented industry can develop their own product platforms, and to examine the platform development process in relation to industry fragmentation.
problem_statement: While product platforms are well studied in manufacturing and increasingly in construction (especially housing), little is known about how specialist consultancy firms (architects, contractors) - rather than product-based manufacturers - can transform their value delivery approach by developing their own product platforms in a fragmented and competitive construction sector.
methodology: Explanatory single case study of a UK construction consultancy firm (ABC) and its architectural partner (DEF), using 15 semi-structured interviews with platform leadership/delivery teams plus three interviews with industry experts and four informal conversations, supplemented by document review, site visits, and steering committee discussions; data analyzed incident-by-incident using constant comparison, with diagrammatic memo-writing and a validation feedback session.
key_background_studies: Nam and Tatum (1992) - describe four strategies to overcome vertical fragmentation, including acquisition, trust-based coordination, contracts, and information integration
Simpson et al. (2001) - distinguish top-down vs bottom-up product platform development approaches
Lessing (2006) - distinguishes technical and process platforms and argues platform development should be separate from project delivery
Jansson et al. (2014) - identify platform support methods for coordinating new components with existing platform elements
Sheffer and Levitt (2010) - framework for vertical, horizontal, longitudinal fragmentation in construction
Gosling et al. (2017) - describe engineering-to-order design/engineering delivery phase in detail
Johannesson et al. (2017) - granular exploration of top-down platform development phases
Barlow et al. (2003) and Winch (2003) - distinguish design/engineering dynamics from physical product delivery in customization contexts
findings: ABC developed a product platform iteratively while continuing project delivery, rather than through standalone top-down or bottom-up approaches. By vertically and horizontally consolidating design, manufacturing, and assembly capabilities within the engineering phase (via a joint venture with DEF and employing manufacturing specialists), ABC achieved early and complete resolution of both product and process specifications. This enabled vertical coordination between engineering and manufacturing phases to be managed through fully specified contracts rather than acquisition of manufacturing facilities, reducing risks of asset redundancy and litigation from incomplete designs. A digital warehouse of coordinated, information-rich components supported reuse of design knowledge across projects, addressing longitudinal fragmentation. The approach moved construction delivery closer to the linear, sequential models found in manufacturing by clarifying and separating the roles of design/engineering, manufacturing, finishing, and assembly, and by minimizing on-site problem-solving and decision deferral.

ideas.idea: Vertical coordination between engineering and manufacturing phases can be managed through fully specified contracts instead of vertical integration by acquisition, reducing risk of asset redundancy.
ideas.quote: This means that vertical coordination between engineering and manufacturing phases can be managed by a fully specified contract, rather than acquisition.

ideas.idea: Historical reliance on contracts struck under incomplete designs as a coordinating mechanism between phases can lead to costly litigation.
ideas.quote: the historical reliance on contracts as vertical coordinating mechanisms between phases, struck almost entirely under incomplete designs, can lead to costly litigation (Li et al. 2012).

ideas.idea: Traditional construction practice defers final design decisions into procurement and site assembly, using vague specifications like 'or equal approved', which introduces inefficiency and compromises spatial optimization.
ideas.quote: early specifiers caveat their outline product specification with "or equal approved". This provides the ultimate product specifier with flexibility in procurement.

ideas.idea: Decision deferral in procurement protects clients through competitive tendering but creates incentives for suppliers to reduce quality to capture value, and can lead to conflict from incomplete contract information.
ideas.quote: Decision deferral also necessitates the use of procurement contracts with incomplete information, introducing misunderstanding and conflict.

ideas.idea: Full specification of components and processes prior to procurement allows competitive procurement from pre-approved manufacturers with pre-agreed pricing, minimizing transaction costs.
ideas.quote: Transaction costs are minimized in this exchange through the complete specification of the contract.

ideas.idea: Traditional procurement institutions and processes (seeking multiple competitive quotes, distinct sequential purchase of design then delivery) are not well suited to product-platform-based bundled design-and-delivery offerings, creating friction for firms like ABC.
ideas.quote: Traditional procurement routes are not set up to purchase buildings in this way, with clients typically procuring a design, and subsequently the means to deliver that design.

ideas.idea: Owning and controlling a fully coordinated platform allows a firm to provide a building warranty, underwritten by an offsite assurance scheme, shifting risk and responsibility from fragmented parties to a single accountable entity.
ideas.quote: Having a unitary team controlling the platform removes the element-by-element price cutting that threatens building quality, and enabled ABC to provide a warranty on the delivered building, underwritten by an offsite assurance scheme.

ideas.idea: Sub-contracting of design and delivery through multiple tiers introduces cumulative margin costs ('margins on margins'), which platform consolidation can eliminate.
ideas.quote: reducing designed-in inefficiency and the loss of value associated with the sub-contracting of the design phase, that is, no more "margins on margins" (interview 6).

ideas.idea: Clients may be required by planning or procurement processes to allow re-tendering of platform-designed buildings to enable competing bidders, which undermines the schedule and cost certainty benefits of the platform approach.
ideas.quote: ABC have previously been asked to re-design buildings to ensure that other bidders can submit tenders for their schemes, despite the negative impacts on delivery cost and schedule certainty.

ideas.idea: Non-contractual, trust-based coordination among project participants is an alternative to acquisition or contracts but carries risk of opportunistic behavior.
ideas.quote: firms can develop non-contractual methods of alignment in which parties coordinate their activities, leveraging long-term relationships, client leadership, or the professionalism of participants (Nam and Tatum 1992). However, such trust-based approaches risk opportunism (Winch 2001).
