Service blueprinting proved effective in visualising the links between service design and the technical, monetary, and perceived value of different service modules, improving shared understanding among actors including TPL providers. However, the late involvement of subcontractors in the innovation/execution phase slowed the co-creation process and limited their perceived and monetary value initially, though value increased with familiarity over time. The study also identified a lack of coordination between the different logistics service modules and their respective TPL providers, since no actor other than the main contractor had an overview of the whole system. Overall, modularisation simplified the design and content of logistics services but increased the number of actors needing coordination, meaning it did not simplify the value co-creation process itself.

ideas.idea: Subcontractors are frequently forced to use logistics modules through contractual stipulation, reducing their voluntary commitment and initial perceived value.
ideas.quote: the customer relationship can stem from municipal or developer demands on using a CLS to decrease disturbances in the vicinity of construction sites

ideas.idea: Mandatory use of logistics modules is written directly into subcontractor contracts with the main contractor.
ideas.quote: Its use by subcontractors is stipulated as part of their contract with the main contractor.

ideas.idea: The uncertain nature of construction projects makes contracts unclear about who bears responsibility for resource-related risks.
ideas.quote: The uncertain nature of construction projects renders resource demands unpredictable, which is a risk, and contracts render the responsibilities for these events uncertain (Loosemore, 1999).

ideas.idea: There is a tendency in construction supply chains to push risk upstream onto subcontractors/suppliers, damaging trust.
ideas.quote: Deep et al. (2022) identify from the literature review that there is a tendency to transfer the value chain or supply chain risks upstream, which leads to a breach of trust, and lack of reliability and commitment.

ideas.idea: Main contractors often view subcontractors mainly as a means for cost savings, which can lead to unfair practices and undermine trust in contractual relationships.
ideas.quote: There is often a tension between main contractors and subcontractors/suppliers, where the former views the latter as key to cost savings, leading to potentially unfair practices and undermining trust (Donato et al. 2015).

ideas.idea: Non-voluntary contractual use of logistics modules by subcontractors delays their involvement in the co-creation process and slows realization of value.
ideas.quote: The subcontractors were non-voluntary customers for two of the three modules, as they had to use them as part of the contract established in the project. Hence, they were not involved in the initial part of the co-creation process.

ideas.idea: Modularisation of logistics services simplifies design and implementation but increases the number of actors that must be coordinated, complicating overall contractual and operational coordination.
ideas.quote: the modularisation simplifies the service content but not the service value creation or the value co-creation process.

ideas.idea: Because no single actor besides the main contractor has an overview of all modules, coordination between different TPL providers responsible for different modules is weak.
ideas.quote: as the only actor with an overview was the main contractor, the interplay between the services of the different modules may not have been completely clear to the different TPL providers.

ideas.idea: The main contractor effectively plays two contractual roles simultaneously—customer of TPL services and de facto supplier/promoter convincing subcontractors to adopt the mandated modules.
ideas.quote: the main contractor has an important role in convincing subcontractors of the advantages of the logistics service modules... the main contractor takes some of the responsibility of selling the logistics service modules.

ideas.idea: Procurement of a new set of logistics modules for each new project resets the co-creation and learning process, indicating a lack of continuity in contractual arrangements across projects.
ideas.quote: the construction setting once again introduced hurdles by procuring a new set of modules in the next project, and the co-creation process must start over again.

objectives: To systematically review the literature (1993-2019) on critical success factors (CSFs) for implementing modular integrated construction (MiC) projects, identifying publication trends, geographical distribution, integrating CSFs into a checklist, and proposing a conceptual model mapping interlinkages among the CSFs.
problem_statement: Although MiC has gained increasing attention as a preferred construction approach, many executed projects have not achieved desired success levels, and despite growing academic attention, no systematic review or common framework of CSFs for MiC projects existed, making it difficult for researchers and practitioners to identify CSFs shared among project types, stages, and territories.
methodology: Systematic literature review using a realist research paradigm and meta-synthesis analytical approach with thematic content analysis. Articles were retrieved from Scopus using a comprehensive Boolean search algorithm, supplemented by snowballing search strategy, yielding 55 included publications (1993-2019) comprising journal articles, conference papers, industry reports, books, and a PhD thesis. Metadata (year, context, reported CSFs) were extracted into a concept matrix; CSFs were ranked by frequency of occurrence. A stage-gate model classified CSFs across project phases, and a conceptual causal loop model was developed using systems dynamics (Vensim) to illustrate CSF interdependencies.
key_background_studies: Rockart (1982) - foundational definition of CSFs as key areas of activity for management attention
Martin (1982) - described CSF methodology as a decision-making tool for prioritizing essential activities
O'Connor, O'Brien & Choi (2014) - identified CSFs for industrial MiC projects including design freeze and owner resources
Murtaza, Fisher & Skibniewski (1993) - identified CSFs for petrochemical MiC projects including early design freeze and standardization
Kamar, Alshawi & Hamid (2009) - identified top CSFs for residential MiC projects in Malaysia
Osei-Kyei & Chan (2015) - prior CEM review methodology establishing CSF framework for PPP projects, used as benchmark
Antwi-Afari et al. (2018) - prior CEM review of CSFs for BIM implementation, used as benchmark for review scale
Jonsson & Rudberg (2015) - classification of MiC production systems and standardization mismatch issues
Gibb (2001) - classification of pre-assembly degrees and modularization considerations
Baldwin & Clark (1997, 2000) - foundational theory of modularity and modularization applied to construction
findings: The review identified and ranked 35 CSFs for implementing MiC projects across 55 studies from 16 countries, with the US, UK, Malaysia, Australia, and Hong Kong as largest contributors. The six most cited CSFs were: (1) good working collaboration, effective communication and information sharing among participants; (2) improved supply chain coordination and management; (3) accurate design, early design freeze and timely owner approval; (4) fully-integrated approach and involvement of key participants throughout the project; (5) suitable procurement strategy and contracting; and (6) standardization and benchmarking of best practices. A stage-gate framework mapped CSFs across conception & planning, design & procurement, and construction phases. A conceptual causal loop model revealed mostly reinforcing feedback loops among CSFs, with effective collaboration, risk management, and stakeholder management identified as highly influential and interdependent factors.

ideas.idea: Selecting an appropriate procurement strategy and contracting method, particularly design-build, is a critical success factor for MiC projects because it integrates design and construction into a single accountable entity.
ideas.quote: Unlike the design-bid-build procurement method, the design-build delivery method brings both design and construction function as one team in a single contractual entity to the owner.

ideas.idea: Early and extensive involvement of fabricators, contractors and other key participants in design decision-making, rather than late-stage engagement, is essential to avoid risky practices and design gaps.
ideas.quote: Thus, it is a risky practice for fabricators to manufacture modules based on design specifications and set of drawings to which they were not privy or involved.

ideas.idea: Contractual and procurement decisions should give module fabricators expanded scope over materials procurement and manufacturing when schedule is critical, and once selected, fabricators should face minimal interference.
ideas.quote: Rentschler et al. (2016) recommended that module fabricators should be offered a greater scope of buying all production materials and manufacturing of the modules in a case where the schedule is critical to avoid the emergence of hindrances to performance.

ideas.idea: Early design freeze, enforced through owner approval discipline, is critical because design changes are especially costly and schedule-sensitive once modules are in fabrication, implying contracts must address change control tightly.
ideas.quote: As design changes are particularly costly, risky and schedule-sensitive in MiC projects, specification, concept and detailed design freezes should be made early to ensure smooth delivery of the projects.

ideas.idea: Standardization of modules and benchmarking are needed to overcome the higher direct costs and lack of economies of scale in MiC, which has implications for how contracts should treat customization versus standardized components.
ideas.quote: This reality is partly due to the lower level of standardization in the modules and the diseconomies of scale in fledgling MiC markets.

ideas.idea: Risk management specific to MiC—covering stakeholder, supply chain, and project execution risks—is a distinct critical success factor, reflecting risks not present in conventional cast-in-situ construction that contracts should allocate for.
ideas.quote: Effective management of stakeholder, supply chain and project execution risks Choi (2014), Choi and O'Connor (2014), Choi et al. (2016), Hjort et al. (2014), Ismail et al. (2012), Kamar et al. (2009, 2010), O'Connor, O'Brien, and Choi (2014), Rashidi and Ibrahim (2017)

ideas.idea: The supply chain for MiC is fundamentally different from conventional construction, spanning modular design, procurement, engineering, manufacturing, transportation, buffer, storage and on-site assembly, requiring contractual coordination across fragmented but interdependent segments.
ideas.quote: the supply chain of MiC comprises modular design, procurement, engineering, manufacturing, transportation, buffer, storage and on-site assembly (Li et al., 2016).

ideas.idea: Because MiC modules are made-to-order and project-specific, scheduling and contractual delivery obligations must be configured differently than in conventional construction to avoid inventory and delay risks.
ideas.quote: scheduling must be configured such that the quantity of each module produced precisely matches its optimum requirement in the project so that its inventory returns to zero on completion of the project

ideas.idea: Owner-furnished long-lead equipment specifications and module envelope limitations are recognized contractual/technical constraints that must be managed for MiC project success, distinct from conventional contracts.
ideas.quote: Owner-furnished long-lead equipment specification Choi (2014), Choi and O'Connor (2014), Choi et al. (2016), O'Connor et al. (2014)

objectives: To identify and rank critical success factors (CSFs) for project planning and control (PP&C) in prefabrication housing production (PHP), explore underlying relationships among these factors, and provide guidance for key stakeholders (designers, manufacturers, contractors) to improve PP&C outcomes in PHP, using China as the empirical setting.
problem_statement: Although PHP is increasingly adopted worldwide and in China, its planning and control face heightened complexity due to more stakeholders, greater coordination and information needs, and specific risks (delays, cost overruns, quality problems). While CSFs have been studied for many project types, few studies comprehensively examine CSFs specific to PHP's planning and control across the full range of stakeholders (design, manufacturing, construction), leaving a research gap that this study aims to fill.
methodology: A mixed literature review, in-depth interviews and pilot study with five PHP experts were used to generate a preliminary list of 23 factors influencing PHP implementation. A questionnaire survey using a five-point Likert scale was distributed via snowball sampling to 400 professionals (designers, manufacturers, contractors) in China's PHP industry in March–May 2017, yielding 136 valid responses (34% response rate). Data were analyzed using mean score (MS) ranking, one-sample t-tests, and exploratory factor analysis (principal component analysis with varimax rotation) using SPSS 19.0 to rank factors and group them into underlying clusters.
key_background_studies: Ismail et al. (2012) – identified management-related factors for PHP but overlooked supply chain, technical and industry-related factors, motivating this study's more comprehensive approach.

Chan et al. (2004) – identified five groups of CSFs for construction project success (project-related, procedures, management actions, human factors, external environment), used as a framework reference.
Zwikael and Globerson (2006) – examined 16 planning processes and identified the most sensitive ones for project success.
Ling et al. (2009) – established 24 project practices correlated with performance of Singaporean firms in China, especially risk management.
Li et al. (2011) – grouped CSFs for green building projects into five components including project manager's competence and coordination of designers.
Liu et al. (2014) – identified CSFs for PPP infrastructure projects such as feasibility analysis and interface/conflict management.
O'Connor et al. (2014) – presented 21 CSFs for modularization projects including owner's planning resources, fabricator capability, heavy lifting equipment.
Heravi et al. (2015) – identified four critical stakeholder groups (owner, developer, designers, contractors) influencing project success.
Deng et al. – provided the methodological framework (mean score and factor analysis) used to study inhibiting factors via questionnaire.
Arif et al. – provided methodological framework (factor analysis, average score) for studying political risk management variables.
Jabar et al. (2013a) – found problem-solving skill to be the most important PM competency in Malaysian PHP market, corroborating this study's findings.
Sacks et al. (2004) – proposed automation of design and detailing tasks for precast concrete.
Haller et al. – proposed sequence deviation quotient (SDQ) method to control design iteration risks in PHP.
findings: 23 CSFs were identified and validated as significant (mean scores above 3.00). The top five CSFs were: designers' experience of PHP, manufacturers' experience of PHP, project manager's ability to solve problems, maturity of techniques used in the detailed design phase, and persistent policies and incentives. Exploratory factor analysis grouped the 23 factors into five clusters explaining 67.2% of variance: (1) technology and method (dominant, 28.6% variance), (2) information, communication and collaboration, (3) external environment, (4) experience and knowledge, and (5) competence of the project manager. Designers, manufacturers and contractors largely agreed on rankings except for designers' distinct emphasis on designer involvement during production/construction. The study concludes that technology/method factors are most critical to PHP success and provides a holistic, multi-stakeholder framework for improving PP&C in PHP.

ideas.idea: Design must be largely finalized before production begins because design changes are costly to accommodate in prefabrication, unlike conventional construction.
ideas.quote: the design must be largely finished prior to the production. The fast production and assembly of building components need accurate design.

ideas.idea: Separation of architectural design and detailed component design creates a subcontracting relationship where the manufacturer depends on and follows the designer's specifications.
ideas.quote: The architectural design and the detailed design of prefabricated components in PHP projects are clearly separate in China. This is evidenced by the fact that the manufacturer is only a subcontractor.

ideas.idea: Late delivery of precast components from manufacturers is a common and critical issue contractors face, tied to manufacturing management quality.
ideas.quote: It has been recognized in PHP projects in Singapore that late delivery by the precast components’ manufacturers is the most common issue for the main contractors

ideas.idea: The project manager plays a central coordinating role between off-site and on-site activities and must resolve problems to keep the schedule on track, especially regarding transportation and lifting logistics.
ideas.quote: The project manager is the person in the PHP project who coordinates on-site and off-site activities and is responsible for the project objectives.

ideas.idea: Detailed design is a distinct, multidisciplinary phase converting architectural drawings into assembly and connection drawings, and any design change requires reprocessing this detailed design, creating rework risk.
ideas.quote: If there are design changes, the detailed design needs to be reprocessed to keep consistent with the overall design of the building.

ideas.idea: BIM adoption in the detailed design phase is limited by interoperability problems between architect software (IFC format) and fabricator software (SAT format), impeding integrated digital design-to-manufacture workflows.
ideas.quote: numerous limitations related to the information exchange in both geometric shape information and other semantically meaningful information between architects (the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) format) and fabricators (the Standard ACIS Text (SAT) format) have impeded the BIM technology in the detailed design phase

ideas.idea: Government policy and incentives are necessary to encourage contractors to adopt unproven prefabrication technology over established methods, especially in early-stage markets.
ideas.quote: When the PHP is still in its infancy, contractors are more willing to choose a mature method rather than new ones without incentives from local government

ideas.idea: Assembly/delivery planning method (push vs pull) affects site congestion and cost; most Chinese contractors use a push-based approach causing site storage problems, whereas lean 'pull' delivery is preferable.
ideas.quote: Most contractors in China adopted the push method. Consequently, all the prefabricated components have been produced beforehand and delivered to the construction site... they will block the construction site

ideas.idea: Early and close coordination among designer, manufacturer and contractor is essential to avoid rework and delays, since design, production and erection activities run in parallel rather than sequentially as in traditional construction.
ideas.quote: Close coordination between prefabrication and construction processes is needed as these two groups of activities run in parallel

ideas.idea: Lack of manufacturer and contractor experience/expertise directly undermines the schedule predictability advantage that prefabrication is supposed to offer.
ideas.quote: a lack of manufacturing experience can cause delays in the flow of deliveries to the construction site; a lack of competence on the part of the contractor can lead to delays in the installation schedule

ideas.idea: Quality issues in prefabricated components (e.g., low precision of junctions, broken nibs) are more costly to fix once detected on site than at the plant, highlighting the importance of upstream quality management.
ideas.quote: Such quality issues often caused repair or rework. As these issues were detected at the construction site, the resulting costs are higher than be detected in the plant.

ideas.idea: Well-developed specifications, regulations and streamlined permitting processes are necessary external conditions supporting successful PHP implementation, but permitting remains slow in practice.
ideas.quote: Although some regions in China have created incentives such as tax exemptions and rewards, the process of obtaining planning permission is slow. The design and construction planning must be approved by several agencies.

objectives: To explore the factors influencing the adoption of Design for Manufacturing and Assembly (DfMA) technologies in Singapore's construction industry, in order to understand strategies needed to encourage private sector buy-in and operationalize government productivity roadmaps.
problem_statement: Despite strong government promotion of prefabrication and DfMA, private sector adoption in Singapore remains low (only 11.2% of national prefabrication level as of 2001), and the factors driving or hindering DfMA adoption are not well understood.
methodology: A questionnaire survey (following a literature review that identified 17 influencing factors across six categories) was distributed to 124 industry professionals (developers, contractors, consultants, architects, engineers, project managers) in Singapore; 30 valid responses (24.2% response rate) were analysed using one-sample t-tests to assess statistical significance of each factor's importance.
key_background_studies: Boothroyd (2005) - originator of DfMA methodology and quantitative evaluation approach
Bogue (2012) - distinguished DfM and DfA approaches and three methods of applying DfMA
Gibb and Isack (2003) - classified four levels of off-site production and client understanding barriers
Ballard and Howell (1998) - described construction as fabrication and assembly, linking design to site assembly
Kamar, Alshawi and Hamid (2009) - identified knowledge and demand factors for IBS/prefabrication adoption
Mao, Shen, Pan and Ye (2015) - identified supporting organizations and legal frameworks as key factors for off-site construction
Park, Yashada, Kim and Ham (2011) - studied Singapore buildability regulations and their effect on prefabrication uptake
Zakaria, Gajendran, Rose and Brewer (2018a,b) - reviewed IBS adoption factors and complexity of adoption in Malaysia
Jaillon and Poon (2008, 2010) - examined client support, design limitations and site constraints in Hong Kong prefabrication
Blismas and Wakefield (2009); Pan, Gibb and Dainty (2007) - identified time reduction and site constraints as key drivers/barriers in UK/Australia off-site construction
Gerth, Boqvist, Bjelkemyr and Lindberg (2013) - proposed Design for Construction (DfC) method integrating constructability evaluation
Fox, Marsh and Cockerham (2001) - studied lack of collaboration among manufacturing, assembly and plant companies
Goulding, Pour Rahimian, Arif and Sharp (2015) - discussed DfMA as value-adding process and need for stakeholder training
findings: All 17 influencing factors positively and significantly affected DfMA adoption success (p=0.00). The three most important factors were 'Reduction in construction time', 'Site constraints and storage', and 'Integration of project team', while the three least important were 'Design limitations due to standardization', 'Presence of government legislation', and 'Presence of government incentives'. Government-related factors played a comparatively minor role, suggesting DfMA adoption in Singapore is driven more by project-specific, design, and performance-related factors than by policy or incentives, partly because government mandates are already well-enforced.

ideas.idea: DfMA is often equated with prefabrication and off-site construction, with major elements manufactured off-site and assembled on-site—a project delivery process.
ideas.quote: Laing O’Rourke (2013) refers to DfMA in construction as being a project-delivery process, where major elements of a product are manufactured offsite and assembled onsite.

ideas.idea: Standardization of design and components is central to DfMA but creates tension with architectural creativity and flexibility.
ideas.quote: the conflict between standardization and flexibility has still not been resolved; as Gibb (2001, pg. 308) put it, ‘it remains as a tension that sometimes leads to design impotence, but should be used to ensure optimal implementation’.

ideas.idea: Early design freeze is critical for successful prefabrication projects, since design changes late in the process cause failures and increase risk for the design team.
ideas.quote: One of the key reasons for the failure of off-site construction is the inability to exercise early design freeze (Blismas, Pendlebury, Gibb, & Pasquire, 2005).

ideas.idea: Fragmentation of the construction industry and lack of collaboration among design, manufacturing and assembly parties undermines effective DfMA implementation, requiring integrated multidisciplinary project teams.
ideas.quote: a multidisciplinary team including building design engineers, architects, contractors, and specialists is needed and these experts must share a common level of commitment and willingness to engage with DfMA technology.

ideas.idea: Government legislation and mandated buildability/constructability scoring systems (B-score, C-score) are used to compel adoption of prefabrication techniques on government land sale sites.
ideas.quote: the Singapore government has introduced two legislations relating to the promotion of DfMA in Singapore... Minimum Buildable Design Score (B-score)... Minimum Constructability Score (C-score).

ideas.idea: Financial incentives and government funding schemes (such as the Construction Productivity and Capability Fund) are intended to offset the cost premium of adopting DfMA, but may be insufficient to change contractor/subcontractor risk allocation.
ideas.quote: companies could offset up to 70% of the cost premium of adopting DfMA with maximum funding of $10 million per application (Ying & Sen, 2017).

ideas.idea: Contractual and financial risk in DfMA projects is distributed unevenly among main contractors, prefabricators and MEP subcontractors, disincentivizing SME participation.
ideas.quote: about 40% of the contract sum would be taken by the main building contractors, with the rest going to the prefabricator and MEP (i.e. Mechanical, Electrical and Plumbing) subcontractors.

ideas.idea: Contractors' willingness to commit capital upfront for prefabrication facilities is a key enabler, and large firms who invest can gain competitive and productivity advantages.
ideas.quote: if contractors are unwilling to put the capital upfront to establish specialized prefabrication factories for the adoption of prefabrication technology, the process will be slowed down (Szwarc, 2013).

ideas.idea: Client and developer decision-making power is decisive in determining demand for prefabrication, and misunderstanding of DfMA benefits by clients is a barrier.
ideas.quote: unless client decision-makers understand its benefits and limitations, their misunderstandings and prejudices will continue to hamper further development.

ideas.idea: Transportation and site logistics constraints (e.g., just-in-time delivery, road permits, storage limitations) are significant practical/contractual considerations for prefabricated construction in dense urban settings.
ideas.quote: Restricted site layouts pose challenges for the placement of prefabricated modules, which results in the project team being reluctant to adopt prefabrication (Blismas et al., 2005).

ideas.idea: BIM is increasingly used as a coordination tool to link design data with manufacturing and assembly processes, improving productivity and reducing errors in prefabricated construction.
ideas.quote: through BIM, digital product data can be exploited in downstream processes and used for the manufacturing and assembly of structural systems.

ideas.idea: Formal institutional systems, such as building codes and mandatory requirements, provide legitimacy and enforcement mechanisms that drive adoption of prefabrication/DfMA more effectively than voluntary incentives.
ideas.quote: As Scott’s (2014) institutional theory notes, formalized systems provide for enforcement, which provides legitimacy to institutional processes.

objectives: To design an optimal government subsidy allocation policy that promotes contractor adoption of modular construction (MC) by explicitly modeling uncertainty in MC price, cast-in-situ cost, MC supply, and future construction volume, using a bilevel stochastic programming framework, and to validate this policy using a Hong Kong case study.
problem_statement: Existing government subsidy schemes for promoting modular construction have been designed using deterministic parameters, ignoring real-world uncertainties in MC selling price, cast-in-situ cost, maximum MC supply, and future construction volumes. This can lead to suboptimal subsidy plans that fail to maximize MC adoption within limited government budgets, and existing solution methods rely on heuristics that sacrifice optimality.
methodology: The study formulates a bilevel stochastic program in which the government (upper level) sets a unit subsidy price to maximize MC quantity used subject to a budget constraint, and contractors (lower level) minimize their costs by choosing between MC modules from multiple factories and cast-in-situ construction, under multiple discrete stochastic scenarios of price, supply, and demand. An exact bisection search algorithm is developed and proven to yield polynomial-time optimal solutions (Propositions 1 and 2), solved via CPLEX. The model is validated using real-world Hong Kong data across 18 districts and 4 Greater Bay Area manufacturing factories, with 20 stochastic scenarios reflecting public/private housing demand forecasts, MC purchase/transport/assembly costs, and cast-in-situ costs, compared against a deterministic mean-value problem and analyzed via sensitivity analysis on budget and cost.
key_background_studies: Wang et al. 2021 - identified reputational and financial incentives among 16 factors influencing contractors' construction method choice, used deterministic subsidy modeling
Yi et al. 2021 - proposed a government-manufacturer subsidy policy via Stackelberg game, showing poorly designed subsidies could increase carbon emissions and reduce prefabrication adoption
Yi et al. 2023a - developed a subsidy scheme analyzing government-manufacturer-contractor relationships, validated with Hong Kong data, providing baseline transportation cost assumptions
Du et al. 2022 - coordinated precast component supply chain under government subsidies in decentralized/centralized scenarios
Du et al. 2023 - used agent-based modeling to compare procurement restriction, carbon credit, and subsidy policies, finding subsidies most motivating
Jiang et al. 2019 - emphasized financial subsidies as more effective than guidelines especially in early MC development stage
Gao and Tian 2020 - empirically studied impact of prefabrication policies on labor productivity, advocating more incentive schemes over standards
Shi et al. 2022 - evolutionary game model examining government-contractor policy interactions
Zhu et al. 2024 - Stackelberg game model analyzing carbon-economy equilibrium between government and contractor in China
Jiang and Qi 2022 - evaluated subsidy effects on manufacturers, contractors, and assemblers via evolutionary game theory
Bertram et al. 2019 - provided cost/productivity data showing MC costs 10% higher than cast-in-situ but potential 20% savings excluding logistics
findings: Without subsidy, only 10.2% of construction work in Hong Kong would use MC modules due to high logistics and purchase costs outweighing benefits. With an optimal subsidy price of HKD166/ton and a HKD100 million budget, MC adoption rises to 52.3%, a fivefold increase, requiring an average subsidy of HKD59.6 million. Incorporating uncertainty (stochastic model) improves the government's expected MC adoption objective by 38% compared to a deterministic mean-value approach. Sensitivity analysis shows increasing marginal budget requirements to achieve higher MC adoption rates (e.g., HKD50M for 30% adoption up to HKD172M for 70%), and that reducing MC costs decreases the needed subsidy price while increasing adoption. Geographic factors matter: contractors near GBA factories (northern/central Hong Kong) adopt MC more readily than those farther away (southern districts) due to transportation costs, and subsidies encourage diversified sourcing across multiple factories rather than reliance on the cheapest single source.

ideas.idea: High initial and logistics costs of MC relative to cast-in-situ construction remain the primary barrier to its adoption, making cost-offsetting subsidy strategies essential.
ideas.quote: high costs represent the foremost barrier to its widespread adoption (Hong et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2018; The Legislative Council 2022; Li et al. 2024).

ideas.idea: Government financial subsidies are more effective at driving MC adoption than technical guidelines or compulsory regulations, especially in early development stages.
ideas.quote: emphasizing that financial subsidies are more effective than other types of supportive strategies, especially during the initial encouraging stage of MC development.

ideas.idea: Existing subsidy optimization studies have ignored uncertainty in future construction volumes, MC/cast-in-situ costs, and supply quantities, producing suboptimal deterministic policies.
ideas.quote: Neglecting these factors can result in suboptimal subsidy plans for governments and further influence the supply chain related decisions made by contractors.

ideas.idea: The interaction between government (subsidy-setter) and contractors (method-choosers) is best modeled as a bilevel Stackelberg-type decision problem where the government anticipates contractor responses.
ideas.quote: the government, acting as the leader, makes the decision about the unit subsidy price offered to contractors for using MCMs and anticipates the reactions of contractors to its optimal decision.

ideas.idea: Cross-border transportation costs of MC modules from manufacturing hubs significantly affect contractors' willingness to adopt MC, creating geographic disparities in adoption.
ideas.quote: the cross-border transportation of MCMs incurs extremely high logistics costs, and therefore contractors in Hong Kong have little incentive to adopt this new method.

ideas.idea: Without subsidies, contractors default to minimal MC usage and rely on the cheapest single supplier, but subsidies encourage diversified sourcing and longer-term supply relationships with manufacturers.
ideas.quote: government subsidies provide diversified procurement strategies for contractors and facilitate a long-term supply-demand relationship between GBA manufacturers and the Hong Kong contractors.

ideas.idea: Larger subsidy budgets yield diminishing returns, with increasing marginal budget required to achieve each additional increment of MC adoption rate.
ideas.quote: The minimum amount of subsidy budget required to increase every 10% of the MC adoption rate progressively increases.

ideas.idea: Reductions in the underlying cost of MC construction reduce the need for government subsidy while still increasing adoption, implying subsidy policy should evolve as technology matures.
ideas.quote: As the overall costs of using MCMs decrease, the adoption rate of MC increases and the optimal unit subsidy price determined by the government decreases.

ideas.idea: Effective subsidy policy design must consider the full supply chain, including manufacturers and logistics providers, beyond just the government-contractor dyad.
ideas.quote: the MC supply chain involves more stakeholders, such as manufacturers and logistics service providers. Designing an optimal MC subsidy policy from a holistic perspective presents a significant challenge that future studies should address.

objectives: To identify and categorize the principal challenges in implementing DfMA in construction projects, and to develop a construction-oriented DfMA deployment framework with recommendations for tackling those challenges.
problem_statement: Despite DfMA's long-standing success in manufacturing, its adoption in construction remains limited due to scattered, poorly understood challenges (contractual, organizational, operational) that prior studies have not comprehensively identified or addressed through an integrated framework.
methodology: Design science research (DSR) approach combining a systematic literature review (232 initial hits, 52 articles retained, qualitative content analysis) to extract DfMA implementation challenges; two focus group discussions (10 and 14 Canadian construction industry experts) to validate and categorize challenges and develop/validate a conceptual framework; and verification of the framework through observation and stakeholder discussions on two real off-site construction case study projects (a multi-residential building in British Columbia under design-build, and a structural steel facility in Ohio under a hybrid design-build/IPD model).
key_background_studies: Wuni et al. [32] - discussed design-for-excellence challenges in industrialized construction, most cited being limited relevant knowledge and practical experience
Gao et al. [15] - categorized DfMA interpretations into philosophy, design process, and evaluation system
[24] - literature review identifying shared practices of DfMA with lean and digital fabrication (design to target value, concurrent engineering)
[25] - systematic review of 23 DfMA articles identifying three perspectives on DfMA and success factors like multi-disciplinary teams and VDC systems
[26] (2020) - reviewed DfMA development in manufacturing/construction, categorized research into implementation strategies, frameworks, and applications
[27] - systematic review on DfMA publications until 2021, identifying analogies between prefabrication and manufacturing
[28] (2022) - reviewed DfMA benefits and barriers including traditional contracting strategies and lack of early supplier involvement, and BIM integration with DfMA
[19] - defined stakeholder integration as stemming from organizational structure, contractual guidelines, and operating systems/processes, central to DSR methodology used
RIBA (2013, 2020) [11] - developed DfMA overlay to Plan of Work, used as basis for the developed framework's stages
findings: The study identified 45 DfMA implementation challenges categorized into eight groups: contractual, technological, procedural, cultural, commercial, geographical, financial, and technical/cognitive, with contractual and operational aspects being most significant. A seven-stage construction-oriented DfMA framework (based on RIBA Plan of Work 2020) was developed and verified on two case studies, showing that integrated business models, relational/collaborative project delivery methods (e.g., IPD), lean operational tools, and digital/I4.0 technologies (BIM, IoT, AI) facilitate successful DfMA implementation, whereas traditional design-bid-build delivery and fragmented contractual/organizational structures hinder it.

ideas.idea: Traditional contract forms create fragmentation among stakeholders that hinders DfMA implementation.
ideas.quote: traditional forms of contracts that create vertical, horizontal, and longitudinal fragmentations (i.e., design–bid–build)

ideas.idea: Lack of risk/reward sharing provisions in contracts is a barrier to DfMA adoption.
ideas.quote: Lack of risk/reward sharing consideration in the contract

ideas.idea: Contracts often lack clarity regarding guarantees, insurance, liabilities and indemnification relevant to prefabricated components.
ideas.quote: many challenges were associated with the contractual and operational aspects of construction projects related to issues such as risks and incentives, dispute resolution, insurance, liabilities and indemnification, and data sharing requirements

ideas.idea: Standard contracts and DfMA platforms are not well aligned with existing Canadian contract forms such as CCDC.
ideas.quote: Lack of DfMA platforms which conform with the CCDC contracts

ideas.idea: Lack of clear scope of work definitions leads to confusion and duplication of responsibilities among stakeholders.
ideas.quote: Lack of clear scope of work, confusions, and duplications

ideas.idea: Contracts fail to reference multiple manufacturers, limiting flexibility for DfMA sourcing.
ideas.quote: Lack of references to several manufacturers in the contract

ideas.idea: Absence of vertical and horizontal integration mechanisms between stakeholders in contracts impedes DfMA collaboration.
ideas.quote: Lack of vertical, and horizontal integration between stakeholders

ideas.idea: Project teams disband at project termination due to lack of longitudinal integration, causing knowledge loss relevant to repeat DfMA use.
ideas.quote: Lack of longitudinal integration, teams disband at project termination

ideas.idea: Unclear roles and responsibilities of stakeholders in contracts is a recurring DfMA challenge.
ideas.quote: Lack of clear roles and responsibilities of stakeholders

ideas.idea: Complex litigation and prolonged negotiation between stakeholders due to contractual ambiguity obstruct DfMA.
ideas.quote: Complex litigation and long negotiations between key stakeholders

ideas.idea: Contracts generally lack agility and flexibility needed to accommodate DfMA/prefabrication processes.
ideas.quote: Lack of agility and flexibility in the contract

ideas.idea: Relational, integrated project delivery methods like IPD, which use multi-party contracts and shared risk/reward, better support DfMA implementation than traditional delivery methods.
ideas.quote: integrated project delivery is a formal approach to integration through signing multi-party contracts and sharing the associated risks and rewards of the project

ideas.idea: DfMA needs to be paired with a contractual framework (such as IPD) that specifically addresses people integration, since DfMA itself focuses on product/process integration.
ideas.quote: While DfMA focuses on product/process integration, it needs to be accompanied by a contractual framework such as IPD, which focuses on people integration.

ideas.idea: In traditional delivery methods, information models remain siloed by phase, discouraging stakeholders from sharing data across project life cycle stages, obstructing DfMA.
ideas.quote: In traditional delivery methods, information models are stuck in phase-based silos, project participants are not motivated to share them beyond the phases to which they are related

ideas.idea: There is a need for further research on developing an optimal IPD contractual guideline that specifically reinforces synergy with DfMA in off-site construction, referencing standard forms like CCDC30.
ideas.quote: several standard forms of IPD contracting are available in North America (i.e., CCDC30 in Canada and AIA C-191 and ConsensusDocs 300 in the U.S.). Further study is needed on the synergic impact of IPD and construction-oriented DfMA

ideas.idea: Case study evidence shows that sub-contracting portions of a DfMA project under traditional design-bid-build delivery undermines integration and collaborative planning.
ideas.quote: in project A, with several traditionally sub-contracted scopes, the joint planning and design tasks were not feasible.

ideas.idea: A hybrid design-build/IPD contractual model with shared risk and joint decision-making fosters the collaborative environment needed for successful DfMA implementation.
ideas.quote: The IPD-type project delivery method provided incentives for stakeholders to collaborate during all phases of the project. For instance, the shared risks and rewards and joint decision-making principles fostered a collaborative project environment.

ideas.idea: Higher design costs and additional organizational investment requirements linked to specialized labor, performance evaluation, and code compliance act as commercial/contractual barriers to DfMA.
ideas.quote: Some scholars have identified “higher design costs” compared to the cost of traditional methods as a barrier to the proper implementation of construction-oriented DfMA methods

objectives: To develop an ethnography-based methodological framework that evaluates, analyzes, and improves the dynamic organizational resilience (efficiency, flexibility, robustness) of prefabricated construction projects (PCPs) from a life cycle perspective, and to validate this framework using a real EPC-contract PCP case in China.
problem_statement: PCPs are interorganizational and involve highly fragmented, interdependent stakeholder relationships that make them vulnerable to disruptions (e.g., COVID-19, supply chain breaks, communication failures). While organizational resilience is recognized as important for project success, existing research has focused mainly on risk management from a project perspective, and there is a lack of a quantitative method to evaluate organizational resilience of PCPs from an organizational/stakeholder-relationship perspective across the project life cycle.
methodology: A mixed qualitative-quantitative framework: (1) an ethnographic method (in-depth interviews, participant observation) to identify stakeholder roles and relationships (coordination, power, control) across five project life-cycle stages (planning, designing, manufacturing/storage/transportation, assembling onsite, operation); (2) a graph theory approach (based on Grossi et al. 2007; Penserini et al. 2009; Yahia et al. 2021) to quantitatively measure flexibility, robustness, and efficiency using performance criteria and metrics on the resulting directed relationship graphs. The framework was applied to a case study of a 2-year EPC-contract prefabricated building project by Poly Real Estate Group in Changsha, China, using eight interviewees, and further tested via disfunction analysis and comparative analysis of BIM, decentralized collaboration platform (blockchain, DCP), and a stakeholder league (GC-DS-M).
key_background_studies: Bhamra et al. (2011) - defined resilience as a system's ability to return to stability after disruption, adopted as the working definition
McManus et al. (2008) - proposed organizational resilience as function of situation awareness, keystone vulnerability, and adaptive capacity
Blay (2017) - updated resilience measurement to adaptive capacity, coping ability, flexibility, including legal/contractual antecedents
Li et al. (2016) - identified stakeholder-associated risk networks in prefabricated housing projects
Luo et al. (2019) - examined supply chain risks tied to stakeholders across PCP phases, informing disfunction analysis of GC/PC/M
Yahia et al. (2021) - provided the relationship typology (coordination, power, control) and graph-theory metrics used to quantify resilience
Grossi et al. (2007) and Penserini et al. (2009) - source of graph theory equations and performance criteria for measuring flexibility, robustness, efficiency
Sydow and Braun (2018) - conceptualized projects as temporary organizations with interorganizational relations relevant to resilience
Nguyen et al. (2021) - systematic review of stakeholder relationships in off-site construction, categorizing relationship patterns
Teng et al. (2017) - highlighted complexity of managing cooperation among multiple PCP stakeholders, supporting GC centrality finding
Ekanayake et al. (2021a,b) - identified supply chain capabilities critical to resilience in industrialized construction using SNA-type approaches
findings: The case PCP's organizational resilience follows a bowl-shaped pattern across the five life-cycle stages, being lowest (most fragile) at the planning stage and highest during manufacturing/storage/transportation, due to unclear project information and contract terms early on. Efficiency performed best while robustness and flexibility required improvement, suggesting a need to manage redundant resources and improve communication and workflow control. Disfunction analysis showed the general contractor (GC) plays the most central role, with its disfunction most damaging resilience, followed by the prefabrication consultant (PC) in design/assembly stages and the manufacturer (M) in manufacturing stage. Comparative analysis showed that partial relationship restructuring (a league among GC, DS, and M) had little effect on resilience, whereas systemic technology adoption—BIM and especially blockchain-based DCP—significantly improved organizational resilience by enhancing communication and, in DCP's case, also improving workflow/data control and delegation-supervision relationships.

ideas.idea: Prefabricated projects involve numerous interdependent stakeholders (owner, GC, designer, manufacturer, subcontractors, consultants) whose relationships change across project phases, increasing coordination complexity relevant to contract structuring.
ideas.quote: the presence of more participants, including but not limited to the general contractor, designers, and manufacturer, makes managing the cooperation relationships among them more difficult and complex

ideas.idea: Under an EPC contract, the general contractor takes on combined design and construction responsibility, differing from traditional contracts where the owner handles early design.
ideas.quote: in a traditional-contract PCP, general contractor is responsible for construction, and the owner/developer takes charge of early design work. Under an EPC-contract PCP, on the other hand, the general contractor is responsible for both design and construction.

ideas.idea: The general contractor is identified as the most centrally important stakeholder whose failure to communicate or perform most damages the project’s organizational resilience, implying contracts should clearly allocate and protect GC-centered communication and control relationships.
ideas.quote: the disfunction of the GC decreases this PCP’s organizational resilience to a great extent, which reflects the central position of the GC in this project.

ideas.idea: Relationships among stakeholders can be categorized into three contractually relevant types—coordination (information flow), power (task delegation/obligation), and control (task supervision, including the right to replace an underperforming party)—that map onto contractual rights and obligations.
ideas.quote: A power relationship means task delegation and responsibility; that is, task delegation from stakeholder x to y ends up in the creation of an obligation directed to y. A control relationship points to task supervision, which means that stakeholder x can legally replace y if the latter cannot complete the task as per the agreed requirements.

ideas.idea: The planning stage is the most vulnerable/fragile point of a PCP because key project information and contract documents remain unclear, suggesting early contractual clarity could improve resilience.
ideas.quote: This result shows that this PCP is fragile at planning stage, which makes sense because considerable volumes of project information and contract issues remain unclear and veiled at this stage. When crucial project information is revealed and key contract documents are formalized, the project tends to be stable.

ideas.idea: Adopting collaborative digital technologies such as BIM and blockchain-based decentralized collaboration platforms can systemically improve communication and workflow/contractual control among stakeholders, enhancing resilience more than piecemeal relationship changes (e.g., forming a sub-league of parties).
ideas.quote: BIM and DCP can significantly improve organizational resilience... Only optimizing part of the structure may not improve organizational resilience even though it improves communication between several nominated stakeholders.

ideas.idea: Blockchain-based platforms not only improve communication but also alter delegation and supervision relationships, showing that emerging technology can reshape contractual-type control relationships in prefabricated projects.
ideas.quote: DCP not only improves information communication, but also upgrades delegation and supervision relationship of stakeholders.

ideas.idea: Existing literature on PCP risk and resilience has largely a project-level lens and neglects the organizational/stakeholder-relationship perspective needed to inform contractual arrangements for resilience.
ideas.quote: There still is a lack of a quantitative method to evaluate the organizational resilience of PCPs. As interorganization projects, it is argued that more research attention should be paid to PCPs from an organizational perspective.

objectives: To develop a scoring framework that quantitatively assesses the feasibility (or infeasibility) of using the Design-Build (DB) project delivery method for bundled infrastructure projects, based on project bundling objectives weighted through expert survey data and statistical analysis.
problem_statement: Agencies bundling multiple infrastructure projects into a single contract face difficulty selecting an appropriate project delivery method (PDM), particularly deciding between DB and DBB, due to limited guidance. No prior research has developed a feasibility assessment tool specifically for DB delivery in the context of bundled (as opposed to single) projects, which differ significantly in risk profile, complexity, and execution considerations.
methodology: A four-step mixed-methods approach: (1) Delphi technique and review of 37 bundled project case studies to identify 25 project bundling objectives, followed by a 5-point Likert-scale survey distributed to 51 industry experts (validated via sample-size calculation, Cronbach's alpha=0.941, and ICC=0.926) to rate objective importance for DB feasibility; (2) Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with KMO/Bartlett tests, Kaiser criterion (5 components retained), and varimax rotation to calculate weights for each objective; (3) calculation of a score per objective (importance × weight) and use of Mann-Whitney U tests to statistically identify seven feasibility tiers with cutoff scores; (4) development of a user-friendly Excel/VBA-based scoring tool calculating a Project DB Feasibility Score (PDFS) and Industry DB Feasibility Score (IDFS) for benchmarking.
key_background_studies: FHWA (2019) - primary source on project bundling practices, PDM options, and DB benefits/challenges for bundled infrastructure projects
Gransberg (2020) - discusses challenges and complexity differences between bundled and singly delivered projects
Qiao et al. (2018, 2019a, 2019b, 2019c) - identify decision-making factors, opportunities, and benefits of project bundling
Tran and Molenaar (2013, 2015) - developed risk-based frameworks and PDM selection matrices for highway projects (DBB, DB, CM/GC)
Assaf et al. (2024) and Assaf and Assaad (2023) - prior work on bundling challenges and PDM decision-making gaps that this study extends
Khwaja et al. (2018) - developed a decision-support tool comparing DBB and DB based on user rankings
Al Khalil (2002) - developed AHP-based model for selecting among DBB, DB, and CM/GC
Zeng et al. (2014) - fuzzy simulation optimization approach for PDM selection minimizing cost and duration
Shan et al. (2023) - case study of DelDOT bundled bridge projects illustrating mutual dependence issues and DB adoption
Xiong et al. (2017) - recommended thresholds for bundle size (e.g., mileage, deck area) for optimal bundling
findings: The scoring framework identified seven feasibility tiers for DB applicability in bundled projects, with Tier 1 (highest feasibility) comprising three schedule-related objectives: (1) having specific scheduling, sequencing, staging, and phasing; (2) meeting tight milestones or deadlines; and (3) completing the overall project on schedule. This indicates DB is most feasible for bundled programs prioritizing schedule-related goals, consistent with DB's fast-track nature from concurrent design and construction. The framework allows users to calculate a project-specific feasibility score (PDFS) and compare it against an industry benchmark score (IDFS) to make an informed go/no-go decision about using DB for their bundled program.

ideas.idea: Bundled contracts differ fundamentally from single-project contracts because they group multiple projects under one contract, creating mutual dependence risks not present in single project delivery.
ideas.quote: this creates additional risks and issues related to mutual dependence between the bundled projects (FHWA 2021b), which is a nonexisting risk or issue in singly delivered projects.

ideas.idea: Under DBB delivery for bundled projects, an issue at a single project location (e.g., ROW or permitting) can delay advertisement of the entire bundled contract, whereas DB can overcome this limitation.
ideas.quote: a complication or issue in ROW acquisition at one location of the bundled projects, can delay the advertisement of the entire bundled contract if delivered under the DBB method. On the contrary, alternative project delivery methods, such as the DB approach, can be used by the project owner (or agency) for bundled projects to overcome this limitation

ideas.idea: In DB delivery, most risks—especially design-related risks—are transferred from the owner to the design-builder, reducing the owner's risk burden compared to DBB.
ideas.quote: most of the risks (especially the design-related risks as most of the construction-related risks are already allocated to the contractor) are transferred from the project owner (i.e., the agency) and allocated to the contactor (i.e., the design-builder); thus, the project owner or agency assumes less risk when utilizing the DB method compared to the DBB delivery

ideas.idea: DB allows construction to start before design completion, enabling fast-tracked project delivery through concurrency of design and construction phases.
ideas.quote: Under the DB contract, the construction phase can start before the full completion of the design, which ensures a fast-tracked completion of the project

ideas.idea: In DB projects, the owner benefits from contractor constructability feedback during design, which helps reduce change orders and delays later in execution.
ideas.quote: in DB projects, the owner can benefit from constructability feedback and analysis since the contractor provides inputs to the design, which helps in reducing change orders and delays later in the project execution phase

ideas.idea: DB provides a single point of responsibility for the owner, since one entity (the design-builder) performs both engineering and construction work.
ideas.quote: In a DB project, a single entity (known as the design-builder) performs both the engineering and construction works (FHWA 2019). As such, the owner will have a single point of responsibility, which is that with the design-builder

ideas.idea: Complex construction sequencing across multiple project locations under one bundled contract is a challenge not present in singly delivered projects, requiring the contractor to coordinate scheduling, phasing, and sequencing across all bundled sites.
ideas.quote: the contractor has to schedule, phase, sequence, and finish all the projects according to the generally aggressive schedule for the entire bundled contract

ideas.idea: Bundled projects increase third-party coordination requirements (utilities, permits, ROW, railroads) since issues at any one project location can affect delivery of the entire bundled contract.
ideas.quote: one issue with one project location could impact the delivery of the entire bundled contract

ideas.idea: DB delivery has notable disadvantages including reduced client control over design, higher costs for client-requested changes, and potential loss of cost savings realized through risk transfer to the contractor.
ideas.quote: These disadvantages include reduced client control, increased cost of client requested changes, client's reduced ability to influence the design, potential higher cost since the contractor assumes most of the risks...

ideas.idea: Existing PDM feasibility assessment tools (e.g., FHWA/Colorado DOT's PDSM) were designed for single projects and are risk-based, qualitative, and burdensome, whereas bundled projects require a different, objectives-based quantitative approach.
ideas.quote: existing frameworks are specifically for individual projects rather than for bundled projects, they are risk-based, they use qualitative evaluations based on the agency's manually entered information, they require a lot of inputs from the agency

ideas.idea: The DB method's feasibility for bundled projects is strongly tied to schedule-related objectives (scheduling/sequencing, meeting milestones, overall schedule completion), reflecting its fast-track, flexible nature.
ideas.quote: It can also be concluded that all three objectives are schedule-related objectives. Thus, this determines that the DB method is highly feasible for bundling programs that have their main goals directed toward enhancing the overall schedule.

ideas.idea: The PDM selection decision occurs at a distinct stage in the bundling process—after candidate projects are identified for bundling but before contract letting—highlighting where contractual delivery method decisions fit within the broader bundling workflow.
ideas.quote: the applicability of the proposed framework in this paper is after the project owner identifies candidate projects to bundle and before the actual letting or execution of the bundled contract.

objectives: To identify and classify the major causes/sources of construction disputes in Kuwait based on actual litigation cases, rank their severity, validate findings through expert interviews, and develop a regression model to predict disputed claim values.
problem_statement: Construction disputes are common and costly, yet most prior research relies on surveys and literature reviews rather than real litigation cases, and there is a lack of guidelines matching dispute sources to avoidance measures. The study addresses this gap by using actual court cases in Kuwait to classify dispute sources and their severity.
methodology: A sample of 177 litigation cases was randomly selected from the Kuwaiti Ministry of Justice Expert Department records (from over 1,000 cases), covering government and private traditional-delivery projects. Case data (contract value, duration, parties, dispute source, phase, offender) were statistically analyzed and classified into four groups: abnormal conditions, financial, project delay, and project management. Ten construction legal experts were interviewed using a Likert scale to validate and rank dispute source severity. A linear regression model (SPSS 27) was built using claim value as dependent variable and contract value and project duration as independent variables, run for all cases and for building-only cases.
key_background_studies: Diekmann and Nelson (1985) - linked incomplete contract documentation and change-related uncertainties to disputes
Kumaraswamy (1997) - classified disputes into root causes (unfair risk allocation, inappropriate contract types) and proximate causes (design/documentation issues)
Love et al. (2011) - classified dispute sources into management, organizational, and people systems, with organizational system tied to contract documentation ambiguities
Cakmak and Cakmak (2014) - categorized dispute causes into seven groups including contract-related ambiguities and interpretation differences
Daoud and Azzam (1999) - noted Middle East contracts are often one-sided favoring the employer, causing misunderstandings of contractual obligations
Awwad et al. (2016) - found contractual concerns are the most common disputes in the Middle East region
Elziny et al. (2016) - identified contract management and contract documentation as top dispute sources in Egypt
Mahamid (2016) - surveyed Saudi contractors finding payment delay, unrealistic contract duration, and variation orders as top dispute causes
Dmaidi et al. (2013) - identified bidding policy and payment delay as key dispute sources in Palestine
Chan and Suen (2005) - proposed recommendations to minimize contractual, cultural, and legal disputes
Mohamed et al. (2014) - proposed measures including owner clarity on needs and stakeholder understanding of contract clauses and risk sharing
Al-Humaidi (2004) and Alrasheed et al. (2023) - attempted to estimate arbitration litigation fees based on claimed values in Kuwait
findings: The most severe dispute sources ranked were payment delay, contract documents (incomplete information, conflict of interest, noncompliance, unawareness), main contractor time delay, and owner time delay. Financial disputes were most frequent (40.68%), with payment delay the single largest source (25.42%). Government projects accounted for 62.71% of cases and 94.83% of total claim value, indicating political and bidding-policy influences. Main contractor time delay accounted for 51.09% of total claim value, and project delay disputes overall accounted for 66.90% of claim value. The regression model showed moderate correlation (R2 ~0.18-0.19) between claim value and contract value/duration, with contract value being the more significant predictor. Expert interviews largely corroborated the case-based rankings, with payment delay, main contractor time delay, back-to-back payments, and owner time delay identified as the most critical dispute sources by both methods. Main contractors were seen as the principal offenders in government contracts, while owners were more often offenders in private contracts.

ideas.idea: Incomplete or ambiguous contract documentation is a major recurring source of disputes, ranking second in frequency among all case types.
ideas.quote: contractual issues could have stemmed from incomplete information, conflict of interest from both parties, noncompliance, and lack of knowledge from both contractual parties. This ranked second in the number of dispute cases.

ideas.idea: The study notes that Kuwait's standard contract documents have not been revised or modernized since their original drafting, contributing to disputes.
ideas.quote: the contracts currently being used are still those that have been designed and referred to since 1971; and as of yet, there have been no upgrades or modifications to make them legitimately acceptable and fair to both contracting parties.

ideas.idea: Payment delay is identified as the single most frequent and severe dispute source across both government and private projects, suggesting contractual payment clauses need strengthening.
ideas.quote: Ranked first as a source of dispute was delay in payments for both government and private dispute cases.

ideas.idea: The allocation of risk and responsibility between contracting parties, particularly regarding time delays, significantly affects claim values and points to weaknesses in project delivery and contractor selection processes.
ideas.quote: The delay caused by the contractor, and which formed a high percentage, seemed to have a reflection on the unreliable process of the project delivery system in Kuwait.

ideas.idea: The identity of the dispute 'offender' differs by contract type: main contractors are primarily blamed in government contracts while owners are more often blamed in private contracts, reflecting differing power dynamics in contractual relationships.
ideas.quote: main contractors were the offenders for the majority of disputes in government contracts by claim value... the scenario differed relative to private contracts, with disputes caused by owners being more significant than those caused by main contractors.

ideas.idea: Recommendations for mitigating disputes related to contract documentation include clarifying ambiguities before tendering and assigning specialized contract administration staff.
ideas.quote: Raising questions during pre-tender meetings to clear any doubts or speculations at the time of bidding and assigning specialized contract specialists.

ideas.idea: Variation orders and changes to scope are treated as a distinct financial/contractual dispute source requiring proper documentation and design review procedures.
ideas.quote: Documenting all changes, applying for proper design review, and having claims in writing.

ideas.idea: The study frames contract clauses on payment terms (including back-to-back payments and penalties) as key contractual mechanisms needing improvement to prevent disputes.
ideas.quote: Applying contract payment terms, studying the project's cash flow ahead of project assignment, wise selection of contractors, applying for bank LC payments, and applying penalties for late payments.

objectives: To evaluate procurement systems enabling early contractor involvement (ECI) in terms of how well they support off-site manufacturing (OSM), and to develop a conceptual two-stage ECI process model for New Zealand that addresses design buildability barriers to OSM adoption.
problem_statement: There is no standard model for two-stage ECI in New Zealand, and OSM adoption faces significant barriers including conservative market culture, design buildability issues, and lack of standardized contractual processes to integrate contractor knowledge into design development.
methodology: Literature review combined with three ethnographic case studies of construction projects in Dunedin, Otago, NZ (2006-2017), document analysis, and legal doctrine analysis distinguishing design buildability obligations from design code compliance. The conceptual model was presented at a conference and refined based on feedback.
key_background_studies: Jorgensen and Emmitt (2007) - ethnographic case studies identifying factors for effective lean integration in design/construction
Mosey (2011) - conditional pre-construction contract model and recommendations for early-stage contract content
Shahzad (2011) - classification of barriers to OSM adoption in NZ into seven categories
Whitehead (2009) - hybrid ECI models in Australia with partnering first stage and DB second stage
Pheng et al. (2015) - two-stage ECI approach maintaining competitive pricing via notional bill of quantities
Rahmani et al. (2013/2014) - two-stage model with non-price contractor selection and open-book target cost
Laryea and Watermeyer (2016) - case studies of two-stage ECI at Wits University with no remuneration for pre-construction involvement
Jergeas and Put (2001) - risk aversion of owners and lack of knowledge as barriers to innovation, timing of contractor involvement
Francis and Kiroff (2015) - perceptions of ECI in NZ, arguing DB is most common form
Kirkham (2007) - decision-making criteria for procurement and diminishing value of change as design develops
findings: ECI offers significant advantages for OSM projects by enabling collaborative design development, risk management, and buildability evaluation. A two-stage ECI model comprising a pre-construction contract followed by a standard-form construction contract can provide collaboration and transparency while maintaining competitive fixed pricing. Key variables requiring clear contractual definition include scope of pre-construction services, payment mechanisms for early involvement, termination grounds, allocation of design/buildability obligations (distinguishing reasonable skill and care for design from fitness-for-purpose for construction/manufactured elements), IP ownership, and milestones. The optimal timing for contractor engagement is once sufficient concept design exists to enable competitive lump sum pricing. A standardized pre-construction contract could help overcome the market culture barrier to OSM adoption by becoming familiar and tested over time.

ideas.idea: Standard-form contracts provide familiarity that can help overcome cultural resistance to OSM adoption.
ideas.quote: standard forms of contract provide familiarity and can be tried and tested over time (Ashworth, 2012)

ideas.idea: Single-stage procurement creates risk that a design will be found unbuildable or difficult to build once tendered, which ECI can mitigate.
ideas.quote: Under single-stage procurement, clients risk commissioning a design which, when tendered, is found to be unnecessarily difficult or even impossible to build. Involving the constructor in design development may reduce this risk.

ideas.idea: Most OSM barriers identified in NZ research relate fundamentally to design buildability issues that early contractor involvement could address.
ideas.quote: Most of the constraints, including difficulties for designers to incorporate OSM technology, connectivity and potential mismatch between design and manufacturing and issues with transportation and site restrictions, may be summarised as design buildability issues.

ideas.idea: A contractor's implied legal duty for construction work is fitness for purpose, a higher standard than the reasonable skill and care duty applied to designers, and this extends to manufacturers of prefabricated elements.
ideas.quote: The implied legal duty imposed for construction work is fitness for purpose. Fitness for purpose imposes a higher standard than that of reasonable skill and care. The standard is absolute guarantee of product performance imposed on manufacturers, which also falls onto contractors in the construction sector

ideas.idea: NZ standard forms reduce contractors' design liability to reasonable skill and care rather than fitness for purpose, contrary to the general default rule.
ideas.quote: published construction contracts in NZ such as the NZS 3910:2013 (clause 5.1.4)... NZIA SCC 2014 (clause 8.6.5)... and the Registered Master Builders Federation of New Zealand's SA-2009 (clause 6.1.1)... all reduce the liability for any contractor's design work to that of reasonable skill, care and diligence.

ideas.idea: Standard physical-conditions relief clauses in construction contracts likely would not cover OSM-specific buildability failures such as oversized prefabricated components or site delivery restrictions.
ideas.quote: such provisions would unlikely cover redesigns required in the event of site restrictions making delivery of pre-cast panels undeliverable, or where pre-fabricated components are designed too large for manufacturing facilities, or where designed windows do not fit prepared openings due to connectivity issues with the design.

ideas.idea: A lump sum contractor implicitly warrants they can build the design for the price offered, so buildability defects become the contractor's risk once accepted.
ideas.quote: By offering a lump sum price, a contractor warrants that (a) they can build what has been designed and (b) they can build it for the price offered. Anything that makes the work more difficult is the contractor's risk, including design defects from a buildability perspective

ideas.idea: Two-stage ECI contracts can maintain competitive lump sum pricing through fixed rates on provisional quantities later remeasured against detailed design, balancing collaboration with price certainty.
ideas.quote: The quantities can then be re-measured once the design is developed to produce a bill of quantities applying the rates of the original tender... and arrive at a lump sum construction price.

ideas.idea: The optimal timing for contractor involvement in OSM-oriented design is once concept design exists, balancing buildability input against risk of losing design creativity or client focus.
ideas.quote: it is contended that the optimum time for contractor engagement is once a sufficient conceptual design exists to enable competitive lump sum pricing for preliminaries and fixed rates against provisional quantities for direct works.

ideas.idea: There are multiple payment models for pre-construction ECI services, ranging from no charge to discounted charge contingent on project proceeding, affecting risk allocation and client cost.
ideas.quote: The contractor does not charge for their involvement... The contractor does not charge, but is reimbursed if the client does not progress the project to construction phase... The contractor charges, but offers a discount if the project proceeds to construction phase.

ideas.idea: Contractors have a legal duty to notify designers of certain design defects once appointed, linking contractual buildability responsibility to proactive risk management.
ideas.quote: Once appointed, contractors are legally required to notify the designer of certain design defects (Glover, 2006).

ideas.idea: A standardized pre-construction contract paired with existing standard-form construction contracts could reduce future disputes over design buildability risk in OSM projects, and consultants might eventually face negligence exposure for failing to recommend ECI on complex projects.
ideas.quote: To the extent that a standard model for two-stage ECI becomes recognised for reducing design buildability risk, it is conceivable that in extreme cases, consultants could potentially be held negligent for not recommending ECI processes for complex projects and exposing their client to unjustifiable design buildability risks.

objectives: To explore the contractual arrangements associated with the adoption of modern methods of construction (MMC) in the UK, examining contract form, contract type, procurement strategy, common amendments, and legislation's role, from the perspective of MMC business leaders.
problem_statement: Despite demonstrated benefits of MMC, UK adoption rates remain low (under 8%), and one understudied contributing factor is the misalignment between traditional contractual arrangements and MMC's characteristics; limited research explains how contracts are shaped or amended to suit offsite construction.
methodology: Qualitative exploratory study using open-ended questionnaires distributed to 40 senior decision-makers (CEOs, COOs, managing directors, managers) in UK MMC businesses, collected over two months. Data analyzed inductively using thematic analysis with NVivo software, generating seven themes: standard forms of contracts, bespoke forms of contracts, preferred contract form, procurement route, procurement strategy, contractual amendments, and legislation's role.
key_background_studies: Farmer (2016) - highlighted the catastrophic housing crisis driving UK government policy on construction innovation
Charlson and Dimka (2021) - identified misaligning contractual arrangements as contributing to clients' indecision on MMC and called for different payment provisions for work due vs work done
Razkenari et al. (2020) - reported design and build (D&B) as the dominant procurement route for MMC due to collaboration facilitation
Koronaki et al. (2021) - called for fundamental transformation of contracts and policymaker action to align legislation with MMC
