ideas.quote: Use of BIM to improve coordination and facilitate communication among project stakeholders

ideas.idea: Training programs for project teams and workers help address the lack of experience with PPVC design and installation, reducing reliance on conventional methods.
ideas.quote: Offering training courses for project team and workers to enhance their knowledge and skills

ideas.idea: Just-in-Time delivery of modules is recommended to mitigate site storage and layout constraints, as demonstrated in the NTU case study where modules were delivered incrementally from a temporary site.
ideas.quote: Just-in-Time delivery was proposed as it can minimize the on-site storage space and thereby improve site management

ideas.idea: Real-world case evidence shows that overseas manufacturing of modules, driven by limited local industrial capacity, significantly increases initial project costs, reinforcing survey findings on cost constraints.
ideas.quote: the vast majority of the modules required by this project had to be manufactured overseas and then imported to Singapore, which increased the project's initial cost dramatically

ideas.idea: Rigid transportation regulations requiring advance approval for oversized vehicle movement create logistical constraints that must be planned around in PPVC projects.
ideas.quote: each movement of the oversized heavy vehicle must apply for approval three working days before the intended date of travel and must follow the approved route

objectives: To develop an automatic incentive-penalty enforcement system (smart contract) for modular construction that motivates reliable performance, using discrete event simulation to establish rules, a blockchain platform to enforce them, and an IPFS-based image-sharing oracle to verify real-world progress.
problem_statement: Modular construction requires coordination among multiple participants (designers, suppliers, prefabricators, contractors), but current practices lack a mechanism to instantly track progress and enforce rewards/penalties in real time; conventional reward/penalty enforcement occurs only near project completion, making it hard to encourage schedule adherence, and there is a gap in research connecting individual participant work-plan reliability to project performance via smart contract rules.
methodology: Case study of a residential high-rise project in Singapore using prefabricated bathroom units (PBUs). Two phases: (A) data collection on PBU delivery and installation (74 PBU_LP assembly durations, 139 hoist-up durations) used to build a STROBOSCOPE discrete-event simulation model of delivery variability, crane availability, and worker assignment scenarios, validated via verification/validation methods (Naylor and Finger 1967; Law and Kelton 2014); (B) development of an Ethereum smart contract (via Remix) encoding 19 incentive/penalty scenarios derived from simulation results, plus a decentralized IPFS-based image-sharing application (using web3.js and React) serving as a blockchain oracle for real-time performance monitoring.
key_background_studies: Ahmadisheykhsarmast and Sonmez (2020) - linked cost/schedule data from Microsoft Project to Ethereum smart contract for secure payments but failed to automate progress payment due to centralized data governance

Hamledari and Fischer (2021a, 2021b) - proposed using reality capture technologies (e.g., UAVs) to fetch as-built data to trigger smart contract progress payments, but lacked concrete smart contract rules
Lee et al. (2021) - integrated digital twins and blockchain for traceable as-built information but did not develop concrete smart contract rules
Lu et al. (2021) - explored smart construction objects as blockchain oracles for supply chain collaboration
Hunhevicz et al. (2021) - investigated digital twins-based oracles for performance-based smart contracts to incentivize delivery
Tao et al. (2021) - developed integrated blockchain-IPFS method for storing design files in BIM-based collaborative design
Peters and Panayi (2015) - defined smart contracts as self-enforcing mechanisms monitoring external inputs
Bamana et al. (2019) and Goh and Goh (2019) - simulation models assessing just-in-time delivery impacts on cycle time and productivity
Liu et al. (2020) - used DES to evaluate supply chain configurations' impact on project performance
Jung et al. (2018) - showed construction and material supply should be viewed as one system
findings: The smart contract successfully automated enforcement of rewards and penalties across all 19 scenarios covering PBU delivery variability, crane availability, and worker assignment. Simulation showed PBU delivery sequence variability significantly affects project duration (40.93 to 50.79 working days) and costs; optimal performance could save 4.7% of overall project cost compared to the benchmark scenario. The developed IPFS-based image-sharing oracle enabled real-time, tamper-resistant documentation of subcontractor performance, increasing transparency and reducing disputes over payment conditions. The framework provides objective, instant feedback on subcontractor performance, an anchor for understanding how performance variations affect schedule/cost, and improved documentation for retrospective review, though it still requires human appraisal of images and functions only as an attachment to conventional contracts without full flexibility for change orders.

ideas.idea: Modular construction success depends on coordination among multiple participants and current contractual practices lack mechanisms to enforce timely, transparent rewards/penalties during the project rather than only at completion.
ideas.quote: In current construction practices, rewards for on-time performance and penalties for delayed completion are usually not enforced until a project is either completed or near completion, making it difficult to encourage adherence to the schedule and work plan during the project.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automate the enforcement of contractual incentive and penalty clauses tied to measurable performance levels, reducing reliance on subjective appraisal and administrative overhead.
ideas.quote: The benefits of using smart contract are enabling tracking on-chain or cross-chain data changes and off-chain data sources in real time and automatically executing contract clauses, resulting in savings in transaction fees and administrative costs, and expediting the transaction process.

ideas.idea: There is a research gap in connecting real-world as-built or delivery data to smart contract triggers because prior studies proposed technology integration without developing concrete contractual rules for varying performance scenarios.
ideas.quote: While both studies proposed using advanced technologies to connect the blockchain network and the real world, they did not develop concrete smart contract rules to respond based on real project performance.

ideas.idea: Delivery sequence variability of prefabricated components has a major contractual and scheduling impact, justifying penalty/incentive structures tied to supplier performance levels.
ideas.quote: The simulation results show that the arrival sequence had a significant impact on project success... The severity became more evident as the number of out-of-sequence events increased.

ideas.idea: Contractual responsibility for performance can be extended beyond the main contractor to subcontractors (crane operators, installation crews, suppliers) via automatically enforced smart contract clauses.
ideas.quote: A similar smart contract execution process can be applied to the crane and workers.

ideas.idea: Using construction site images as blockchain oracles provides tamper-proof documentation that can serve as contractual evidence for verifying performance and triggering payment, reducing disputes.
ideas.quote: Due to the uniqueness of the images, it is difficult for subcontractors to argue about what has been clearly recorded in the images.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts as currently implemented function only as an attachment to conventional contracts and lack the flexibility to handle change orders, indicating a limitation for full contractual integration.
ideas.quote: the developed smart contract functions as the attachment to the conventional contract; it lacks the flexibility to deal with multiple change order scenarios.

ideas.idea: Blockchain-based documentation improves record-keeping compared to conventional construction documentation practices, which are often poorly maintained and lost after project completion.
ideas.quote: improving the poor conventional documentation processes for construction data, wherein records are often defectively filed and simply lost after project completion.

objectives: To identify and rank liability factors involved in the process from digital design to digital fabrication, and to develop a conceptual framework for contract design that helps project stakeholders manage these liability factors across the four common project delivery models (DBB, CM, DB, IPD).
problem_statement: The adoption of digital fabrication in construction introduces new liability uncertainties in the process linking digital design to fabrication, which can increase disputes and claims; however, these liability factors and how contracts should address them have received little scholarly attention, particularly in relation to existing project delivery models.
methodology: A two-stage single case study approach: Stage 1 involved descriptive case study research (project document review and 21 semistructured interviews) on Case R within Project Q, a Taiwanese theater project, to map the digital design-to-fabrication process via a swimlane process map. Stage 2 involved a three-round Delphi survey of 14 selected project stakeholders to identify and rate 163 liability factors across eight categories (actors, resources, conditions, attributes, processes, artifacts, values, risks), from which 85 important factors were derived and organized into a conceptual contractual framework with four provisions (A-D).
key_background_studies: Bock and Linner (2015) - foundational work on digital fabrication and robot-oriented design (ROD) fostering automation in construction
Ng et al. (2021) - developed design for digital fabrication (DfDFAB) concept and studied integration between design and fabrication value chains
Hamdi and Leite (2014) - identified liability factors for conflicts in BIM implementation including model ownership and cost control
Alwash et al. (2017) - studied legal uncertainties in BIM adoption including shared information risks and negligence from professionals
Celoza et al. (2021a) - identified legal factors for information management in digital projects including risk allocation and standard of care
Celoza et al. (2021b) - found necessary contractual conditions for BIM cost success including contractual BIM requirements and BIM execution plans
Hall and Bonanomi (2021) - applied Ostrom's common pool resource governance theory to manage collaborative resources in IPD projects
Touran et al. (2011) - described financial liability and risk allocation differences across DBB, CM, and DB delivery models
Fischer et al. (2017) - described IPD's multiparty relational contracting and qualification-based selection
findings: The study identified 163 liability factors across eight categories, with management capability and BIM expertise (both resources) ranking as the most important liability factors, followed by general contractor (actor), BIM modeling coordination platform (resource), and reduce errors (value). 85 factors exceeded the importance threshold and were organized into four contractual provisions (A-D) based on mean importance and standard deviation of agreement. The study concludes that IPD requires fewer supplementary contractual considerations for digital fabrication compared to DBB, CM, and DB, though IPD may need additional considerations for BIM protocols and target-value practices to govern collaborative resources. The findings support inclusion of liability factors via supplementary agreements (e.g., PCSA, BIM protocol), supplementary clauses (e.g., prescriptive tender specifications), and supplementary practices (e.g., concurrent engineering, design-to-target value) tailored to each delivery model.

ideas.idea: Digital fabrication creates new liability uncertainties because faulty fabrication downstream may result from poorly constructed upstream digital design models, and fragmented understanding of machine constraints among project teams contributes to this risk.
ideas.quote: a faulty digital fabrication operated by a downstream contractor could be due to a poorly constructed three-dimensional (3D) design model with inadequate design information passed from upstream design teams.

ideas.idea: Understanding liability factors upfront allows contracts to allocate responsibility clearly, helping avoid negligence claims and disputes.
ideas.quote: To address the liability uncertainties and avoid disputes, a clear understanding of the liability factors in the process is needed for project stakeholders to consider when designing the contracts. This helps eliminate negligence of responsibility or tort liability.

ideas.idea: Different project delivery models (DBB, CM, DB, IPD) allocate risk, cost liability, design flexibility, and contractor involvement differently, which affects how digital fabrication liabilities should be contractually addressed.
ideas.quote: DBB usually involves two fragmented procurement steps and two solicitations... project owners usually control the assets and operations including project teams and schedules and thus they are financially liable for costs of any errors and omissions (E&O) in construction.

ideas.idea: Design-Build models restrict design flexibility partly because standard professional liability insurance may not cover design dissatisfaction, creating a contractual gap relevant to prefabrication/digital fabrication adoption.
ideas.quote: DB can lead to restricted design flexibility because the typical design professional liability insurance policy, commonly known as an E&O policy in the US, might not cover dissatisfaction of design.

ideas.idea: Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) fosters systemic innovation and adoption of digital fabrication and prefabrication through early contractor involvement, risk-and-reward sharing, and specification of innovative construction methods in multiparty agreements.
ideas.quote: The early contractor involvement and risk-and-reward sharing mechanism foster systemic innovation across disciplines and adoption of digital fabrication with cost control (Ng and Hall 2021)... innovative construction methods such as prefabrication and modular construction are usually specified in IPD contracts such as the Integrated Form of Agreement (IFOA).

ideas.idea: On-site constructability is a critical condition for digitally fabricated/prefabricated systems, since off-site fabricated components must integrate properly with on-site assembly.
ideas.quote: a system fabricated digitally off-site should be integrable with other building parts during on-site assembly.

ideas.idea: Early contractor involvement is a key contractual mechanism to manage constructability and design-for-manufacture issues in digital fabrication and prefabrication contexts.
ideas.quote: The condition of early contractor involvement is relevant to 'design for constructability,' as stated by one surveyed expert.

ideas.idea: Physical mock-ups and precise 3D BIM models function as key artifacts/contractual deliverables that reduce risk in digital fabrication and prefabrication processes, particularly for pricing and quantity takeoff under DBB.
ideas.quote: Precise 3D BIM construction model ranks first. This artifact is in particular important for DBB projects because it is usually the model that provides 'construction information and pricing,' including the 'bill of materials and quantity takeoff.'

ideas.idea: Liability factors can be incorporated into contracts through three mechanisms: supplementary agreements (e.g., preconstruction services agreements, BIM protocols), supplementary clauses (e.g., prescriptive tender specifications, selective tendering criteria), and supplementary practices (e.g., concurrent engineering, design-to-target value).
ideas.quote: Liability factors can be included in a supplementary agreement such as a preconstruction services agreement (PCSA) or a BIM protocol; Factors can be included in a supplementary clause in a standard agreement... Factors can be included as a supplementary practice, such as concurrent engineering and design-to-target value.

ideas.idea: Preconstruction services agreements (PCSA) are recommended in DBB and CM projects to enable early involvement of digital fabrication trade contractors, which is otherwise absent in these more fragmented delivery models.
ideas.quote: PCSA is recommended for a DBB or CM project to enable the early involvement of the digital fabrication trade contractor to participate in the design process.

ideas.idea: IPD requires fewer supplementary contractual provisions for digital fabrication because early contractor involvement and integrated contracting are already built into the model, though it may still need enhanced BIM protocols and governance mechanisms for shared/commons resources.
ideas.quote: the authors evaluated that, among the other three project delivery models, IPD requires fewer supplementary considerations when designing the contract for design for digital fabrication. IPD could require more considerations, in particular, in the BIM protocol and with design-to-target value practice to manage projects commons.

ideas.idea: Digital fabrication adoption requires rethinking design management to integrate process, organization, and information across the design-to-construction value chain, which existing project delivery models do not fully address.
ideas.quote: Digital fabrication entails a rethinking of management for the design process (Ng et al. 2020). It requires process, organization, and information integration between upstream design and downstream construction value chain.

objectives: To analyze particular conditions of FIDIC-based construction contracts using a machine learning-driven multifunctional (Control, Coordination, Adaptation) perspective, identifying which aspects good particular conditions focus on to mitigate risks when modifying general conditions.
problem_statement: While general conditions of FIDIC contracts have been analyzed for their multifunctional risk-mitigating properties, particular conditions—which modify general conditions to suit specific projects—can introduce additional risks by unevenly redistributing obligations, yet have not been systematically studied from a contract-functional theoretical perspective; existing studies on particular conditions are practice-oriented and narrowly focused.
methodology: Content analysis and supervised machine learning classification. Human coders classified 5,785 sentences from FIDIC 1999 Red Book, FIDIC 2017 Suite (Red, Yellow, Silver Books), and five particular conditions (based on FIDIC 1999 Silver Book) into 11 subfunctions under 3 functions (Control, Coordination, Adaptation), following Chen et al. (2018b)'s coding scheme. Four ML algorithms (NB, SVM, LR, RF) were compared; TF-IDF with SVM (linear kernel, C=10, unigram+bigram+trigram) was selected as optimal and used to code four additional particular conditions. Chi-square tests compared functional/subfunctional distributions across nine contracts (5 human-coded, 4 machine-coded) containing particular conditions versus the general conditions of the FIDIC 1999 Silver Book.
key_background_studies: Chen et al. (2018b) - first applied the three-function multifunctional perspective and content analysis coding scheme to dissect FIDIC 1999 general conditions, establishing the 11-subfunction coding scheme this study extends to particular conditions.

Mellewigt et al. (2012) and Schepker et al. (2014) - proposed and developed the multifunctional perspective identifying Control, Coordination, and Adaptation as contract functions addressing different risk types.

Lawrence (2017) - argued particular conditions can inadvertently transfer risks (e.g., of nominated subcontractors) unreasonably, motivating the need to carefully examine particular conditions for hidden risk transfers.

Lee et al. (2020b) - used rule-based NLP to measure how risk allocation is modified by employers in particular conditions, providing a related practice-oriented approach this study builds theoretical grounding upon.
Bodea and Purnus (2016) - analyzed how particular conditions affect financial arrangement/management of contractors, representing a narrow single-aspect study of particular conditions.
Lee et al. (2019) - built an NLP system to automatically extract 'poisonous clauses' from contracts to help contractors identify risks, an antecedent practice-oriented risk-detection approach.
Schwartz and Scott (2003) - theorized that stable, efficient contractual terms remain unchanged in standard/model contracts, supporting the finding that general conditions form a stable boilerplate.

Yao et al. (2019, 2021) - showed coordination provisions reduce misunderstandings and disputes and mitigate performance risks through communication, informing the discussion on Coordination amendments enhancing trust.
findings: The optimal model (TF-IDF + SVM) achieved acceptable classification accuracy (above 60%, often above 80%) for coding particular conditions. No significant difference was found in functional or subfunctional distribution between complete contracts (general + particular conditions) and the general conditions alone (chi-square tests non-significant), indicating particular conditions are coherent extensions of general conditions rather than substantial redistributions of risk. Particular conditions most heavily added Obligations and Task Descriptions clauses (Control and Coordination subfunctions), indicating an emphasis on clarifying what parties should do to mitigate risks. Interpretations subfunction (Coordination) was the most numerously adjusted (both added and deleted), reflecting clarification of contract meaning for specific project circumstances. Adaptation function was the least adjusted, with Task Changes never modified across the nine contracts, suggesting that provisions dealing with unforeseeable future contingencies remain stable in general conditions and are not substantially altered by particular conditions.

ideas.idea: Standard/model contracts (like FIDIC) are widely adopted and modified rather than rewritten from scratch for each project, but such modifications (particular conditions) can introduce unforeseen contractual pitfalls and uneven risk distribution.
ideas.quote: some particular conditions can set certain contractual and legal pitfalls to bring additional risks to the employer or contractor by deleting some fair clauses or adding some clauses to distribute risks unevenly

ideas.idea: Particular conditions, despite modifying general conditions, do not significantly alter the overall functional (risk-mitigation) distribution of a contract, suggesting they function as coherent extensions rather than fundamental redesigns.
ideas.quote: there is no significant difference in construction contract functional distributions between a mature contract (containing general and particular conditions) and its underlying model contract (general conditions).

ideas.idea: Particular conditions most often add clauses clarifying parties' obligations and task descriptions, which is a way of explicitly assigning responsibilities to avert risk before it materializes.
ideas.quote: particular conditions should concentrate more on explicitly illustrating both parties’ obligations and tasks prudently to mitigate potential risks

ideas.idea: Increases in obligation-related clauses may reflect a transfer of risk to one party for specific project circumstances (e.g., local site conditions), which contract managers must watch for since it can shift the risk allocation balance.
ideas.quote: the changes in Obligations need to be paid attention to because they may involve the transfer of risks and may influence the risk allocation balance between parties.

ideas.idea: Detailed amendments in Coordination-related clauses (clarifications, task descriptions) should not be seen as signs of distrust between parties but rather as tools that reduce misunderstanding and can strengthen the relationship, given the complexity of construction tasks.
ideas.quote: Amendments in Coordination often serve for clarification and a better understanding of the whole contract... the relationship between the two parties, instead of being damaged by detailed Coordination sentences, can be enhanced

ideas.idea: Adaptation-related provisions, which deal with future uncertainty, are the least modified because such contingencies are inherently difficult to foresee even during drafting of project-specific particular conditions, so general/mature provisions are largely retained.
ideas.quote: Adaptation is the least adjusted function due to the difficulty of foreseeing future contingencies.

ideas.idea: Task Changes provisions (e.g., variation procedures, value engineering) remain completely unmodified across all examined particular conditions, indicating that procedures for handling scope/standard/sequence changes are treated as rigorously fixed regardless of project specifics.
ideas.quote: The number of Task Changes adjusted by particular conditions is all zero, indicating that the Task Changes subfunction of construction contracts, such as value engineering and variation procedures, has been rigorously set in general conditions and their modification is tightly restricted.

ideas.idea: Interpretation clauses (defining terms and clarifying meanings) are the most heavily modified subfunction in particular conditions, reflecting the primary role of particular conditions in tailoring general definitions to specific project circumstances rather than changing risk allocation fundamentally.
ideas.quote: Interpretations take up the largest number and proportion of sentences in particular conditions, and explaining specific situations is the most important task for particular conditions to avert risks.

ideas.idea: Because model/general contract clauses tend to be efficient and stable if consistently used across many transactions, contract managers are advised to make only minor, targeted modifications rather than extensive rewrites when drafting particular conditions.
ideas.quote: it is less risky to modify some parts of the general conditions only slightly according to the project situation.

objectives: To quantify the marginal benefits of prefabrication (prefab) building systems in terms of cost, time and productivity improvements compared to traditional building systems (TBS), and to examine how these observed benefits may be affected by 'building type' as a fixed independent factor.
problem_statement: Although prefabrication is widely credited with numerous benefits over traditional construction, evidence supporting these claims has been anecdotal or fragmented, based on isolated case studies rather than statistically robust, quantified analyses across building types, particularly in the New Zealand context. This lack of empirical evidence contributes to low industry uptake of prefab technology.
methodology: A mixed method of archival research and case study analysis was used. Historical records of 66 completed prefab building projects in Auckland (commercial, houses, apartments, educational, community) were collected via purposive sampling through contacts with contractors and the Registered Master Builders Federation. Data included final contract sums, completion dates, gross floor areas and number of floors. Equivalent TBS costs and durations were derived from the Rawlinsons Construction Handbook and designer/contractor feedback. Marginal cost saving, marginal time saving, and productivity improvement (product of cost and time savings) were computed per project and averaged by building type. Single-factor ANOVA was used to test whether building type significantly affected cost, time, and productivity outcomes.
key_background_studies: Shahzad and Mbachu (Shahzad & Mbachu, cited as [1]) - argue little differentiation exists between conventional and prefab building types based on componentization/panelization thresholds, and note owner preference for bespoke design as a barrier.
Bell [3] - discusses socio-cultural stigma and misperceptions about prefab quality from post-WWII reconstruction era.
Lu [14] - notes prefab offers more reliable cost estimates and investment outlays.
Egan [26] - argues prefab offers speed, lower cost, reduced skilled labour need, and up to 30-40% productivity improvement.

Burgess et al. [27] - New Zealand case study finding prefab did not yield better economic outcomes than onsite construction, citing Kaufmann and Remick [28], Atkin and Wing [29], and Bell [3] on 30-60% time savings for residential applications.
Mbachu and Shahzad [7] - distinguish strategic productivity (cost/schedule based) from economist's input-output productivity measures.
findings: Prefab delivered average marginal cost savings of 19% (highest in community buildings at 24%), average marginal time savings of 34% (highest in house projects at 50%), and average productivity improvement of 7% (highest in house projects at 11%). ANOVA results showed building type had no significant effect on cost saving or productivity improvement outcomes, but had a significant effect on time savings. This suggests cost and productivity benefits of prefab can be generalized across building types, whereas time saving claims should be reported specific to building type. Findings partly align with international studies (e.g., Egan) but contrast with some NZ studies (e.g., Burgess et al.) that found less favorable economic outcomes for prefab.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication and conventional construction are not always clearly distinguishable, since most buildings contain some componentized or panelized elements, complicating classification for contractual and analytical purposes.
ideas.quote: there is increasingly little differentiation between the conventional building types and the "componentized" and the "panelized" prefabrication types.

ideas.idea: A quantitative threshold (over 50% of building value from prefab components) is proposed to classify a building as prefab versus conventional, which has implications for how contracts might define scope.
ideas.quote: a building is classified as a prefab building where the prefab component is more than 50% of the total building value, or vice versa.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication reduces flexibility for owners to make bespoke design changes during design and construction, unlike traditional construction which more readily accommodates change management.
ideas.quote: the prefab approach usually limits the extent of the owner's changes to the standard designs. If significant changes are made, especially at the construction phase, the outcomes for the prefab technology in terms of costs, speed and wastage will be less desirable

ideas.idea: Long lead times for ordering and supplying prefabricated components are a recognized issue that could affect project scheduling and contractual timelines.
ideas.quote: the long lead time required for ordering and supply of prefab components, and the lack of flexibility to permit bespoke designs at the design phase

ideas.idea: Logistics challenges such as expensive haulage/cranage and site interface/connection problems are inherent risks in prefab construction that traditional contracts may need to address.
ideas.quote: Other issues include the logistic challenge (especially for projects located in traffic congested areas), onsite connection or interface problems, and the reality that construction-phase changes are bound to be made due to the variability of site conditions from the initial design assumptions.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication offers better compliance with building codes and faster processing of permits/inspections, which has implications for contractual administration and approval processes.
ideas.quote: Other advantages of the modular prefabrication over and above conventional construction methods include better compliance with the Building Codes, quicker processing of the building consents/permits, and fewer building inspections

ideas.idea: The benefits of prefab (cost, time, productivity) are not uniform across all building/project types, implying that generalized contractual provisions for prefab may not suit all project contexts equally.
ideas.quote: claims about the superior benefits of prefab can only be generalised in respect of cost and productivity improvements across all building types, whereas claims about time savings should be cautiously applied to specific building types.

ideas.idea: Site condition variability during construction can necessitate design changes that undermine the presumed cost/time benefits of prefab, suggesting risk allocation for late-stage changes is a contractual concern.
ideas.quote: the reality that construction-phase changes are bound to be made due to the variability of site conditions from the initial design assumptions. In these circumstances, the conventional building method proves to be more suitable than the prefab system.

objectives: To develop, pilot and validate a robust, empirically-based decision-support tool that helps engineering construction clients, contractors, consultants and suppliers make early, informed decisions about whether to adopt modularisation/offsite construction on a project.
problem_statement: Existing decision-support tools for assessing project suitability for offsite modular construction are limited, outdated, or not tailored to the engineering construction sector, leading decisions to be based mainly on capital cost, experience or intuition rather than holistic, value-based evaluation.
methodology: Mixed-method study conducted 2014-2016 with European Construction Institute (ECI) members (clients, contractors, consultants, suppliers) using a non-random, single-stage sample. Phase 1 used an explanatory sequential mixed method: web-based questionnaire (n=18), semi-structured phone interviews (n=12), a Delphi-style plenary questionnaire (n=46) and workshop with focus groups (n=28) to identify drivers/constraints. Phase 2 used a convergent parallel mixed method: additional literature review, workshop 2 (n=12), an online questionnaire to the ECI modularisation task force (n=10), and a validation workshop 3 (n=25) in Farnborough, UK. Data were thematically analysed and used to build a multi-criteria decision analysis tool (Simple Multi-Attribute Rating Technique) implemented in Excel/VBA (the Ecimod tool).
key_background_studies: Tatum et al. (1987) - seminal work defining modularisation and modules, foundational to research into large engineering construction projects.
Gibb (1999) - established importance of early project-wide strategy to maximise offsite benefits and definitions of modularisation/offsite.
Pan et al. (2008) - identified lack of metrics for evaluating offsite benefits, decisions based on cost/experience/intuition; developed a decision-support matrix for housing build system selection.
Haas and Fagerlund (2002) - developed Modex, the earliest identifiable modularisation decision tool, and used the SMART rating technique.
Emes (1992) - argued offsite strategy must be evaluated from an 'overall project view' rather than 'element view'.
Blismas et al. (2006) - noted that offsite benefits depend on project specifics and cannot simply be listed and assumed to apply universally.
Cigolini and Castellano (2002) - discussed modularisation relevance to engineering construction sector and offshore industry influence.
Padron et al. (2007) - developed Autmod3, a planning tool for modular building systems focused on implementation stage rather than early decision-making.
Farmer (2016) and Egan (1998)/Latham (1994) reports - identified persistent inefficiencies in UK construction and advocated offsite as improvement strategy.
findings: The study identified 46 drivers and 41 constraints for modularisation adoption in engineering construction, categorised into client objectives, site characteristics, project execution/management approach, and EPC/contractor/industry status. These were used to build a three-level decision-support tool (Ecimod) assessing initial selection, applicability (likelihood of benefits) and feasibility (capacity to implement). The tool uses a SMART-based scoring system with fixed impact values and user-input Likert-scale weightings. Validation workshops showed acceptable levels of disagreement (20-22%) with the tool's factors, mostly related to project-specific nuances rather than fundamental disagreement. The tool was successfully piloted and refined into an Excel/VBA-based application, representing the first globally-applicable, empirically-based decision-support tool for early-stage modularisation decisions in engineering construction, though further validation via real-life case studies was recommended.

ideas.idea: Early decision-making in construction projects is often made without full information or stakeholder involvement, leading to poor option selection and downstream cost, delay and quality problems.
ideas.quote: early decisions concerning a project are often made without full knowledge of all options and without direct involvement of some of the relevant parties

ideas.idea: A lack of standardized metrics for evaluating offsite/modular benefits means decisions are driven by cost, experience or intuition rather than systematic value assessment.
ideas.quote: A lack of existing metrics to assess the benefits of offsite has been identified in the past, with decisions based around capital cost, experience or intuition

ideas.idea: Modularisation should be evaluated as early as possible and from a whole-project perspective rather than an element-by-element view, since a project-wide strategy is essential to realize benefits.
ideas.quote: Emes (1992) states that the offsite strategy must be evaluated from an ‘overall project view’ rather than an ‘element view’.

ideas.idea: Benefits of modularisation are not universal but depend heavily on project-specific circumstances, specifications and combinations of techniques used.
ideas.quote: benefits deriving from offsite depend on the project specifications, circumstances and combination of construction techniques employed. One cannot simply list them and be sure of their realisation in every project

ideas.idea: Modularisation shifts risk allocation between parties, for example from engineering design to engineering construction, and introduces significant transportation risk.
ideas.quote: Risk allocation shift (e.g. from engineering design to engineering construction)

ideas.idea: Early freeze of design and decisions is both a driver (certainty/predictability) and a constraint (limits ability to make late changes), highlighting a contractual tension around design finality in modular projects.
ideas.quote: H: Early freeze of design and decisions ... H: Limited late changes due to early freeze of design and decisions

ideas.idea: Increased engineering and design effort is required upfront for modularisation, including designing specifically for transportation, which affects project cost and schedule allocation between parties.
ideas.quote: H: High engineering and design effort, mainly detailed engineering, necessity to design for transportation and maturity of the information at the early stage

ideas.idea: Coordination and communication requirements increase significantly with modularisation, especially during transportation and installation phases, requiring closer supplier relationships.
ideas.quote: M: Higher coordination and communication required during transportation and installation

ideas.idea: Contractors' and industry players' propensity to recommend a modular approach may be influenced by their own economic interests rather than objective suitability, creating a potential conflict of interest in delivery method selection.
ideas.quote: H: Economic interests in advising a modular approach (e.g. design hours payment) ... H: Economic interest in advising a stick build approach

ideas.idea: Lack of contractor experience and risk evaluation capability specific to modular projects is a significant constraint to adoption, including poor management of transportation and installation risk.
ideas.quote: Lack of consolidate methods and management procedures in facing modular projects ... Lack of risk evaluation and mitigation (e.g. during transportation and installation)

ideas.idea: Transportation of modules introduces unique risks (damage, loss) and cost/logistics challenges not present in traditional stick-build construction, requiring specific contractual and planning attention.
ideas.quote: H: Transportation cost of the module ... H: High transportation risk (module damaged or lost)

objectives: To develop Shapley value–based smart contracts that quantify subcontractors' marginal contributions in modular construction and automatically assign fair rewards/penalties to motivate reliable task-level collaboration, and to deploy these payment rules in a blockchain environment for self-enforcement.
problem_statement: Construction projects, especially modular construction with multiple interdependent subcontractors, lack an objective mechanism to fairly allocate rewards and penalties and to motivate reliable bottom-up collaboration instantly; existing blockchain/smart contract and game-theory studies on incentives remain largely theoretical and unvalidated, and it is unclear how smart contracts can handle multiparty coordination, derive fair incentive-penalty rules without human judgment, and decentralize construction management at the task level.
methodology: Case study of a high-rise residential building in Singapore using modular construction (prefabricated bathroom units, PBUs) fabricated in China and installed via crane and workers. Empirical delivery/installation data (74 PBU loading platform assemblies, 139 hoisting activities) were collected and fitted to statistical distributions (PERT, gamma). A discrete-event simulation model (built in STROBOSCOPE) exhausted 27 combinations of high/middle/low reliability levels for PBU fabricator, crane, and workers to quantify marginal cost/duration impacts. Shapley value calculations were applied to the simulation outputs to determine fair reward/penalty allocations for each subcontractor. These payment rules were encoded into Ethereum smart contracts (Solidity, Remix-Ethereum IDE) and deployed on a Ganache blockchain network with MetaMask wallets and Truffle compiler, then validated through test transactions including detection of malicious/incorrect payments.
key_background_studies: Shapley (1953) – introduced the Shapley value concept used as the core fair-allocation mechanism in this study
Pishdad-Bozorgi and Srivastava (2018) – analyzed IPD contracts via game theory, showing incentivized parties stay in coalitions and minimize cost overruns, informing the incentive design rationale
Hall et al. (2018) – demonstrated IPD's inter-organizational governance model for collaborative management, referenced in relational contracting discussion
Elghaish et al. (2020) – developed a smart contract framework for IPD risk/reward sharing, cited as a case-based incentive study needing further validation

Hunhevicz et al. (2020, 2021, 2022a, 2022b) – explored blockchain governance, DAO concepts, and performance-based smart contracts with financial incentives, forming the theoretical basis for decentralized autonomous organizations and incentive mechanisms
Lu et al. (2021a) – used blockchain reputation scores with incentive mechanisms for offsite logistics and onsite assembly, referenced as related incentive work
Javanmardi et al. (2018) – linked cooperative game theory and relational contracting to construction collaboration
Assaad et al. (2020) – noted that subcontractor interactions are shaped by contractual relationships, framing the collaboration problem
Grigg (2004) – highlighted the need to pair smart contracts with legal contracts for enforceability, discussed in limitations
findings: The simulation showed that as subcontractor reliability increased, project duration and costs decreased, though marginal benefits diminished without corresponding improvements from other parties. The Shapley value method produced consistent incentive structures: penalties for low reliability, no payment for middle reliability, and rewards for high reliability, with 'pest player' effects amplifying penalties when only one party underperforms. High individual reliability was shown to be a dominant strategy, and rational players were incentivized to encourage others' high performance, enabling peer negotiation toward system-wide reliability. Investing in higher reliability produced lower total costs overall despite higher upfront investment. The smart contract successfully automated reward/penalty payments matching Shapley value calculations on a blockchain (Ganache/Ethereum), and could detect and reject malicious/incorrect payment attempts, demonstrating feasibility of decentralized, self-enforcing incentive contracts without centralized human judgment.

ideas.idea: Traditional centralized contractual and hierarchical structures create slow responses and cannot guarantee reliable subcontractor collaboration, motivating decentralized alternatives.
ideas.quote: coercive forces from hierarchical authority or contractual terms cannot guarantee reliable collaboration or reduce opportunistic behaviors (Henisz et al. 2012)

ideas.idea: Coordination provisions in contracts define responsibilities and structure collaboration to mitigate risk, but current contracts rely on centralized inspection and control layers.
ideas.quote: Coordination provisions are often included in contracts, and they define each party's responsibility and structure the means of efficient collaboration to mitigate potential risks (Salbu 1997).

ideas.idea: Relational contracting approaches such as partnering and integrated project delivery (IPD) attempt to align incentives through shared risk/reward ('pain-share, gain-share') mechanisms as alternatives to traditional contracts.
ideas.quote: Project teams jointly take responsibility for completing the projects and share the achievements or failures of the projects based on the "pain-share, gain-share" mentality (Yeung et al. 2007).

ideas.idea: IPD contracts are more effective at maintaining collaboration and minimizing cost overruns when they include financial incentives.
ideas.quote: parties that were financially incentivized would stay in the coalition and complete the project satisfactorily with a minimized cost overrun.

ideas.idea: Implementing IPD and smart contracts practically is hindered by lack of effective technology, difficulty determining fair early-phase reward sharing, and financial transparency challenges — problems this study's Shapley-value approach seeks to resolve.
ideas.quote: determining fair rewards and sharing in the early phases and achieving financial transparency can be challenging (Kahvandi et al. 2019; Rodrigues and Lindhard 2023).

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automate payment, reduce transaction costs, and improve trust/communication, offering a technological mechanism for enforcing contractual incentive terms without centralized management.
ideas.quote: Smart contracts provide a standardized formula for basic transaction-based interactions without the centralized party (Mason 2019), which can reduce transaction costs (Elghaish et al. 2020), achieve payment automation (Das et al. 2020)

ideas.idea: A major limitation of current smart contracts for construction is their inability to handle unexpected or exceptional cases, raising questions about legal enforceability and compatibility with real contracts.
ideas.quote: it is necessary to pair smart contracts and contracts so that the smart contract can be consistent with legal enforcement.

ideas.idea: Cooperative game theory, and specifically the Shapley value, provides a rigorous, quantitative basis for fairly allocating risk and reward among contracting parties based on marginal contribution, which could be embedded directly into contract payment terms.
ideas.quote: The Shapley value, introduced by Shapley (1953), is a mechanism in cooperative game theory that provides a unique and equitable distribution of additional costs when working in a coalition

ideas.idea: Embedding calculated incentive/penalty rules into smart contracts can decentralize risk allocation, removing the need for a central manager to judge and assign rewards or penalties.
ideas.quote: Establishing a fair benefit distribution system for construction projects... There is a lack of objective mechanism for construction projects to motivate reliable workflow automatically and instantly.

ideas.idea: Reward/penalty structures based on marginal contribution can create negotiation dynamics among subcontractors, incentivizing each party to encourage others' higher performance—an emergent form of peer-enforced contractual behavior.
ideas.quote: This rational player is also motivated to encourage other players' high performance to achieve high reliability to maximize overall rewards, enabling peer production.

ideas.idea: A single underperforming party in an otherwise reliable coalition ('pest player') should bear disproportionately higher penalties, reflecting how marginal-contribution-based contractual liability differs from equal-share penalty clauses.
ideas.quote: the PBU fabricator becomes the only so-called pest player in the team in Case 9, who should be blamed most for the cost overrun.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automatically detect and reject incorrect or malicious payment attempts, suggesting potential for self-enforcing compliance mechanisms in construction payment contracts.
ideas.quote: Smart contracts can automatically detect and reject malicious operations... This triggers an error window that pops up to indicate the potential failures for transactions

ideas.idea: Unresolved risk allocation issues remain for handling contractual change orders and extreme/unforeseen ('black swan') events within automated smart contract frameworks, an important gap for contract drafting involving MMC/prefabrication.
ideas.quote: there is no such pledge that it can handle an event that comes as a surprise but has a major effect, which is categorized as a black swan event

objectives: To identify and address the obstacles currently preventing further expansion of off-site prefabrication of timber and MEP services, examining the coordination and processes between builders and suppliers in Australia.
problem_statement: There are limited empirical and qualitative studies addressing the detailed processes and performance obstacles in coordinating off-site prefabrication between builders and suppliers, particularly regarding timber and MEP services, despite prior research on defects and algorithms for these components.
methodology: Qualitative field research using 40 unstructured, face-to-face interviews with approximately 2 participants from each of four builder organizations and four supplier organizations in Melbourne, Australia. Data were coded and analyzed thematically using NVivo software, with content analysis conducted separately for builders and suppliers, followed by a comparative analysis.
key_background_studies: Bildsten (2014) - identified traditional lack of collaboration and coordination between builders and suppliers in construction supply chains
Johnsson and Meiling (2009) - studied defects in completed off-site prefabricated timber modules
Tserng et al. (2011) - developed an algorithm for efficient assembly of modular MEP services on-site
Yunis et al. (2016) - revealed deficiencies between off-site prefabrication and in situ construction
Salama et al. (2017) - established a 'Modular Suitability Index' to optimize coordination of prefabricated components with in situ construction
Laurent and Leicht (2019) - defined integrated project delivery (IPD) and cross-functional team management for off-site prefabrication
Masood et al. (2021) - studied supply chain challenges for prefabricated houses from supplier perspectives in New Zealand
findings: Builders' obstacles included sustainability, quality assurance, mass production, CAD/BIM, technological support, commercial arrangements, system building, buffering in supply, schedule monitoring, productivity, flexibility, engagement, risks, and multiple supply arrangements. Suppliers' obstacles included design, financing and subcontracting, coordination, recognized practices, risks, multiple supply arrangements, and constraints. The study concludes these obstacles can be addressed through improved collaboration and coordination, as there is traditionally a lack of both between builders and suppliers. Findings align with international studies (e.g., Masood et al. 2021) on competitive pricing, international competition, and technology adoption challenges.

ideas.idea: Builders typically include contractual clauses such as bank guarantees and insurance certificates to manage cash flow and risk with prefabrication suppliers, reflecting contractual risk allocation practices relevant to prefabrication procurement.
ideas.quote: Bank guarantees allow the builders to deposit payments, which helps them obtain materials, plant and/or equipment necessary for contending with construction project-specific risks.

ideas.idea: Variation orders (VOs) by project clients significantly disrupt prefabrication suppliers' cycles of preparation, resourcing, quality control, coordination, and installation efficiency, showing a contractual risk area unique to off-site work.
ideas.quote: each variation order (VO) by the project client inevitably changed their cycle of preparation, resources invested, QC, as well as coordination, thereby jeopardizing the functions of logistics, scheduling, meeting deadlines, constructability, and installation efficiency.

ideas.idea: Large Tier 1 builders often impose onerous subcontract terms on prefabrication suppliers that rigidly require delivery regardless of circumstances, indicating an imbalance of contractual risk allocation.
ideas.quote: Tier One (1) builders mightn’t budge . . . There’s no excuse because those contracts blindly say you will deliver.

ideas.idea: Suppliers sometimes act as Nominated Subcontractors engaged directly by the project client, altering the typical contractual chain and risk allocation in prefabrication projects.
ideas.quote: The construction project client would then engage the builder, with Supplier P2 included as a Nominated Subcontractor.

ideas.idea: Lack of timely and thorough design information (shop drawings) before prefabrication starts creates downstream risks including unforeseen costs, delays, defects, and safety hazards, often requiring contentious negotiations to remediate.
ideas.quote: without the timely shop drawings with adequate information from off-site prefabrication suppliers, risks of associated unforeseen costs, delays, defects, OH&S hazards, and project client distress would ensue, which normally require remediation measures through potentially hostile negotiations.

ideas.idea: Builders sometimes deliberately engage multiple competing suppliers for the same or similar scope to mitigate the risk of late or failed delivery, showing a contractual risk-management strategy distinct from single-source subcontracting.
ideas.quote: Builder C1 has previously subcontracted duplicate precast concrete and joinery trades for the construction of two mixed-use high-rise towers, yet each of these competing companies had been assigned work packages to undertake in a separate tower.

ideas.idea: Payment terms and timing of progress claims for prefabricated work are a source of contractual friction, requiring third-party quantity surveyor approval and additional insurance measures to manage cash flow risk.
ideas.quote: Builder C2 stressed that this arrangement—for them to submit monthly progress payment claims for the project client to approve—is contentious because such approval sometimes happens when deemed acceptable by a third-party quantity surveyor (QS).

ideas.idea: Suppliers protect intellectual property in their designs by withholding detailed shop drawings until formally subcontracted, reflecting a contractual/commercial tension around design responsibility and IP in prefabrication supply chains.
ideas.quote: The latter is a measure to protect their IP, which would only be divulged if the builder proceeds to subcontract their shop drawing design and off-site timber prefabrication.

ideas.idea: Integrated Project Delivery (IPD), as a relational multiparty contract model, is identified as better suited to off-site prefabrication coordination than traditional procurement, highlighting a contractual delivery method relevant to MMC.
ideas.quote: IPD has recently been defined by Laurent and Leicht (2019) [33]... as when "multiple stakeholders from the design and construction team join a relational, multiparty contract".

ideas.idea: Some builders internalize prefabrication capability entirely (system building in-house) to bypass subcontracting risks altogether, representing an alternative to standard contractual supplier relationships.
ideas.quote: The years of investment and efforts by Builder C4 toward establishing their holistic in-house system afforded them the luxury of being able to bypass the abovementioned risks by undertaking all design, prefabrication, logistics, lifting/loading, construction, and fit-out themselves.

ideas.idea: Design freeze once agreed reduces the ability to make contract variations for prefabricated components, showing how MMC affects the variation/change process typically governed by standard contracts.
ideas.quote: Designs are frozen once agreed, reducing contract variations.

ideas.idea: Off-site prefabrication requires earlier and more comprehensive decision-making and planning discipline than traditional construction, since design errors are harder and costlier to correct once components are fabricated off-site.
ideas.quote: Design errors tend to only be identified on-site, which adversely affects planning... More difficult and time-consuming to fix any errors.

objectives: To examine the impact of postpandemic inflation on construction project budgets and costs in Canada, identify high-risk inflationary building divisions, and demonstrate how off-site construction (OSC) can be used as a strategic response to mitigate inflation-driven cost overruns.
problem_statement: Persistent, high, and volatile inflation following the COVID-19 pandemic has significantly increased construction material and labor costs in Canada, leading to cost overruns, budget deviations, and project delays; existing budgeting practices do not adequately identify which divisions of work are most sensitive to inflation or how off-site methods can offset these effects.
methodology: A four-phase mixed methodology combining a case study of a volumetric modular (off-site) construction project (an administrative complex in Northern Ontario) with statistical analysis: (1) collection of historical Building Construction Price Index (BCPI) and material price data for Montréal; (2) elemental cost analysis (ECA) of the case project using the National Master Specification breakdown; (3) assessment of inflation-induced change orders and claim amounts; (4) Spearman's correlation and sensitivity coefficient (SC) analysis to examine the relationship between inflation rates and claim amounts by division. Data were validated by the client, a design-build company, an external cost consultant, project management consultants, and financing institutions.
key_background_studies: Musarat et al. (2020, 2021) - established inflation as a critical driver of construction cost overruns and outlined economic factors affecting inflation monitoring
Alaloul et al. (2021) - discussed inflation's role in cost estimation and its links to housing and material prices
Bertram et al. (2019) - highlighted efficiency gains and cost/time savings from off-site construction (OSC)
de Laubier et al. (2019) - emphasized OSC's controlled factory environment enabling stable, skilled workforce and reduced labor dependency
Goulding and Rahimian (2019) - advocated OSC as a holistic solution to mitigate cost overruns from material waste and delays
Smith and Quale (2017) - defined OSC as prefabrication of components before site assembly
Ribeirinho et al. (2020)/McKinsey Global Institute (2017) - underscored widespread cost overruns in construction and potential of OSC/productivity improvements
Kamar et al. (2011) - defined industrialization/off-site construction terminology
findings: Inflation contributed to a 14% increase in the contract sum for the case project, primarily driven by Metals (highest inflation, 21% approved for claim) and Special Construction/prefabricated divisions. Spearman's correlation coefficient (r=0.6044) showed a strong positive relationship between inflation rate and claim amount by division. Sensitivity coefficient analysis identified Metals (SC=0.27), Special Construction (SC=0.14), and HVAC (SC=0.12) as most sensitive to inflation. These high-sensitivity divisions, comprising about 35% of project scope, were identified as suitable candidates for off-site construction, which reduces material waste, enables bulk purchasing with fixed pricing, and shortens timelines, thereby mitigating inflation-driven cost overruns. The study concludes OSC is an effective strategic and collaborative approach for managing inflation risk and improving budget resilience.

ideas.idea: Off-site/modular construction is presented as a strategic method to reduce cost overruns caused by inflation, material waste, and project delays.
ideas.quote: Off-site construction is a suitable approach for divisions identified as high-risk inflationary works. This construction method can significantly reduce material waste and minimize project delays, two factors that exacerbate cost overruns during inflationary periods.

ideas.idea: OSC centralizes production in a factory setting, improving control over material usage and quality compared to traditional site-based construction.
ideas.quote: OSC involves the prefabrication of building components in a factory setting before transporting them to the construction site for assembly (Smith and Quale 2017). By centralizing production, OSC allows for better control over material usage and quality, thereby minimizing the risk of cost overruns due to material waste and project delays (Goulding and Rahimian 2019).

ideas.idea: OSC reduces reliance on scarce and costly on-site labor by shifting work to controlled factory environments with more stable, skilled workforces.
ideas.quote: OSC addresses the critical issue of workforce shortages by reducing the dependency on on-site labor, which has become increasingly scarce and expensive... The controlled factory environment in OSC enables the use of a more stable and skilled workforce, further enhancing the efficiency and reliability of construction projects.

ideas.idea: A Stipulated Price Contract (CCDC-14 Design-Build) was used for the case project, meaning the contract price could not be increased due to inflation, requiring the design-build firm to allow for inflation risk in its bid.
ideas.quote: A Design–Build Stipulated Price Contract (CCDC-14) was applied to the project, meaning that the contract price was not to be increased due to inflation. As such, the design–build company made allowances for inflation in its bid based on the benchmark of the inflation rate from 2018 to 2019.

ideas.idea: Change orders driven by inflation in material costs were formally claimed against the contract sum, with a defined methodology approved by stakeholders for calculating claim amounts by division.
ideas.quote: The percentage of inflation served as the basis for computing the claim amount attributable to inflation for each building division. This methodology, approved by the key stakeholders, provided insights into the impact of inflation on individual components of the project.

ideas.idea: Bulk purchasing enabled by off-site/modular construction can lock in fixed pricing for volatile materials like steel, protecting projects from inflation spikes.
ideas.quote: the use of OSC enables bulk purchasing of materials, such as steel, which is highly susceptible to price fluctuations, further insulating projects from inflationary pressures. (Bulk purchasing agreements often come with fixed pricing, which protects against sudden price hikes.)

ideas.idea: Divisions most sensitive to inflation (high sensitivity coefficient), such as Metals and Special Construction (prefabricated elements), are identified as prime candidates for shifting work off-site, illustrating a contractual/procurement strategy tied to MMC adoption.
ideas.quote: The results show that the divisions most affected by inflation (i.e., those with a high SC), such as metals and special construction, are good candidates to be studied using the OSC approach.

ideas.idea: Successful use of OSC to manage inflation risk required collaborative agreement and validation among multiple stakeholders including designer-builder, project management consultant, client, and financing institutions.
ideas.quote: various stakeholders, including the design and build team, project management consultants, clients, and financial institutions, mutually agreed on the OSC approach and collaborated closely to minimize the negative impact of inflation on the total project cost.

ideas.idea: The study frames OSC/MMC adoption not just as a technical efficiency measure but as a contractual risk-mitigation tool against inflation, relevant to how contracts allocate inflation risk between parties.
ideas.quote: OSC techniques not only address immediate challenges but also serve as a proactive measure, fortifying project budgets against the compounding impacts of inflation.

objectives: To develop a constraint programming based optimization approach that generates an optimal module assembly plan for a module yard, minimizing the total waiting time of small (off-shore fabricated) modules given supply chain uncertainty, contractual delivery deadlines, and limited assembly resources (crews and bays).
problem_statement: Off-shore prefabrication for modular construction projects creates increasingly complex and uncertain supply chains, with delays commonly occurring in module fabrication and shipping. Existing improvised, experience-based scheduling responses to these disruptions are non-optimal and can increase crew idling and waiting waste. There is a need for a systematic optimization approach that integrates logistics data, contract-derived delivery deadlines, and resource constraints to reduce waiting waste on the module yard.
methodology: The study formulates a constraint programming (CP) mathematical model with an objective function minimizing total waiting time of small modules, subject to constraints derived from three data sources: (1) logistics management database (predicted arrival times of overseas-fabricated small modules), (2) construction contract documents (expected delivery/on-site demand deadlines), and (3) crew/resource availability (bays and crews). The model is solved using IBM ILOG CPLEX Optimization Studio V12.6. A case study abstracted from a real modular construction project in Alberta, Canada is used, involving 10 large modules assembled from 40 off-shore fabricated small modules, tested under two supply scenarios (baseline and delayed) to demonstrate feasibility and effectiveness.
key_background_studies: Ballard and Howell (1998) - introduced the concept of lean construction as foundation for applying lean principles to prefabrication/modularization.
Wu and Lu (2013) - documented benefits of modular approach in Northern Alberta oil sands mega-projects (cost, duration, quality, safety).
Choi and Song (2014) - described the modular construction method and off-shore fabrication practices to improve labor productivity and reduce on-site duration.
Koskela et al. (2002) - discussed the need to balance off-site fabrication, transportation, and on-site installation to minimize waste.

Tommelein et al. (2003) and Dubois and Gadde (2002) - highlighted difficulty of achieving effective supply chain management in construction compared to manufacturing, and contractor tendency toward early delivery to mitigate late-delivery risk.
Ohno (1988) - originator of waste categories (inventory, overproduction, waiting waste) underlying the lean framework used.

Liu and Lu (2016) - showed that improvised, common-sense scheduling strategies to mitigate material delay actually increase crew idling time and cause further project delay, motivating need for optimization.

Liu and Wang (2012) and Menesi et al. (2013) - demonstrated use of constraint programming for construction scheduling problems (multi-skilled crews, time-cost trade-off), supporting methodological choice.
findings: The proposed constraint programming framework successfully generates an optimal module assembly schedule (start/finish times for each large module) that minimizes total waiting time of small modules while respecting contractual delivery deadlines and crew/bay resource limits. In the case study, total waiting time was 298 days for the baseline scenario and increased to 311 days when some containers were delayed, demonstrating that supply disruptions increase idling/waiting waste and that the optimization approach can adapt to updated supply information to mitigate this increase. The framework can be rerun iteratively as new logistics data becomes available, providing decision support for both crew work planning and materials logistics planning, and can be used to estimate associated storage costs.

ideas.idea: Contract documents are used as a direct data source defining on-site demand deadlines that constrain the module assembly schedule.
ideas.quote: construction contract documents for on-site demand information

ideas.idea: The expected delivery time specified in the contract imposes a hard constraint on module assembly finish times, requiring modules to be completed with buffer time before contractual delivery.
ideas.quote: The expected delivery time for each large module is extracted from the contract document and listed in Table 3.

ideas.idea: Contractual delivery deadlines directly limit the scheduled finish time of each module, formalized as a mathematical constraint in the optimization model.
ideas.quote: the expected delivery time Tj getiver of large module j limits its finish time SF;, which equals to the summation of the scheduled start time SS; and the duration Dj... the large module j has to be finished before the expected delivery time.

ideas.idea: Off-shore prefabrication and overseas shipping introduce significant contractual and logistical risk due to uncertainties in marine environment, transport availability and regulations, which can disrupt contractually planned assembly and delivery schedules.
ideas.quote: There are lots of uncertainties over the shipping process such as variable marine environment, the availability of transportation vehicle and local road regulations... unexpected interruptions to module fabrication and shipment can easily disrupt the original plan.

ideas.idea: Reliance on subjective, experience-based scheduling decisions to cope with supply delays is shown to be contractually and operationally inefficient, reinforcing the need for systematic planning tools that also consider contract deadlines.
ideas.quote: decisions resulting from subjective experience often turn out to be less efficient and non-optimal. For example, Liu and Lu (2016) demonstrated "improvised" schedule strategies based on common sense to mitigate material delay would actually increase the crews' idling time and lead to further project delay.

ideas.idea: The contractor's tendency to deliver materials or modules as early as possible to mitigate late-delivery risk (rather than just-in-time) reflects a contractual risk-avoidance behavior that generates waste, highlighting a tension between contractual risk allocation and lean efficiency.
ideas.quote: instead of adopting a just-in-time (JIT) delivery method, the contractor tends to deliver the materials or pre-fabricated modules at the earliest time in order to mitigate the risk of late delivery.

objectives: To develop and empirically test a theoretical framework showing how collaboration forms (project delivery models) within prefabricated modular high-rise building projects should be organized to overcome current process-related barriers to modular construction.
problem_statement: While modular building methods offer significant advantages for high-rise construction, process-related barriers such as lack of team integration, poor cooperation between contractors, and communication issues persist. Prior research has examined barriers to modular construction but has not focused on which collaboration forms or project delivery models (PDMs) best fit modular high-rise projects.
methodology: A multiple holistic case study of three international high-rise modular projects (The Fizz Spartaan in Amsterdam, CitizenM Bowery in New York, and Mapleton Crescent SW18 in London), using semi-structured interviews with 10 stakeholders (at least 3 per case) at management level, supplemented by document review and project materials for data source triangulation. Data were coded in Atlas.ti using template analysis with open, axial, and selective coding; within-case analyses were compared via cross-case analysis. A 17-criteria PDM selection framework (adapted from Hosseini et al. 2015) was used to score and compare client profiles against PDM characteristics via spider charts.
key_background_studies: Blismas et al. (2005) - identified process-related barriers including need for intensive collaboration, effective communication, and client risk-aversion toward single suppliers
Hosseini et al. (2015) - developed the 17 selection criteria framework for comparing project delivery models
Jonsson and Rudberg (2014) - discussed modularity as encompassing architecture, organizations and processes
Wuni et al. (2019, 2020) - examined difficulties in achieving early design freeze and key decision-making in modular projects
Peltokorpi et al. (2018) - framed modularization as a concept explaining product architecture and organizational processes
Hough and Lawson (2019) - discussed suitability of modular buildings for cellular-type repetitive structures
De Ridder (2011) - proposed theory of Product Delivery Models with standard contracts akin to consumer transactions for modular systems
findings: The three cases used three different PDMs (Turnkey, Design-Bid-Built, and Design & Build), indicating no single PDM is a generic best fit for modular high-rise projects. In all cases, clients sought minimal execution responsibility, and modular knowledge was required early in the design phase, though implemented differently in each case. Traditional Design-Bid-Built is poorly suited to modular construction due to late contractor involvement; more integrated PDMs (Early Contractor Involvement, Design & Build, Turnkey) are more suitable because they reduce the rigid separation between design and execution. None of the cases used serial tendering or framework contracts, reflecting the construction industry's project-based rather than product-based character. The study concludes that current PDMs may not adequately meet the needs of modular concepts, and that long-term, fixed partnerships (a shift toward Product Delivery Models) would better serve modular construction; until such change occurs, the best PDM match should be selected based on a client profile assessed against 17 selection criteria.

ideas.idea: Modular construction requires early design freeze due to the need for manufacturers to begin production before the design is fully finalized on-site, making early decision-making critical.
ideas.quote: This requires making early key decisions, which is experienced as difficult. The customer or the designer is often not able to freeze the design and specification early enough within the construction project process

ideas.idea: Successful modular projects require a multidisciplinary integrated process to prevent information loss between phases and involve manufacturers early in design.
ideas.quote: There must be a multidisciplinary integrated process (Hwang et al. 2018). A process in which all parties work together in all phases of the process.

ideas.idea: Traditional Design-Bid-Built delivery models are poorly suited for modular construction because contractors are brought in too late to influence design for modular optimization.
ideas.quote: In general, the traditional DBB model is not particularly well-suited to modular construction methods. When tendering out the project the design has advanced to the point where the team may be unwilling or unable to make changes to optimize for modular construction.

ideas.idea: More integrated project delivery models (ECI, Design & Build, Turnkey) blur the separation between design and execution, better accommodating modular construction's need for early manufacturer input.
ideas.quote: This calls for more integrated PDMs such as Early Contractor Involvement, Turnkey, or Design & Build... In these PDMs, the hard separation between the design phase and the implementation is blurred, so that the design and implementation have an overlap with each other.

ideas.idea: Clients are reluctant to bear risk or responsibility for a construction method tied to a single supplier, preferring to shift responsibility to contractors/suppliers who developed the modular system.
ideas.quote: a client doesn't want to commit to a single one supplier as a risk-averse measure.

ideas.idea: Selection of an appropriate project delivery model is fundamental to project success and depends on matching client characteristics to PDM characteristics via a defined set of criteria.
ideas.quote: Zhu et al. (2020) state that selection of an appropriate PDM is the basis of success in every construction project.

ideas.idea: The absence of serial tendering or framework contracts between clients and modular suppliers reflects the construction industry's project-based paradigm, which conflicts with the product-based nature of modular systems that benefits from long-term partnerships.
ideas.quote: none of the cases uses a framework contract or serial tendering between a client and a modular supplier, whereby a declaration of intent is signed for several buildings. Up to now, contracts have always been a project-to-project approach.

ideas.idea: Modular construction represents a shift from traditional project-based collaboration to product-based development, requiring different contractual and organizational approaches than current standard PDMs provide.
ideas.quote: It can be said that modular construction is a change from project collaborations to product development.
