ideas.idea: Current standard PDMs may not adequately serve modular concepts; new Product Delivery Models with standardized contracts akin to consumer product transactions could better support modular construction.
ideas.quote: Making a strong argument for new Product Delivery Models such as described in the theory of De Ridder (2011), who argues that the modular supplier not only deliver the product but also has a standard contract that belongs to the product, including terms and delivery conditions

ideas.idea: Heavily administrative PDMs such as DBFMO and Partnership models are unsuitable for modular construction because their rigid organizational structures cannot support the fast decision-making modular projects require.
ideas.quote: heavily administrative PDMs such as DBFMO and Partnerships cannot meet the fast decision needs associated with modular construction.

ideas.idea: Assigning the manufacturer a larger, more determining role during the design phase can help overcome process-related barriers by ensuring production constraints are considered early.
ideas.quote: One way to achieve this is by assigning a larger and more determining role of the manufacturer during the design phase. Managing this process is seen as the biggest process-related barrier to modular construction.

ideas.idea: Pre-construction service agreements (e.g., Pre-Service Contract Arrangements) can help resolve technical feasibility doubts about modular methods before committing to a final contract form.
ideas.quote: Thanks to the Pre Service Contract Arrangement (PSCA), the modular contractor, together with its regular consultant partners, has been able to remove these doubts.

objectives: To explore practical project governance approaches (project organizational structure and governance mechanisms, i.e., contract and trust) that achieve inter-organizational collaboration (IOC) between stakeholders in off-site construction (OSC) projects, adopting a dynamic/adaptive systems perspective rather than treating collaboration as static.
problem_statement: Existing research treats project organizational structure and project governance mechanisms (contract, trust) separately and as substitutes, and portrays IOC as a static relationship; there is a lack of understanding of how these governance approaches combine and evolve dynamically to produce IOC in OSC projects, which are characterized by high linkage between design, production and site construction and by frequent design changes that undermine formal contracts.
methodology: A two-stage mixed-method design: Study 1 is a survey of 178 valid responses (59.3% response rate) from frontline professionals in 30 OSC projects across 15 Chinese cities, using validated Likert-scale measures for contract, trust, project organizational structure and IOC, analyzed via Mplus (CFA, reliability/validity, regression and bootstrapped mediation analysis). Study 2 is a system simulation experiment using a Belousov–Zhabotinsky (B–Z) reaction/Oregonator dissipative-structure model, implemented in MATLAB, to simulate dynamic evolution of the IOC system under scenarios dominated by contract, trust, IOC willingness, and dual contract-trust governance.
key_background_studies: Winch (no year given) and Cicmil, Williams, Thomas and Hodgson [5] - established that project organizational structure functions to allocate responsibilities/rights among stakeholders
Müller and Turner [6], Ning [16], Yan and Zhang [9] - found that formal contractual and informal relational governance mechanisms are necessary for resource exchange and information sharing
Camilo, Andreas, Geert and Jörg [25] - source of the contract and trust measurement scales used in the survey
Modig [60] - source of the project organizational structure measurement scale
Wu, Chuang and Hsu [61] - source of the IOC measurement scale
Woolthuis, Hillebrand and Nooteboom [51] - showed trust affects project team IOC, e.g., lack of trust between owners and contractors leads to poor partnerships
Zhang, Liu, Gao and Ma [13] - stated that contract provides a legal atmosphere for formal collaboration in construction projects
Gokpinar, Hopp and Iravani [39] - found project control affects collaborative relationships through compliance behaviors
Arya and Zhiang [55] - found organizational structure affects collaborative relationships through contract type and performance
Lu et al. [45] - found relationships/dependency among project team members improved via standardized business process management in organizational structure
findings: Project organizational structure, contract, and trust all directly and positively affect IOC; project organizational structure positively affects both contract and trust, which mediate its effect on IOC (supporting H1-H8). Simulation results show IOC improves with greater contract or trust, with contract governance having a more evident effect than trust; project organizational structure's impact on IOC is more significant when governance is contract- or trust-dominated than when IOC is driven mainly by willingness to collaborate. Trust moderates the relationship between organizational structure and IOC. Overall, project organizational structure and governance mechanisms (contract and trust) are complementary rather than substitutive, and their relationship is dynamic rather than static, evolving across project stages.

ideas.idea: Off-site construction requires precast components to be manufactured in factories and installed on-site, creating high linkage between design, production, and construction that heightens the need for stakeholder collaboration.
ideas.quote: OSC is an off-site construction method in which components are precast at the factory (i.e., precast stairs, precast slabs, precast walls), and then transported and installed into buildings on-site

ideas.idea: Reliance on formal contract governance alone is problematic in OSC because frequent design changes create out-of-contract tasks leading to disputes and delays.
ideas.quote: OSC projects relying solely on formal contract governance are prone to a high level of contract disputes, schedule delays, and quality issues

ideas.idea: Fragmented/traditional contracting modes (separate contracts with designers and contractors) reduce communication and collaboration across design, production and construction stages, raising costs and causing delays.
ideas.quote: The conventional contractual way reduces the communication and collaboration amongst stakeholders in design, production, and construction stages, leading to high production costs of precast components, high construction costs of OSC projects, and schedule delays

ideas.idea: Integrated delivery methods such as design-build, EPC, and IPD are increasingly favored for OSC but still face practical difficulties such as unclear task requirements and negotiation problems.
ideas.quote: The implementation of the designbuild (DB), design, procurement, and construction (EPC) has been favored by OSC project managers, but it also faces many dilemmas, such as unclear requirements for construction tasks, the phenomenon of kicking, and the difficulty of negotiation.

ideas.idea: Because construction bidding often treats projects as one-time transactions, deep trust is lacking among participants, increasing opportunistic behavior and reducing collaboration.
ideas.quote: Considering existing bidding regulations, most project participants view the project as a one-time construction task that lacks deep trust... Participants tend to undertake one-time cooperation, increasing the probability of opportunistic behavior and reducing collaborative performance with their partners

ideas.idea: Contract incompleteness in OSC necessitates informal relational governance (trust) to handle work that falls outside written contract terms.
ideas.quote: When work outside the contract appears, project participants who have not signed the contract still collaborate to complete the project tasks in terms of consultation and communication based on trust

ideas.idea: A flatter organizational structure under integrated delivery models (EPC, IPD) promotes trust and collaboration compared to traditional vertical/hierarchical structures typical of conventional contracting.
ideas.quote: Compared to the traditional vertical organizational structure, the organizational structures corresponding to EPC and IPD promote the emergence of relational governance such as trust because clear contract terms are lacking considering cross-operation amongst design, production, and on-site instalment

ideas.idea: Contract and trust governance mechanisms should be combined (dual governance) rather than used singly, as this is more effective for promoting IOC in OSC projects.
ideas.quote: A dual governance mechanism including contract and trust is more effective for promoting the OSC project IOC than a single governance mechanism such as contract and trust.

ideas.idea: Governance approaches should evolve across project stages: formal contracts establish cooperation early, while trust becomes more important as the project progresses to resolve conflicts and unforeseen issues.
ideas.quote: In the early stage, participants establish the content and form of cooperative work by signing formal contracts, which provide legal safeguards for their collaborative endeavors. As the project progresses, trust helps to mitigate conflicts and contradictions among OSC project participants.

ideas.idea: The choice of organizational structure should match the governance approach: vertical structures pair with contract-dominated governance while flat structures pair with trust-dominated governance for OSC teams.
ideas.quote: When project participants opt for a project organizational structure with a robust vertical structure, the contract governance approach holds greater significance than trust among OSC project team members. Conversely, when participants choose a flat organizational structure, the trust governance approach proves to be more effective than the contractual governance approach.

ideas.idea: Long-term relational contracting and alliances among OSC-specific stakeholders (designers, precast manufacturers, contractors) are recommended to build mutual trust and reduce transaction costs, given the close operational linkage in OSC.
ideas.quote: It suggests a long-term alliance might be built to collaborate between stakeholders related to OSC projects, such as designers, precast component manufacturers, and general contractors, through a relational contract and mutual trust.

objectives: To develop a structured decision-making approach and preliminary feasibility framework to help Australian construction industry professionals choose between in situ and precast concrete during early design stages, by identifying influential factors, key decision makers, preferred precast building types, and prioritized concrete construction systems.
problem_statement: Australia lags in adoption of prefabrication/modular construction compared with other countries, and construction decision-making is subjective, reliant on experience/intuition, and lacks documented decision-support approaches; early project decisions are often made without comprehensive understanding of options or involvement of relevant parties.
methodology: Mixed-methods study: extensive literature review and pilot study with four experienced construction professionals to develop and validate a list of 32-33 decision factors; online Likert-scale survey distributed to Australian construction professionals across seven states, yielding 107 valid responses (38% response rate); reliability analysis (item analysis, Cronbach's alpha=0.893); statistical analysis using Relative Importance Index (RII), Severity Index (SI), mean scores, factor analysis (PCA with Varimax rotation, KMO and Bartlett tests), two-sample t-tests and one-way ANOVA to compare groups (public/private sector, states, occupations) using SPSS 27.
key_background_studies: Hussein et al. (2014) - identified key decision factors for off-site construction adoption in house building, categorizing drivers and constraints.
Chen et al. (2010) - categorized decision attributes into seven economic, social, and environmental dimensions.
Sharafi et al. (2018) - classified modularization decision criteria into four major areas: quality/safety, cost/sustainability, productivity/efficiency, constructability/design.
Kamali and Hewage (2017) - reviewed sustainability indicators in modular vs conventional buildings, noting increasing emphasis on social dimension.
Abdul Nabi and El-adaway (2020) - emphasized uncertainty in escalating alternative requirements and need for comprehensive decision criteria understanding.
Hosseini et al. (2018) - argued that off-site production cost is a substantial obstacle.
Mesaros and Mandicak (2015) - highlighted production/site equipment, construction time, integration, coordination, transportation factors.
Jin et al. (2018) - discussed factors influencing modularization decisions and off-site construction complexity.
Navaratnam et al. (2022) - noted industry challenges in understanding off-site construction concept, contributing to adoption barriers.
Wuni and Shen (2022) - highlighted site conditions, project-specific requirements, and location factors in modularization adoption decisions.
findings: Schedule control (F10) is the most significant factor influencing choice between in situ and precast concrete; 12 factors rated High importance, 19 High-Medium, 1 Medium (contractor's experience/knowledge lowest). Factor analysis identified six main clusters: HSEQ management, project scheduling and control, project characteristics, quality management, value management, and logistics management, explaining over 65% of variance, with results suggesting a shift toward prioritizing environmental considerations over cost alone. No significant differences found between public/private sectors, states, or occupations for factor importance or key decision makers, though some differences emerged for preferred building types and precast adoption across states. Main contractor, structural engineer, and client are the primary decision makers; project manager and designer follow, scheduler least influential. Preferred precast building types: industrial, office, educational, parking, and hotel; least preferred: religious buildings. In situ concrete remains the most preferred construction system overall, followed by large panel systems and tilt-up production.

ideas.idea: Schedule/time control is identified as the single most important factor driving the choice between precast and in situ concrete, reflecting the criticality of avoiding delays.
ideas.quote: schedule control emerges as the most significant factor influencing the choice between in situ and precast concrete in construction projects, emphasizing the importance of adhering to project timelines.

ideas.idea: Early project decisions are frequently made without full stakeholder involvement or comprehensive understanding of construction method options, a gap this decision framework aims to address.
ideas.quote: early project decisions are frequently made without a comprehensive understanding of available options and without the direct involvement of relevant parties.

ideas.idea: Multiple stakeholders with potentially conflicting interests (clients focused on cost, contractors wary of higher upfront prefabrication costs) complicate collaborative decision-making on construction method selection.
ideas.quote: project clients often prioritize cost considerations when selecting a construction method... contractors may be reluctant to adopt prefabrication if its costs remain higher than those associated with traditional on-site construction.

ideas.idea: The main contractor, structural engineer, and client are identified as the key decision makers determining whether to use precast or in situ concrete, with schedulers having least influence—highlighting where contractual responsibility for this choice tends to sit.
ideas.quote: the main influencers in the decision-making process between in situ and precast concrete are the main contractor, structural engineer, and client, who hold considerable sway.

ideas.idea: Logistics and transportation of large precast components (crane requirements, factory-to-site transfer) are significant cost and planning considerations affecting method selection, particularly in dense urban sites.
ideas.quote: Transporting large precast components over long distances can present particular challenges.

ideas.idea: Site access and storage constraints in densely populated urban areas pose practical/logistical barriers to adopting precast/volumetric prefabrication, which must be planned for contractually and operationally.
ideas.quote: expert opinions underscore potential logistical challenges, particularly with volumetric prefabrication in densely populated urban areas, including issues with site access and on-site storage constraints.

ideas.idea: Early contractor involvement and early design freeze are recognized as important factors for successful modularization decisions, implying a need for procurement/contractual structures that enable early collaboration.
ideas.quote: Early design freeze or early contractor involvement... Modularization offers several advantages, such as early involvement in design, engineering, and construction.

ideas.idea: Regulatory and standard constraints during the design stage are prioritized more by public sector practitioners, suggesting that contract type/sector affects how compliance and regulatory risk are weighted in method selection.
ideas.quote: Public sector practitioners tend to prioritize regulatory and standard constraints during the design stage.

ideas.idea: Despite growing environmental awareness, in situ concrete remains the most preferred overall construction system among professionals, indicating persistent industry inertia against greater use of off-site/precast methods.
ideas.quote: in situ concrete remains the preferred construction method among practitioners in the industry. This underscores its continued popularity and suggests that this traditional construction method will remain significant in the foreseeable future.

ideas.idea: A documented, structured knowledge base of decision criteria is lacking in industry practice, and consolidating expert knowledge into feasibility tools is needed to support informed method selection at early design stages—relevant to how contracts might formalize such early decision processes.
ideas.quote: There appears to be a lack of documented sources of information and a need to consolidate expert knowledge into a structured resource that covers both managerial and operational aspects.

objectives: To analyze current practices of electrical construction prefabrication and identify a set of data-driven best practices and future improvement opportunities, particularly considering the dependency of prefabrication on supply chain collaboration and labor union relations.
problem_statement: While prefabrication offers proven safety, time, and cost benefits and is increasingly adopted by electrical contractors, prior research has given limited attention to electrical construction prefabrication, and no study had investigated the impact of supply chain collaboration and labor union relations on the successful implementation of electrical prefabrication.
methodology: A three-phase industry-sponsored qualitative/mixed-methods study: (1) data collection via semistructured interviews with a 12-member industry taskforce, site visits to prefabrication and vendor distribution facilities, acquisition of case studies, and an online questionnaire distributed to NECA's ~2,925 member firms (84 responses, 78 usable, response rate 2.9%, from 32 states); (2) development of best practices in three categories (operational/design requirements, vendor's role, manufacturer's role) validated against questionnaire data and taskforce feedback; (3) identification of future improvement opportunities focused on labor union relations and lean management implementation.
key_background_studies: Bogus et al. 2009 - the only prior ELECTRI-sponsored study identifying best practices of operating an electrical contractor prefabrication facility
Mullens and Kelley 2004; Nahmens and Ikuma 2012 - studies of lean manufacturing principles in modular/manufactured housing construction
Lu et al. 2011; Moghadam et al. 2012 - studies on BIM benefits in design/construction of modular buildings
Neelamkavil 2009 - adoption of automation and robotics in modular building manufacturing
Voordijk et al. 2006; Jeong et al. 2013; Said et al. 2014 - supply chain management as integral to construction prefabrication
El Asmar et al. 2013 - integrated project delivery (IPD) systems improving project outcomes by combining design and construction expertise
Kent and Becerik-Gerber 2010 - contractors' familiarity with IPD benefits but hesitancy toward full implementation
Warszawski 2003 - long-range planning framework for industrialized building fabrication capacity, used as basis for suggested prefabrication capacity roadmap
Pagh and Cooper 1998 - concept of 'postponement' from mass customization applied to standardized flexible electrical component design
MHC 2011 - McGraw Hill Construction industry report on prefabrication trends and project type applicability
findings: The study identifies best practices in three categories: (1) operational/design requirements including BIM use, systematic labeling/packaging, assemblies modularization/standardization, prefabrication scope identification, and capacity planning in phased roadmap; (2) vendor's role including strategic partnerships, early involvement in projects, material management agreements, and preassembly kitting/area-based packaging; (3) manufacturer's role including training workshops, packaging/labeling services, and customized cataloged prefabricated assemblies. IPD was found to be helpful but not essential for successful prefabrication because electrical specifications are largely performance-based and flexible. Labor union (IBEW) relations were found to create significant resistance to both onsite prefabrication and outsourcing to vendors/manufacturers, though resistance was lower for contractors with existing prefabrication facilities. Lean principle implementation was found to be underused but positively correlated with higher prefabrication volume. Two major improvement opportunities were identified: promoting win-win union-contractor relations and increasing lean implementation.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication success depends heavily on supply chain collaboration among contractors, vendors, and manufacturers, an aspect prior research neglected.
ideas.quote: there was no recorded investigation of the impact of supply chain collaborations and labor union relations on the successful implementation of electrical construction prefabrication.

ideas.idea: Labor union relations can either enable or constrain prefabrication adoption, representing a key contractual/relational risk.
ideas.quote: labor union relations and agreements can either motivate or discourage construction and general contracting companies to adopt prefabrication and industrialization approaches.

ideas.idea: BIM serves as a critical coordination and communication tool linking contractors, vendors, and manufacturers for prefabrication scope definition.
ideas.quote: BIM helps the EC to communicate the project information with the project design team and collaborate with the firm’s vendors and manufacturers.

ideas.idea: Labeling and packaging systems are essential to manage the logistical complexity created by splitting work between offsite fabrication and onsite installation.
ideas.quote: A clear, informative and consistent labeling/packaging system is therefore needed to distribute the assemblies correctly to their final rooms with the required installation instruction.

ideas.idea: Standardization and modularization of components, including flexible interconnections, reduce coordination risk between offsite and onsite work.
ideas.quote: The inherent modularization and standardization of electrical systems can be used and leveraged to increase the compatibility between prefabricated assemblies and minimize the interfacing effort between offsite and onsite workmanship.

ideas.idea: Integrated Project Delivery, while beneficial, is not a prerequisite for successful prefabrication because performance-based electrical specifications already provide flexibility.
ideas.quote: insignificant dependency was found between successful prefabrication implementation and the existence of integrate project teams... IPDs can improve the prefabrication implementation process... but they are not a hard prerequisite.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication increases rework risk since errors discovered onsite require costly return, redo, and resupply of offsite-fabricated parts.
ideas.quote: prefabrication increases the magnitude of the rework risk as the major bulk of the work is performed offsite away from the final installation onsite location. Coordination errors and changes can result in great cost implications to return, redo, and resupply the prefabricated parts.

ideas.idea: Formal vendor partnership agreements allocate responsibilities across communication, materials, delivery, payment, technology, and training, functioning as quasi-contractual arrangements supporting prefabrication.
ideas.quote: Vendor partnerships are formed as legally nonbinding agreements that clearly outline the mutual responsibilities of the two parties.

ideas.idea: Early involvement of vendors in project planning correlates strongly with successful prefabrication operations, suggesting a need for earlier contractual engagement of supply chain partners.
ideas.quote: Electrical contractors with prefabrication operations need greater vendor involvement in the early planning phases of the project... A vendor’s early involvement is critical in projects with prefabrication operations to reduce the complexity of integrating onsite and offsite work.

ideas.idea: Union resistance to prefabrication and outsourcing is a significant barrier requiring negotiated labor portability agreements and certification programs as improvement strategies.
ideas.quote: The IBEW union locals tend to resist prefabrication in the form of strict policies because of the fear that it will result in fewer work hours for their workers... These discussions can be supported by systematic scientific research of the limitations of current union policies and suggestions for improvement in the form of labor portability agreements of required certification programs for assembly fabricators.

ideas.idea: Manufacturers cataloging prefabricated assemblies as standard products (rather than customized assemblies) can help circumvent union resistance to outsourced prefabrication.
ideas.quote: transforming the item description from an assembly to a catalog product may help in complying with current electrician union constraints.

ideas.idea: Lean production principles are underutilized in electrical prefabrication but show a clear positive relationship with prefabrication volume and efficiency.
ideas.quote: Fig. 18 shows a clear relation between the increased level of lean implementation and the increased contribution of prefabrication to the firm’s total work volume.

objectives: To evaluate prefabrication levels of buildings through the assembly rate and develop Stackelberg game models to determine optimal prefabrication decisions and coordination contracts within a prefabricated construction supply chain (PCSC) under government subsidies.
problem_statement: Government subsidies intended to promote prefabricated construction have not achieved the expected prefabrication levels, and existing literature lacks analysis of how developers and general contractors make prefabrication decisions (via the assembly rate) under different subsidy schemes, and how to coordinate the resulting supply chain to avoid double marginalization and misaligned incentives.
methodology: Analytical/mathematical modeling study using Stackelberg game theory to model a two-echelon PCSC (developer as leader, general contractor as follower) under two government subsidies (unit price subsidy and incremental cost subsidy). Decentralized and centralized decision scenarios are formulated and solved analytically (first-order optimality, inverse induction), followed by numerical simulation (MATLAB) with parameter values drawn from prior literature to illustrate impacts of subsidies and to test coordination via a subsidy revenue-sharing contract and an improved transfer payment contract.
key_background_studies: Gao & Tian (2020) - compared directive vs supportive prefabrication policies in China, showing only strong incentive policies encourage adoption
Liu et al. (2020) - used evolutionary game theory to show government subsidy alone cannot sustain adoption of prefabricated construction by construction units
Li et al. (2018) - surveyed construction enterprises showing subsidy policy significantly affects willingness to accept prefabrication
Pan et al. (2007) - identified cost, complexity, and lead-time barriers to precast construction adoption in UK housebuilders
Lopez & Froese (2016) - compared cost-effectiveness of panelized vs modular prefabricated homes
Chen & Hong (2015) - established government subsidy model under asymmetric and complete information affecting developer/government benefits
Jin et al. (2020) - tripartite evolutionary game (government-contractor-consumer) suggesting tax and subsidy incentives for contractors
Wang and Liu (2020) - designed cooperative game profit incentive and collaborative pricing mechanism for PCSC stakeholders
Dou et al. (2021) - found negative investment behavior of developers is main obstacle to prefabrication promotion in Changchun
findings: The optimal assembly rate under centralized decision-making exceeds that under decentralized decision-making, indicating efficiency loss due to double marginalization. A subsidy revenue-sharing contract with a 100% sharing coefficient can coordinate the PCSC and achieve Pareto improvement in assembly rate, but it disproportionately benefits the general contractor while reducing developer profit. An improved transfer payment contract, combined with the revenue-sharing contract, can achieve overall Pareto optimality by allowing the general contractor to bear the fixed cost to reach the assembly rate benchmark while the developer bears subsidy investment beyond that benchmark, ensuring both parties benefit when the transfer payment falls within a specific 'Pareto zone'.

ideas.idea: Government subsidies are transferred from developers to general contractors through revenue-sharing contracts to incentivize higher assembly rates, reflecting a contractual mechanism for risk/benefit allocation.
ideas.quote: Developers could transfer the subsidies to incentivize the general contractors to improve prefabrication levels via a revenue-sharing contract.

ideas.idea: Developers hold dominant bargaining power in the supply chain relationship, controlling decision authority while general contractors are subordinate, creating asymmetric contractual power that affects prefabrication outcomes.
ideas.quote: Within the decision system, developers are in the dominant position and general contractors are subordinate.

ideas.idea: General contractors bear greater economic and quality risk in delivering prefabricated construction compared to developers, reflecting a specific allocation of project risk in contracts.
ideas.quote: The general contractors respond to the needs of the emerging industrialized construction market and assume more responsibility and risk in terms of economic and engineering quality.

ideas.idea: A simple revenue-sharing contract alone is insufficient to fully coordinate the supply chain fairly, since it can create profit losses for the developer despite gains for the contractor, showing limits of basic incentive contracts.
ideas.quote: Although a higher value of the subsidy revenue-sharing coefficient increases the assembly rate of prefabricated construction, it affects the profit of the developers.

ideas.idea: An improved contract combining transfer payments with revenue-sharing can more fairly allocate risks and costs between developer and contractor, with the contractor covering baseline costs and the developer covering incremental subsidy-related investment.
ideas.quote: the general contractor will bear the fixed cost required to achieve the assembly rate benchmark (via the transfer payment). In contrast, the developer bears the subsidies investment required to enhance the prefabrication level beyond the assembly rate benchmark.

ideas.idea: Contractual coordination mechanisms (transfer payment contracts) are necessary to ensure that all supply chain participants benefit, illustrating the importance of designing appropriate risk/reward sharing clauses in prefabrication contracts.
ideas.quote: Only by involving the transfer payment term can the system surplus be fairly allocated so as to reach a win–win situation.

ideas.idea: Setting an appropriate assembly rate benchmark in government policy or contracts is critical, as overly high benchmarks discourage enterprises from adopting prefabrication due to increased cost burden.
ideas.quote: when the assembly rate benchmark stipulated by the government is higher than 0.7, the enterprises are unwilling to construct prefabricated buildings, which is not conducive to promoting the development of prefabricated buildings.

ideas.idea: Cooperative, centralized decision-making between developer and contractor yields higher overall profit and higher assembly rates than independent (decentralized) contractual decision-making, underscoring the value of collaborative contractual arrangements.
ideas.quote: PCSC profit under the decentralized decision is lower than under the centralized decision, which is consistent with Proposition 3. This phenomenon indicates that there exists efficiency loss in the two-echelon supply chain.

objectives: To identify and validate key principles for implementing strategic organizational changes in design and construction companies (especially SMEs) seeking to successfully adopt offsite construction (OSC) in multifamily housing projects in the USA.
problem_statement: While OSC offers benefits for addressing the US multifamily housing affordability and labor shortage crisis, adoption remains incipient due to risks, insufficient standards/policies, and lack of professional experience; prior research has identified factors affecting OSC adoption but few studies propose concrete, expert-validated strategies/principles for companies (especially SMEs) to implement OSC successfully, particularly in the US multifamily market.
methodology: Multi-phase mixed-methods research: (1) a Delphi survey with 14 experts across three panels (contractors, designers, consultants/manufacturers/academics) to validate and rank factors and changes needed for OSC adoption; (2) an online survey with 25 professionals to obtain a reliable ranking of the most significant changes; (3) deductive qualitative analysis using the WEF (2016) framework to draft principles, followed by semi-structured validation interviews with 12 AEC professionals (6 design, 6 construction) to refine and finalize eight principles.
key_background_studies: Gibb (2001) - proposed the widely accepted categorization of OSC by level of offsite work (component, non-volumetric, volumetric, modular)
Gusmao Brissi et al. (2021a) - prior systematic literature review identifying 27 factors affecting OSC adoption in US multifamily projects across social, environmental, economic dimensions
World Economic Forum WEF (2016) - framework of 30 practices to transform AEC industry at company, sector, government levels, used as basis for organizing principles
Bertram et al. (2019) - identified demand for real estate and labor shortage as key US drivers for OSC adoption and associated risks
Sexton and Barrett (2003) - discussed SMEs' lack of organizational slack limiting their ability to test strategies and commit to long-term investments
Dodge Data and Analytics (2020) - survey showing multifamily buildings have high potential for modular construction adoption among A/E and GC/CM professionals
Colton and Ahluwalia (2019) - survey of home builders showing limited current use of wall panels and modular construction in multifamily housing
Akintoye and Main (2007) - discussed partnership benefits for SMEs including risk sharing and access to innovation
Lessing and Brege (2015, 2018) - discussed industrialized housing business models, logistics, and vertically integrated companies
Bock and Linner (2010) - described industrialized construction roles analogous to automobile manufacturing, assemblers managing supply chains
findings: The study identified eight final principles for OSC adoption in multifamily design/construction firms: (1) develop product-oriented business models, (2) promote leadership and mindset engagement with OSC, (3) engage in partnerships and innovative contractual models, (4) shift toward digital transformation and automation, (5) develop training and knowledge management strategies, (6) adopt lean construction practices, (7) improve monitoring and quality control, and (8) integrate logistics and supply chain management with AEC processes. Sustainability was not validated as a driving principle but rather seen as a consequence of OSC adoption. Early stakeholder involvement and new permitting/inspection models were considered important but outside direct control of design/construction firms and thus excluded from the final principle set. The research also noted potential emergence of new industry roles (assemblers, vertically integrated firms) as OSC adoption deepens.

ideas.idea: Adopting more innovative contracting models that share responsibilities, risks, profits, and expenses is identified as a significant change needed for successful OSC adoption.
ideas.quote: Adopt more innovative contracting models sharing responsibilities, risks, profits, and expenses

ideas.idea: Design and construction professionals often lack authority over contract/delivery method decisions, which are typically controlled by owners or developers, creating friction with OSC implementation.
ideas.quote: designers and construction professionals often do not have the power to decide on the type of contract that defines the delivery method

ideas.idea: Collaborative, relational contract models such as Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) support early stakeholder engagement, reduce adversarial relationships, and encourage multidisciplinary collaboration important for OSC success.
ideas.quote: Adopt collaborative delivery methods (such as IPD) that support early engagement between parties, reduce adverse relationships and encourage true inter-and multidisciplinary collaboration and transparency throughout the process.

ideas.idea: Partnerships between contractors, subcontractors, and manufacturers are primarily established to share risk and facilitate access to innovation, which is especially critical for SMEs with limited resources.
ideas.quote: Partnerships are primarily established to share risk, meet customer needs, facilitate access to innovation and technology and promote more efficient use of resources, which are essential for SMEs (Akintoye and Main, 2007).

ideas.idea: Vertically integrated business models—combining design, manufacturing, and construction under a single company—are emerging as OSC adoption deepens, changing traditional contractual/organizational boundaries.
ideas.quote: the advance of industrialized construction, which begins with the growing use of OSC, may lead to the emergence of more vertically integrated companies, that is, the processes of design, engineering, manufacturing of construction parts, as well as the control of logistics and assembly on-site will all be performed by a single company

ideas.idea: Early involvement of all project stakeholders (owners, developers, designers, manufacturers) is broadly recognized as critical, but is often outside the direct control of design/construction firms, implicating contractual arrangements and project delivery structures.
ideas.quote: All interviewees (n 5 12) clearly defended this principle, but they also commented that in many cases this is not an attribution of design or construction companies, but of the owners or developers, who may not have a clear perception of the benefits that this strategy can bring to the project as a whole.

ideas.idea: OSC adoption requires design and construction teams to collaborate closely on defining module dimensions, lifting points, and other interface issues, extending traditional contractual scopes of coordination.
ideas.quote: design and construction teams collaborating to define the dimensions of modules and components, temporary reinforcements, lifting points, etc., for these issues impact the transport and handling of the components

ideas.idea: Insufficient laws, policies, and standards for OSC, along with lack of professional experience, are structural barriers that affect risk allocation and contractual certainty in OSC projects.
ideas.quote: insufficient laws, policies and standards for OSC and lack of experience of the professionals involved (Bertram et al., 2019; Gibb and Isack, 2003; Wu et al., 2019).

ideas.idea: Risk related to module interfaces involving multiple stakeholders is a distinct contractual/coordination challenge in OSC projects requiring stricter quality control across design, production, transportation, and site phases.
ideas.quote: it is also important to carefully consider potential risks related to module interfaces, which may involve multiple stakeholders (Da Rocha and Koskela, 2020).

objectives: To investigate how BIM contract practices impact stakeholder BIM implementation on AEC projects, specifically to (1) evaluate the association between BIM implementation and contractual BIM requirements, and (2) examine stakeholder perceptions of the impact of contract requirements on BIM implementation at the project level.
problem_statement: While numerous BIM contract documents and academic recommendations exist, there is little understanding of how these contracts are actually implemented on projects and how they impact BIM use by key stakeholders, nor of stakeholder perceptions and experiences with BIM-related contract requirements at the project level.
methodology: Mixed-methods approach: (1) A survey distributed via email and LinkedIn (available March-May 2020 and Sept-Oct 2021) collected BIM-related project data (36 usable responses) on stakeholder BIM use, BIM contractual requirements, and BEP use/requirement; analyzed using Fisher's exact test for associations between categorical variables. (2) Semistructured interviews with 23 AEC professionals (21 interviews, average 20.5 years experience, various organization types: owner, contractor, designer/engineer, legal firm/claims consultant) conducted virtually Aug 2021-April 2022, analyzed using grounded theory qualitative coding (open, axial, selective coding) in NVivo, with peer review validation.
key_background_studies: Arshad et al. 2019 - developed a contractual framework for BIM-enabled design/bid/build projects, recommending model ownership by author, licensing for use, and defining authorized uses/deliverables
Ashcraft 2008 - discussed responsible control, admissibility of digital data, copyright, standard contracts reducing transaction costs, and evolving standard of care with BIM adoption
ConsensusDocs 2016/2015 - developed the 301-BIM addendum template allowing parties to choose precedence between model and 2D drawings, and designation of a BIM manager

AIA E203-2013 - defined authorized uses of the model and stated that without defined authorized uses, reliance on the model is at the receiving party's sole risk; also defined Level of Development (LOD)
Messner et al. 2019 (CIC BIM Project Execution Planning Guide) - provided structure/template for BIM execution plans, process maps, and information exchanges
Celoza et al. 2021b - evaluated relationship between BIM contract requirements and project performance
Assaad et al. 2020 - recommended contractually requiring BEPs to mitigate BIM risks and limiting use of shared data to project parties' scopes of work
Chong et al. 2017 - recommended that the party providing data is responsible and liable for it, related to standard of care changes
Hensel Phelps Construction Co. v. United States - legal case illustrating conflicts between specifications and drawings and order of precedence disputes
findings: Fisher's exact test revealed significant associations between each stakeholder's (A/E, contractor, subcontractor) BIM use and their respective BIM contractual requirement, and a significant association between BEP implementation and its contractual requirement. Qualitative interview analysis identified four main categories of contract requirements impacting BIM implementation (deliverables, BIM-related meetings, workflow documents, software requirements) and four main categories of BIM-related contractual challenges (model-related challenges, reliance on 2D contract documents, lack of BIM standard practice, and BIM regulatory challenges). Despite significant associations, less collaborative delivery methods (DBB, CMAR) dominated the sample (53%), potentially limiting full BIM benefits due to lack of direct contractual relationships between A/E and contractor. The study concludes there is still much room for improvement in BIM implementation at the project level and underscores the importance of moving toward BIM-based project delivery prioritizing BIM over traditional 2D documents.

ideas.idea: Contracts often designate a hierarchy of precedence between the 2D drawings and the BIM model to resolve conflicts, with parties choosing which document governs.
ideas.quote: The two options are (1) the model takes precedence over 2D drawings or (2) the 2D drawings take precedence over the model when discrepancies arise.

ideas.idea: Regulatory limitations on permitting authorities accepting only 2D drawings drive continued reliance on 2D documents even on BIM-enabled projects.
ideas.quote: A driver of developing 2D drawings during project delivery is the limitation on what types of documents can be submitted to permitting agencies or authorities having jurisdiction (AHJs) (Sacks et al. 2018).

ideas.idea: Absent explicit contractual definition of authorized uses of the model, reliance on the model by other parties is entirely at their own risk, limiting the model's contractual reliability.
ideas.quote: any use of, transmission of, or reliance on the Model is at the receiving Party’s sole risk

ideas.idea: Clear rules on model ownership and licensing are recommended, with the model author retaining ownership while other parties needing a license to use it, and use limited to relevant scopes of work.
ideas.quote: It is recommended that whoever authors a model should retain ownership of it (Arshad et al. 2019). However, this also requires that whoever must use and rely upon that model throughout the project needs a license for use.

ideas.idea: Standard contracts and defined BIM execution plans support successful collaborative processes such as kickoff meetings, coordination sessions, and clash detection, which need to be defined for project participants.
ideas.quote: These meetings, stakeholders required, and purpose are typically documented in the BIM execution plan (Messner et al. 2019; Arshad et al. 2019).

ideas.idea: Designating a BIM manager or information manager role helps centralize responsibility for coordinating BIM processes among stakeholders.
ideas.quote: ConsensusDocs 301 includes Section 3.1, which allows for the owner to designate a BIM manager (e.g., constructor, design professional, other), which is responsible for the overall BIM process (ConsensusDocs 2016).

ideas.idea: Contractually requiring a common software platform is recommended to reduce interoperability challenges and data loss, though this can conflict with differing stakeholder practices, including prefabrication/CNC equipment compatibility.
ideas.quote: [T]he majority of our contractors aren’t utilizing Revit. [...] even for the more advanced projects, their CNC [Computer Numerical Control] equipment, their [...] prefabrication [machines don’t] utilize Revit.

ideas.idea: BIM is frequently not treated as a formal contract document, undermining reliance on it in favor of traditional 2D drawings even when models are actively used in design and construction.
ideas.quote: BIM is not considered a contract document, so it cannot be relied upon in the same way 2D drawings are relied upon.

ideas.idea: Repeated translation of information between 2D and 3D formats throughout a project's lifecycle introduces inefficiencies and data loss risks, undermining full realization of BIM/model-based benefits.
ideas.quote: The exchange of project information from 2D to 3D and back to 2D can result in a number of interoperability problems, including data loss or corruption, which can result in conflicts between project stakeholders.

ideas.idea: Lack of direct contractual relationships between designers and contractors in traditional delivery methods (e.g., design-bid-build, CMAR) can create information exchange gaps and liability shortfalls when models lack sufficient construction detail.
ideas.quote: The lack of a direct contractual relationship between the A/E and the contractor could lead to potential information exchange challenges.

ideas.idea: Inconsistent levels of development (LOD) among stakeholders' models create coordination and liability challenges, suggesting the need for contractually defined LOD standards per element and party.
ideas.quote: Project teams can develop a model element author table, which assigns LOD, associated project milestone or phase, and responsible party (AIA 2013b).

ideas.idea: Assigning liability for model elements is contractually ambiguous when multiple parties can access and edit a shared/federated model.
ideas.quote: Chong et al. (2017) recommends that the party that provided the data is responsible and liable for it.

ideas.idea: The absence of industrywide standardized BIM practices leads to bespoke, organization-specific BIM processes that can conflict across project stakeholders, increasing rework and coordination challenges.
ideas.quote: Each organization develops and adopts its own BIM processes to achieve their specific objectives, which may or may not support other project organizations’ processes or objectives.

ideas.idea: Regulatory and professional liability concerns (stamping/sealing) currently restrict acceptance of BIM models as authoritative documents, reinforcing continued reliance on 2D drawings for legal compliance.
ideas.quote: I don’t know if I’d be comfortable stamping or certifying a model, because it seems like it would just be vulnerable to changes, and then what?

objectives: To investigate the impact of Prefabricated Bathroom Unit (PBU) delivery reliability on on-site installation productivity, and to establish a situation-awareness-based Smart Contract using Blockchain technology to motivate reliable prefabricated construction material delivery.
problem_statement: Construction site managers face challenges tracking progress, managing interruptions, and motivating reliable work plan commitment of specialty trades, especially under supply chain uncertainty caused by COVID-19 disruptions in modular construction. Current practice enforces penalties for delay only near project completion, and there is a lack of research using simulation to generate incentive/penalty strategies or fully automate progress-based payments via Smart Contracts.
methodology: Case study of a high-rise residential project in Singapore using PBU modules. Data on PBU loading platform assembly and hoisting durations were collected (74 and 139 activities respectively) and fitted to statistical distributions. A STROBOSCOPE discrete-event simulation model was built to quantify the impact of PBU delivery variability (classified into five levels via k-means clustering) on project schedule and cost across 100 runs per scenario. Based on simulation results, Smart Contract rules were developed and implemented on the Ethereum Blockchain platform (via Remix-Ethereum) to automatically assign incentives or penalties based on detected delivery variability levels.
key_background_studies: Bamana et al. [4] and Goh and Goh [6] - simulation models assessing impacts of just-in-time deliveries, showing reduced cycle time and improved labor productivity
Liu et al. [13] - discrete event simulation evaluating supply chain configurations, showing multi-supplier setups boost manufacturing efficiency
Jung et al. [10] - showed construction and material supply should be viewed as one system, with on-site storage useful under uncertain supplier capability
Mason [15,14] - introduced Smart Contract as a logical extension of BIM, argued full automation requires broader social/legal change
Li et al. [12] - reviewed Blockchain applications in AEC industry with case studies demonstrating feasibility
Wang et al. [16] - developed a Blockchain platform to detect if modular component delivery matches planning in a precast project
Elghaish et al. [5] - proposed using real-time BIM 4D/5D data to assign incentives and penalties to crews
Ahmadisheykhsarmast and Sonmez [3] - built construction contract platform linking Microsoft Project data to Ethereum Smart Contract for secure payments
Hamledari and Fischer [8] - proposed using reality capture technologies to trigger Smart Contract progress payments, at conceptual level only
findings: Simulation results showed that PBU delivery variability strongly affects project duration and cost: low variability (0-6) scenario finished in 40.9 days with lower total cost, while high variability (22-24) scenario extended to 50.8 days with higher costs. Using scenario 2 (variability 6-12) as benchmark, the Smart Contract algorithm calculated incentive payments (in Ether) for better-than-benchmark delivery and penalties for worse-than-benchmark delivery. The Blockchain-based Smart Contract was successfully tested to automatically transfer incentives or penalties based on input delivery variability levels, and rejected incorrect payment attempts, demonstrating enforceability and transparency. The system provides objective, instant, and quantifiable feedback on supplier performance, offers an anchor point for understanding delivery variability's schedule impact, and reduces management burden. Limitations include the need for GC-verified manual data entry (not fully decentralized) and the model only considering PBU delivery impact, not other participants' reliability.

ideas.idea: Delivery reliability of prefabricated modules directly affects on-site installation productivity and overall project schedule/cost, which can be quantified via simulation.
ideas.quote: investigate the PBU delivery reliability impact on on-site installation productivity

ideas.idea: Current contractual practice fails to timely enforce delay penalties, only doing so near project completion, which limits its motivational effect on suppliers.
ideas.quote: the penalty of delayed completion is usually not enforced until project completion or near completion

ideas.idea: Smart Contracts encoded on Blockchain can automate incentive and penalty payments based on measurable delivery performance, reducing manual monitoring effort.
ideas.quote: Smart Contract alleviated the time-consuming work of tracking and paying by automating the consensus algorithms.

ideas.idea: There is a gap in existing research regarding using simulation outputs to generate customized incentive/penalty structures for suppliers to encourage reliability.
ideas.quote: few studies used the simulation to generate the incentives and penalties strategies that can motivate the supplier to perform higher reliability

ideas.idea: Smart Contracts cannot be fully automated under current legal, social, and economic systems and require some human intervention.
ideas.quote: He argued that the Smart Contract can not be fully automated or can be semiautomated with limited human intervene because the full intelligence of the Smart Contract requires the change of the current social, economic, and law system.

ideas.idea: Blockchain-based Smart Contracts provide transparent, objective, and tamper-proof records of transactions and performance, improving on the subjective nature of current subcontractor performance appraisals.
ideas.quote: In many current practices, subcontractor performance appraisal tends to be subjective and qualitative.

ideas.idea: The developed Blockchain/Smart Contract system currently relies on manual verification and input by the general contractor, making it not fully decentralized.
ideas.quote: the inputs for Blockchain platform need to be verified and entered by the GC. So at the current stage, the Blockchain platform is not a fully decentralized system.

ideas.idea: The approach can be generalized and customized for other modular construction projects to manage supply chain risk and incentivize reliable delivery.
ideas.quote: With the suitable adjustment, the Blockchain platform developed in this research can be customized to other types of modular construction projects.

objectives: To develop a comprehensive framework for identifying and classifying sources of ambiguity in construction contracts, and to validate this framework by analyzing motives of litigation in relevant Supreme Court of Canada construction cases.
problem_statement: Existing research on causes of construction claims and disputes is fragmented, taking niche perspectives or discussing sources of ambiguity qualitatively and subjectively, without a comprehensive, quantifiable framework linking common causal factors in contract documents to actual litigation outcomes.
methodology: A two-phase qualitative and quantitative approach: Phase 1 involved a comprehensive literature review (105 articles, 1985-2019) to extract 104 unique sources of ambiguity, which were clustered into a hierarchical fishbone model (5 categories, 15 subcategories, 62 classes, subclasses) and quantified by frequency of occurrence in the literature. Phase 2 involved screening 30,500 Supreme Court of Canada cases down to 285 construction-related cases, then narrowing via topical, temporal, and geographic criteria to 50 cases for first-level analysis and 13 cases for detailed analysis, cross-examining litigation motives against the fishbone model categories/classes.
key_background_studies: Cakmak and Cakmak (2013) - identified 28 common causes of disputes across contractor, contract, design, owner, project, human behavior, and external factors
Mahamid (2016) - studied dispute causes in residential building projects, ranking 29 reasons by frequency
Odeh and Battaineh (2002) - identified 28 reasons for delay in traditional contracts via interviews with contractors and consultants
Broome and Hayes (1997) - studied clarity of NEC ECC contracts, identifying word order, layout, and jargon as key ambiguity sources
Wright and Fergusson (2009) - studied benefits of standard contract forms and cost impact of wording ambiguity (up to 5% of budget)
Chehayeb et al. (2007) - analyzed motives of court cases related to CCDC-2 general conditions
Chan and Ann (2005) - studied clarity of design liability and contractual provisions in design-build contracts, finding roles/responsibilities poorly defined

Azghandi-Roshnavand et al. (2019) - proposed the original five-category conceptual framework (language, contract, design, stakeholders, external factors) for classifying ambiguity sources, which this study's fishbone model builds upon
Ali (2016) - studied legal text layout issues when translating standard contracts
Gilson et al. (2014) - emphasized need for clear contract language as basis for judicial reasoning
Shahtaheri et al. (2015) - identified need for fault-tolerant design in modular construction to minimize on-site rework
Fateh et al. (2017) - emphasized need for proper procurement route selection, particularly for modular/industrialized construction
Nasrollahzadeh et al. (2016) - described recycling contracts from previous projects without modification as a common industry barrier
findings: Incomplete and/or redundant information in contract documents were identified as the core reasons for conflict between contracted parties in the Canadian construction industry. Literature analysis ranked poor contract draftsmanship, ambiguity in contract terms, modification issues, and lack of local industry readiness as top sources of ambiguity, while court case analysis found ineffective contract management/administration, incomplete contract documents, and redundant information as top motives for litigation. Four of the top five categories were common between literature-based and case-based analyses, though ranked differently. The contract and stakeholder categories emerged as most prominent across both analyses. External factors related to modular/off-site construction, though emphasized in literature, were not represented in the SCC cases studied, indicating a gap in judicial data for MMC-related disputes.

ideas.idea: Standard contract forms, while intended to reduce misunderstanding, are frequently modified to meet specific project needs, which can itself introduce new sources of ambiguity and dispute.
ideas.quote: in practice, however, these standard contract forms are often modified to satisfy the project requirements given by owners (and other parties involved).

ideas.idea: The literature places particular emphasis on the need for proper contractual arrangements and procurement guidelines specifically for modern/modular and industrialized construction projects, which existing standard forms may not adequately address.
ideas.quote: The need for contractual arrangement guidelines, particularly in modern construction (such as industrial and modular) projects, is highlighted in the literature (Fateh et al. 2017).

ideas.idea: Modular/off-site construction lacks separate, adequate specifications compared to conventional construction, contributing to missing information disputes.
ideas.quote: Insufficient specifications in conventional construction and the lack of separate specifications for modular and off-site construction (MOC) are pointed out in this regard by the literature.

ideas.idea: In modular construction, design choices are constrained by transportation/shipment method limitations, creating a distinct category of design-related ambiguity not present in conventional construction.
ideas.quote: depending on the choice of shipment method, there would be limitations and constraints to the module design (Schoenborn 2012). As such, we defined a separate subcategory for design optimization in modular construction, under which classes such as design limitation of modules, design standardization and repetition, and module damage and interfacing problems are included.

ideas.idea: Fault-tolerant design systems are necessary in modular construction to reduce on-site rework caused by assembly interface problems between prefabricated modules.
ideas.quote: Shahtaheri et al. (2015) identified that the systematic design of fault-tolerant systems is required to minimize rework during the assembly of modules on-site.

ideas.idea: External factors specific to modular construction—such as volumetric transportation difficulties, contradictory transport regulations across jurisdictions, and lack of building codes for modular construction—are significant unavoidable sources of contractual ambiguity not addressed in current frameworks.
ideas.quote: Volumetric transportation difficulties in modular construction can negatively affect the overall control of the project's cost, schedule, and productivity (Song et al. 2005). As such, lack of proper supply chain management and logistics planning as well as transportation restrictions and/or contradictory transportation regulations among different territories can become the source of claims and disputes.

ideas.idea: The level of industry maturity and adoption of modern/efficient construction practices such as industrialization and automation strongly affects project progress and should be considered in contract drafting, yet lack of local industry readiness was a literature-identified concern absent from actual court cases studied.
ideas.quote: the level of local industry maturity and the adoption level of modern/efficient construction practices (e.g., digitalization, industrialization, and automation) in the workplace can strongly affect the progress of construction and must be overseen and taken into consideration in the contract.

ideas.idea: The study notes that despite literature emphasis on external factors correlating with modular and off-site construction methods, none of the analyzed Supreme Court cases involved such projects, indicating a research and judicial data gap regarding MMC-related contractual disputes.
ideas.quote: Some of the categories, such as external factors, which have considerable support in our literature analysis, particularly correspond with modular and off-site construction methods. However, the relevant court cases at the SCC did not include any projects of this type.

ideas.idea: Sources of ambiguity and contractual confusion are strongly correlated with the project procurement strategy and delivery method chosen, an area the study could not fully examine due to lack of available case information on contract type.
ideas.quote: it must be noticed that the common sources of confusion or ambiguity in construction contracts can be strongly correlated with the project procurement strategy adapted (e.g., delivery method, contract type).

ideas.idea: Recycling standard contracts from previous projects without proper modification for new project conditions is a common industry barrier that introduces redundant or inconsistent contractual information.
ideas.quote: Nasrollahzadeh et al. (2016) described recycling contracts from previous projects without proper modifications as one of the top barriers frequently occurring in the industry.

objectives: To identify and prioritize stakeholder-associated supply chain risks (SCRs) in prefabricated building projects (PBPs) in Hong Kong, and to examine the dynamic interactions between these risks using social network analysis (SNA).
problem_statement: Existing SCR research has mainly focused on static, individual risk perspectives, with little attention paid to the dynamic interactions between SCRs and their associated stakeholders in prefabrication supply chains. This limits understanding of how risks propagate through the fragmented, cross-border supply chains typical of PBPs in Hong Kong.
methodology: A mixed-methods case study approach combining literature review, expert interviews, a focus group, and social network analysis (SNA). Thirty stakeholder-associated SCRs were identified through literature review and validated by three experts. A public housing case project in Tuen Mun, Hong Kong (five buildings, 34–38 storeys, 2015–2017) was studied; stakeholders (client/designer, manufacturer, transporter, main contractor, assembly subcontractor) participated in a focus group to assess likelihood and impact of risk interactions using a five-point Likert scale, producing a risk structure matrix. The matrix was analyzed in Netminer 4 software to compute network measures (density, cohesion) and node/link measures (nodal degree, betweenness centrality, status centrality, brokerage, ego size).
key_background_studies: Koskela (2003) - explained the complexity of SCM for PBPs from four perspectives (longer chain, larger design work, longer error correction period, higher dimensional accuracy requirements).
Christopher and Peck (2004) - proposed the five-category SCR classification (process, control, demand, supply, environment) adopted as the study's risk categorization method.
Pfohl et al. (2011) - highlighted high interconnectedness and manifold nature of SCRs and their negative impacts on supply chain performance.
Yu et al. (2017) - provided the methodological approach for assessing risk interrelationships via stakeholder-rated likelihood/impact questions, adopted in this study's focus group method.

Yang et al. (2016) and Mok et al. (2017) - demonstrated successful use of SNA to investigate stakeholder-related risks and interactions in complex construction projects, justifying SNA's application here.
Li et al. (2016) - identified schedule delay issues in Hong Kong PBP supply chains related to information and logistics problems.
Choi et al. (2017) - identified site access, on-site storage, site operations, and labor productivity as barriers to PBP implementation in Hong Kong, echoed by this study's findings.
Zhai et al. (2017) - identified lead-time hedging issues from contractors informing manufacturers of component requirements too early.
Chiang et al. (2006) - argued that control over the supply chain, not prefabrication itself, provides sustainable competitive advantage.
findings: Thirty SCRs across seven stakeholder groups (client, designer, main contractor, manufacturer, transporter, assembly subcontractor, government) were identified. SNA of the case project's risk network (43 nodes, 195 links) revealed high complexity (density 0.108, cohesion 0.309). Nine critical risks and eleven critical links were identified, converging into three major challenges: (1) poor supply chain planning (e.g., inaccurate initial time/resource estimation by main contractor, leading to labor shortages and quality issues); (2) poor control of working flows (e.g., delayed delivery of precast elements, delayed assembly schedule, poor factory/site layout management); and (3) poor information sharing between stakeholders (e.g., design changes not communicated promptly, obsolete communication channels like email/WhatsApp/hard copies). Removing the key nodes and links substantially reduced network density (by 62%) and cohesion (by 79%), confirming their central role in propagating risk through the network. The manufacturer and main contractor were found to play critical hub roles connecting different stakeholders and risk categories.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication supply chains require close integration among stakeholders from the design stage onward to coordinate labor, materials, and equipment across factory and site environments.
ideas.quote: Prefabrication should be integrated at the outset of the design stage, which requires a high degree of integration among stakeholders to ensure close coordination in maintaining labor, materials, and equipment

ideas.idea: The complexity of prefabrication supply chains stems from longer chains spanning two production environments, greater upfront design work, longer error-correction periods, and higher dimensional accuracy requirements.
ideas.quote: Koskela (2003) explained the complexity of SCM-PBP from four perspectives: (1) a longer chain caused by two or more production environments, namely, factory and site; (2) larger amounts of design work and earlier design for cast-in-situ construction because of prefabrication lead time; (3) longer error correction period; and (4) higher requirements for dimensional accuracy.

ideas.idea: Design changes originating from the client frequently cause downstream delays in assembly, illustrating how contractual/process risk from one party propagates through the supply chain.
ideas.quote: a design change originated from the client often leads to the delayed assembly of precast components by the assembly subcontractor, resulting in cost overruns and schedule delay of the entire project.

ideas.idea: Poor and outdated modes of communication between designer, main contractor and manufacturer (e.g., email, WhatsApp, hard copies) are root causes of costly design-change and delivery problems, suggesting a need for better contractual/coordination mechanisms for information flow.
ideas.quote: the stakeholders interact with each other mainly by email, WhatsApp, and hard copies of project documents. Such obsolete ways of communication and the unawareness of frequent information exchanges between stakeholders are the root cause of many problems in the supply chain.

ideas.idea: Inaccurate initial time and resource estimation by the main contractor is the most influential risk, propagating widely into labor shortages and quality problems, highlighting the importance of allocating planning responsibility clearly in contracts.
ideas.quote: The risk network shows that poor planning of resources and schedule is a very significant risk in the case project and generates many propagated impacts. The master program has been revised seven times, indicating the poor estimation of resources and schedule (S3R14).

ideas.idea: Delayed delivery of precast elements and delayed assembly schedules are critical nodes reflecting poor control of working flows between manufacturer and assembly subcontractor, indicating a need for clearer contractual delineation of responsibility for schedule coordination between off-site and on-site parties.
ideas.quote: Delayed delivery of precast elements to the site (S4R6) and delayed assembly schedule (S6R23) are two important nodes that reflect the poor control of working processes in both the upstream and the downstream chains and cause significant schedule and quality problems.

ideas.idea: The manufacturer often serves multiple clients simultaneously, causing poor coordination of resources among different projects that has downstream effects on a specific project's supply chain performance—a risk not typically addressed in bilateral construction contracts.
ideas.quote: the manufacturer does not work for only one project but has signed contracts with multiple clients. The factory, therefore, has to plan resources for several projects at the same time but suffers from poor coordination of resources among different projects.

ideas.idea: The main contractor, manufacturer, and client occupy the most central roles in the risk network, indicating that contractual risk allocation should particularly focus on these parties' obligations around planning and communication.
ideas.quote: the risks related to the main contractor, the manufacturer, and the client locate in the very central status of the circle, indicating their significant roles in coordinating the supply chains of PBPs.

ideas.idea: Cross-border transportation and customs processes (e.g., prolonged custom declaration) introduce contractual and logistical risk in prefabrication supply chains that traditional single-jurisdiction contracts may not adequately address.
ideas.quote: most precast factories are in the Pearl River Delta area of Mainland China from which the components are transported by trucks through customs to Hong Kong, resulting in substantial uncertainty and task complexity during the transportation process.

objectives: To evaluate and compare the effects of a subsidy mechanism versus a reward-penalty mechanism on environmental responsibility (ER) decisions of contractors and suppliers in the prefabricated construction supply chain (PCSC), using a Stackelberg game framework, and to identify applicable scenarios for each policy type.
problem_statement: Prefabricated construction shifts environmental burdens from on-site construction to off-site factories, requiring both upstream suppliers and downstream contractors to share environmental responsibility. Existing literature treats government policy as exogenous, examines fabrication and construction stages in isolation, and relies on single-dimensional indicators (e.g., emissions) without considering government financial expenditure, leaving a gap in understanding how subsidy versus reward-penalty mechanisms shape ER allocation and profitability across the decoupled PCSC.
methodology: A three-level Stackelberg game model with government as leader and contractor/supplier as followers is developed. Backward induction is used to derive optimal ER decisions and profit functions under a subsidy mechanism (Model A) and a reward-penalty mechanism (Model B), compared against a no-policy baseline. A real-world case study of a Beijing prefabricated construction project (2018) with parameterized values (price, cost, quantity, cost coefficient, subsidy cap) is used to numerically simulate and validate the theoretical findings via OEB (optimal environmental benefit) and NEB (net environmental benefit) indicators.
key_background_studies: Wang and Wang (2023) - showed unit cost subsidies reduce emission intensity but may increase total emissions under volumetric schemes
Wang et al. (2024) - found green subsidies and unit subsidies yield equivalent carbon allocation outcomes in PCSCs, supporting this study's finding of equal ER allocation
Yi et al. (2024) - designed a government-manufacturer-contractor three-tier subsidy model for sustainability
Weng et al. (2023) - demonstrated reward-penalty intensity drives decarbonization but risks an incentive-intensity paradox
Zhao et al. (2020) - showed reward-penalty schemes in remanufacturing supply chains optimize buyback pricing and recycling performance
Chen and Ulya (2019) - found reward-penalty mechanisms incentivize green production and product return rates
Jia et al. (2017) - proposed combining penalties, waste disposal fees and subsidies for construction and demolition waste management

Rathore and Sarmah (2021) and Wang et al. (2022) - found reward-penalty mechanisms improve waste/product collection rates more effectively than subsidies, though this study finds contrasting profitability effects
Liu et al. (2021) - noted the role of subsidies in promoting environmental participation
findings: Under both subsidy and reward-penalty mechanisms, contractor and supplier adopt equal ER levels (50% each), achieving equitable allocation of environmental responsibility. The subsidy mechanism increases both agents' profits relative to baseline but yields lower environmental benefits, especially once the subsidy cap is reached. The reward-penalty mechanism yields higher ER levels and greater environmental benefits (higher OEB and NEB) but reduces both agents' profits below baseline, since compliance costs exceed incentives; rewards only occur when the environmental benefit coefficient exceeds 1/2. Policy recommendation: prioritize reward-penalty mechanisms in environmentally critical/economically robust regions and subsidy mechanisms in economically vulnerable regions, potentially phasing from subsidies to reward-penalty over time.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication relocates environmental impacts from on-site construction to off-site factories, creating a supply-chain-wide responsibility issue requiring coordination between contractors and suppliers.
ideas.quote: this shift also creates a systemic challenge: while downstream environmental impacts are reduced, new environmental burdens emerge upstream at component manufacturing facilities

ideas.idea: The contractor is modeled as the central coordinator responsible for committing to the overall ER level of the project, reflecting industry practice of contractors being the main liaison with regulators.
