ideas.quote: the contractor serves as the central coordinator, reflecting industry practice where general contractors often serve as the main liaison with regulatory bodies. It is therefore assumed that the contractor is responsible for committing to the overall ER level for the entire construction project.

ideas.idea: The supplier's ER contribution is determined in response to the contractor's overall project-level ER commitment, establishing a sequential decision structure between supply chain parties.
ideas.quote: The supplier, in response, determines the extent of its own ER contribution based on the contractor's overall commitment.

ideas.idea: Under both government policy mechanisms, contractor and supplier end up sharing ER responsibility equally (50/50), suggesting a natural equilibrium allocation regardless of policy type.
ideas.quote: both government policies lead the supplier and contractor to undertake the same optimal ER levels for the supply chain... if they agree to undertake half of the overall ERs of the supply chain.

ideas.idea: Reward-penalty regulatory mechanisms achieve stronger environmental compliance than subsidies but impose net profit losses on contracting parties, creating a trade-off between environmental performance and contractor/supplier profitability.
ideas.quote: Reward-penalty mechanisms demonstrate superior environmental performance yet impose systemic profit loss, as compliance costs exceed governmental incentives.

ideas.idea: Subsidy caps limit the effectiveness of subsidy-based incentives, meaning contract and procurement strategies tied to subsidies must account for these ceilings to avoid under-incentivizing ER adoption.
ideas.quote: If the subsidy cap is set too low, it may fail to encourage higher levels of ER... policymakers should carefully design subsidy ceilings to maintain incentives while controlling public expenditures.

ideas.idea: Policy selection for construction projects should be context-sensitive, tailored to regional environmental urgency versus economic vulnerability, which has implications for how contracts might be structured differently across jurisdictions.
ideas.quote: prioritizing reward-penalty mechanism for environmentally critical regions and subsidy mechanism for economically vulnerable areas.

ideas.idea: Inter-organizational coordination mechanisms, such as green procurement contracts or shared ER targets, are recommended to align contractor and supplier environmental efforts within supply chain contracts.
ideas.quote: Formal collaboration mechanisms, such as green procurement contracts or shared ER targets, can align efforts and reduce inefficiencies.

objectives: To develop and validate a text mining risk assessment-based model that extracts contractual obligations from the general conditions of construction contracts and quantifies the risk-sharing pattern between the client and contractor based on probability and impact on project objectives, using the NSW GC21 contract as a case study.
problem_statement: General conditions of construction contracts are a major source of unquantified, implicit risk allocation between parties, and while text mining has been applied to construction contracts for extracting requirements, poisonous clauses, or exceptions, no prior model combined obligation extraction with a systematic risk analysis to assess the overall risk balance of a standard form contract.
methodology: A two-stage rule-based approach: (1) text mining using MATLAB Text Analytics Toolbox with a lexicon of Promisor-Determiner Nouns (PDN) and Obligation-Maker Verbs (OMV) developed from FIDIC 1999 Red/Yellow/Silver Books, applying preprocessing, POS tagging, tokenization, lemmatization and IF-THEN extraction rules to identify obligations in the NSW GC21 (2nd ed.) general conditions; (2) risk analysis using expert judgment (14 experts) to score probability and impact of obligation breach on five project objectives (cost, schedule, quality, safety, environment) via a three-point scale, followed by correction using lateral latent factors (proximity, controllability, manageability, dormancy, detectability). Model validated against a two-round Delphi expert panel using Precision, Recall, F-measure.
key_background_studies: Hassan and Le (2020) - developed NLP/machine learning framework with rule-based keyword lexicon to classify contract text into requirements/no-requirements
Marzouk and Enaba (2019) - proposed three-tier system integrating contract analysis, 5D BIM and correspondence text analysis to monitor project performance
Lee et al. (2019) - extracted 'poisonous clauses' representing risk to contractor using lexicon-based extraction rules across 11 risk types
Roshnavand et al. (2019) - text mining method to identify ambiguity/confusion sources in modular construction contracts using NLTK
Gao et al. (2012) - extracted 'exceptions' (indemnities) from contracts using noun phrase pattern extraction
Chui and Bai (2010) - content analysis of AIA-A201 and Chinese GF-1999-0201 general conditions categorizing clauses into six content categories
Manderson et al. (2015) - analyzed general conditions content in ten thematic areas relevant to BIM adaptation
William and Ashley (1987) - analyzed >90 clauses across 36 projects to measure impact on six performance indices, finding risk distribution between owner and contractor
findings: The model extracted 109 main contractual obligations from GC21 (76 contractor, 33 principal), achieving Precision 81.55%, Recall 77.06%, F-measure 79.25% against expert panel results. The ten most critical obligations (e.g., paying advance payment, notifying non-compliance with code, paying scheduled amounts, providing site information, notifying faults in contract documents) were identified and ranked, then re-ranked using lateral latent factors. Obligation sharing was found fairer for cost and schedule objectives but unequal for quality, safety and environmental objectives, with the principal bearing about 15% more importance than the contractor on top obligations, though overall 69.7% of all obligations belonged to the contractor versus 30.3% to the principal. The study concludes that general conditions clauses vary greatly in strength/importance and that a systematic, text-mining-supported risk analysis can help both parties develop balanced contract strategies before and after contract signing.

ideas.idea: Standard form contracts are typically drafted or heavily influenced by the client/owner, limiting contractor input and skewing risk allocation.
ideas.quote: almost all construction contracts are concluded based on a standard form, are drafted by the client-side of the contract, or at least the contract is customized and amended by the client

ideas.idea: Risk should be allocated to the party best able to manage it, otherwise project cost and time overruns result.
ideas.quote: each risk should be assigned to the party who could manage it best (Tao 1994). Otherwise, the consequences of the risk will increase and the project will face cost and time overruns

ideas.idea: Unmanaged or unbalanced contractual risk-sharing leads to disputes and increased contractor pricing to cover risk.
ideas.quote: unmanaged contract risks have a major impact on project costs, because contractors increase their price proposals to cover the risks. Disputes become unavoidable when there is unbalanced risk-sharing or ambiguities

ideas.idea: The general conditions document is the principal legal instrument for allocating risk and reducing uncertainty if clearly drafted.
ideas.quote: The principal legal platform for risk-sharing in a construction contract is the general conditions that have an unexampled role to reduce project uncertainty if they have been drafted clearly

ideas.idea: Clauses in a contract are not equal in importance; some are essential 'conditions' while others are minor 'warranties' or intermediate 'innominate' terms, affecting how risk should be prioritized.
ideas.quote: the terms and conditions of an agreement that are expressed through clauses of a contract are not equal in strength and are divided into three types by their relative emphasis on critical issues

ideas.idea: Transferring unpredictable risk to one party via disclaimer clauses increases overall contract costs substantially.
ideas.quote: transferring the unpredictable risks to one party using contractual terms, such as disclaimer clauses that could increase the contract costs between 8% and 20%

ideas.idea: Standard forms of agreement improve fairness in risk-sharing, facilitate risk management, and provide a reliable tendering basis compared to bespoke drafting.
ideas.quote: The use of standard forms of agreement leads to fairness in sharing risks between two parties, facilitates risk management, and establishes a reliable basis for bids during tendering

ideas.idea: Obligations related to design completion, site access, and payment are recurrent early-phase contractual risk points that critically affect cost, schedule and quality outcomes.
ideas.quote: 7 out of 10 significant commitments related to the early phases of the project and 30% only related to the design phase of the project

ideas.idea: Distribution of significant obligations between contracting parties can be numerically unequal even though total obligation counts favor one party, revealing hidden risk imbalance despite apparent balance in raw counts.
ideas.quote: the principal bears approximately 15% more important than the contractor, and the number of shared obligations were 60% and 40% for the contractor and the principal, respectively. The mentioned ratio, for 109 main clauses was 69.7% for the contractor and 30.3% for the principal.

ideas.idea: A systematic obligation/risk extraction model can support both parties and the contract-drafting body in achieving a more balanced, risk-aware contract prior to signing and during administration.
ideas.quote: using the proposed model in the precontract phase of a project, the drafting party could assess the contract risk balance to evaluate the general terms and conditions; the contractor could adjust the bid markup and cover the risk exposure during tendering

objectives: To explore the impacts of emerging off-site industrialized construction technologies (specifically bathroom pods) on construction subcontractors in the Australian residential high-rise sector, using the resource based view (RBV) of the firm as a theoretical lens.
problem_statement: While there is extensive research into the impacts of industrialized construction on the construction sector generally, there has been little research into the specific impacts on subcontractors, despite subcontractors operating at the coalface of the industry and facing different innovation challenges than large firms.
methodology: Qualitative exploratory study using semi-structured interviews with senior executives/managers of six major subcontracting firms (hydraulic, mechanical, electrical trades) in Australia with experience of bathroom pod projects, selected via non-probability snowball sampling. Interviews covered firm background, pod experience, and impacts on financial, physical, intellectual, human, social and organizational resources. Data analysed using Leximancer software (automated concept/theme mapping) combined with narrative analysis of interview transcripts.
key_background_studies: Gibb and Isack (2003) - hierarchical model of industrialization levels and need for supply chain coordination
Blismas and Wakefield (2009) - drivers, constraints and reductions in on-site labour from off-site manufacture
Koebel et al. (2004) - innovation diffusion patterns among different builder types in US residential market
Sexton et al. (2008) - subcontractors' smaller scale and lack of resources for innovation
Barney (1991) - foundational RBV theory on resources and competitive advantage
Priem and Butler (2001a,2001b) - critique of RBV's tautological nature and limited empirical grounding
Goulding et al. (2014) - finding that subcontractors need more help adapting to off-site than designers/manufacturers
Lu and Liska (2008) - barriers of design inflexibility and skills gaps among contractors/architects/engineers
Loosemore (2014) - innovation creates winners and losers, disturbing power/reward structures in construction
Pan et al. (2008) - survey of UK house builders on quality drivers and cost barriers for off-site prefabrication
findings: Key subcontractor resources affected by bathroom pod adoption are human, financial, intellectual and social capital; physical and organizational resources were less impacted. Financial impacts varied by trade (negative for hydraulic, positive for mechanical/electrical) due to reduced scope of work and reward capture by head contractors. Human resources saw reduced site labour but stable management levels, with concerns about deskilling and apprentice training. Intellectual resources became more important for competitive advantage through new planning, logistics and coordination skills. Social resources required new supply chain partnerships and collaboration with manufacturers/designers, though these remained project-based rather than long-term. Organizational structures showed little change. Overall, subcontractors need to develop new skills, knowledge, networks and deeper supply chain collaborations to turn risks of off-site into competitive opportunities.

ideas.idea: Off-site prefabrication requires significant upfront investment that challenges subcontractors' financial resource strategies, forcing a shift from conservative to more aggressive working capital approaches.
ideas.quote: off-site prefabrication requires significant up-front set-up costs, requiring a firm to move towards a more aggressive working capital strategy, at least in the short term, as capability is built-up.

ideas.idea: Financial benefits from off-site efficiency gains tend to be captured by head contractors rather than subcontractors due to competitive pressures and traditional contracting power structures.
ideas.quote: Competition is so high we don’t get to retain any of the savings or indirect cost benefits for ourselves. We still end up making the same margin as per usual because everyone just passes the cost savings along. R3

ideas.idea: Reduced scope of work under off-site prefabrication reduces subcontractor revenue while overhead costs for site management remain constant, squeezing margins.
ideas.quote: Say a 5 million dollar contract I don’t do the fit out and I don’t supply the fixtures so it reduces the 5 to a 3.8 but I still have my managers on site for the whole project ... so while my workload reduces my overhead stays the same. R6

ideas.idea: Off-site prefabrication increases the need for early subcontractor involvement in design and closer collaboration between designers, manufacturers and constructors to achieve successful outcomes.
ideas.quote: We had to be heavily involved in the initial design process and design of the connections ... I would say we will need to communicate more with people and other trades ... R6

ideas.idea: A breakdown in communication between designed pod specifications and what actually arrives on-site can hinder project success and relationships between subcontractor, head contractor and manufacturer.
ideas.quote: respondents noted that pod designs agreed was not always what arrived on-site, a breakdown in communication which hindered project success and new relationships between subcontractor, head contractor and the pod manufacturer.

ideas.idea: Off-site technology reduces the amount of on-site trade labour needed while management/coordination staffing levels remain stable, requiring more intricate workforce planning.
ideas.quote: As far as human resources go you still have your site manager, your leading hand. It is hard to measure however, we reduced the workforce a little. R6

ideas.idea: Moving tradesmen from site-based work to factory environments can create motivation and mental welfare issues due to repetitive work, despite safety benefits claimed in the literature.
ideas.quote: The thing with the pod factories they go out and get local labour and trade professionals and they basically work on the production line... it would kill our guys to work in that sort of environment. Doing that kind of repetitive work all day. R3

ideas.idea: Apprentices and young tradesmen risk losing essential trade skills and experience when working primarily on pod projects rather than traditional installations.
ideas.quote: If you’re a young apprentice if you work on three pod projects you will be finished [the apprenticeship] and will have never set a bathroom you have never set a pan, put a basin in or put a shower on the wall that is a huge risk [to my company]. R6

ideas.idea: Off-site prefabrication increases the importance of intellectual resources such as new planning, logistics, scheduling and coordination skills, though firms differ in strategies to protect this knowledge as a competitive advantage.
ideas.quote: Firm strategies to retain intellectual resources as forms of competitive advantage differed. For example, R6 did not document knowledge since he saw them as 'the family secrets'... In contrast, R5 had begun to document or codify the knowledge gained.

ideas.idea: Subcontractors' social capital and supply chain relationships shift as reliance on traditional material suppliers decreases while new relationships with pod manufacturers must be developed.
ideas.quote: Take for example (supplier name) the largest tap ware and sanitary supplier in Australia. Our relationship with them will reduce because we will not be purchasing the product any longer. R5

ideas.idea: Organizational structures of subcontracting firms show little immediate change from adopting off-site technology, though this may evolve as the technology becomes more widespread.
ideas.quote: We didn’t change the organisational structure on the job you couldn’t we still had the same number or management people there from day one for the start up to the end of the project. R6

ideas.idea: Successful transition to off-site technology in other industries has relied on joint product development and relational contracts, which are currently lacking in construction subcontracting relationships.
ideas.quote: in contrast to the relational contracts found in other industries that effectively use OSM (Helper and Henderson 2014), our respondents were hampered by traditional subcontracts which resulted in rewards being passed up the line to head contractors.

ideas.idea: High levels of supply chain coordination between designers, developers, builders, manufacturers and suppliers are necessary to fully realize the benefits of off-site prefabrication.
ideas.quote: Gibb and Isack (2003) highlight the need for high levels of supply chain co-ordination between designers, developers, builders, manufacturers and suppliers to enable the benefits of off-site prefabrication to be fully realized.

ideas.idea: Off-site prefabrication requires an early design freeze, which conflicts with the construction industry's traditional practice of allowing designs to evolve throughout construction.
ideas.quote: inflexibility of design was a major challenge because off-site prefabrication requires and an early design freeze, whereas the industry has become accustomed to projects progressing with incomplete designs which involve numerous changes and adaptions throughout construction.

objectives: To clarify the real meaning and relevance of collaboration for digital transformation in the construction industry, exploring what collaboration looks like in the real world of digitalized construction projects among AEC professionals.
problem_statement: Despite frequent use of the term 'collaboration' in policy, technical, and governmental reports related to digital transformation and Industry 4.0 in construction, the concept remains vague, undefined, and lacking a grounded theoretical framework, leading to unclear understanding of what collaboration actually entails in practice at the project level.
methodology: An exploratory qualitative study using content analysis of literature, standards, and guidelines combined with 13 open-ended semistructured interviews of AEC industry experts (middle- and senior-level management from large infrastructure projects across UK, India, US, Ireland, and Malaysia), recruited via snowball sampling. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using three-phase coding (open, axial, selective) in NVivo 14 to generate concept maps, project maps, and themes.
key_background_studies: Hughes et al. (2012) - defines construction-specific collaboration emphasizing non-adversarial, early-involvement team-based practices via appropriate contracts
Hartono and Holsapple (2004) - defines collaboration in information systems as participatory, knowledge-based process among autonomous participants
Bedwell et al. (2012) - human resources management definition of collaboration as joint activity engagement to achieve project goals
Schöttle et al. (2014) - construction definition emphasizing joint project organization, trust, shared risks/rewards
Bouwen and Taillieu (2004), Stout and Keast (2021), Otjes and Rasmussen (2017) - support theme of multiple parties' involvement in collaboration definition
Verheij and Augenbroe (2006), Chowdhury et al. (2021) - support theme of workflows in place as part of collaboration definition
Aarts and Van Woerkum (2006), Parkhe (1998) - relate to open-mindedness toward problem resolution as collaborative behavior
Bradley et al. (2010), Tuuli et al. (2010) - relate to self-managing teams as key collaborative behavior
Chakkol et al. (2018), Han (2023) - support importance of nation-specific guidelines and standards for collaboration
Eriksson (2017), Akintan and Morledge (2013) - support role of appropriate procurement strategy in facilitating collaboration
Bond-Barnard et al. (2018), Ekung et al. (2015) - support theme of personality traits integrated into BIM process as key interdependency
findings: The study identified that collaboration is defined primarily through multiple parties' involvement and workflows in place. Key collaborative behaviors within alliance/integrated delivery included self-managing teams and open-mindedness toward problem resolution. Appropriate procurement strategy and nation-specific guidelines/standards were found important for realizing collaboration. Technology, particularly BIM, email, cloud environments, and Microsoft Teams, was confirmed by all experts as facilitating smooth collaborative workflows. Members' personality traits integrated into the BIM process emerged as the most influential interdependency for realizing collaboration in project teams.

ideas.idea: Appropriate procurement strategy is linked to and improves the importance of collaboration within construction project delivery.
ideas.quote: an appropriate procurement strategy seemingly improves the importance of collaboration, which again echoes the existing studies (Eriksson 2017; Akintan and Morledge 2013).

ideas.idea: Collaboration importance varies across contract types, with experts asked specifically about traditional, design-build, EPC, and design-build-operate arrangements.
ideas.quote: How important is collaboration (formal and informal) within different forms of contracts (e.g., traditional, design and build, EPC, design-build-operate) in your sector of construction work?

ideas.idea: Partnering, alliancing, and integrated project delivery (IPD) contracts share a common objective of shared pain/gain among stakeholders to maximize collaborative behavior legally and in business terms.
ideas.quote: partnering, alliancing, and integrated project delivery contracts share the same objective (Hughes et al. 2012): all stakeholders in project teams share both the pain and the gain associated with ultimate project performance to maximize collaboration behavior within a project team's culture legally as well as business environment

ideas.idea: Collaborative practice in construction requires a cultural shift from hierarchical decision-making to a 'best for project' rather than 'best for me' approach with equal risk/reward distribution.
ideas.quote: creating a collaborative team where risks and rewards are equally distributed and no decision is made from the hierarchical fashion, and the ultimate decision is changing from best for me to best for project.

ideas.idea: Self-managing teams and open-mindedness toward problem resolution emerged as the most critical collaborative behaviors within alliance and integrated project delivery arrangements.
ideas.quote: two themes, i.e., self-managing teams and open-mindedness toward problem resolution, emerged as the most important

ideas.idea: Nation-specific guidelines and standards facilitate recognition of the importance of collaboration in construction projects.
ideas.quote: Three of the 13 experts trusted that nation-specific guidelines and standards would facilitate the recognition of the importance of collaboration

ideas.idea: BIM, alongside cloud environments and collaboration platforms like Microsoft Teams, acts as a critical enabler of smooth collaborative workflows in digitalized construction projects.
ideas.quote: collectively all the experts confirmed that building information modeling (BIM) and email communications, cloud environment and Microsoft Teams facilitated smooth collaborative workflows.

ideas.idea: The personalities and traits of project team members, integrated into the BIM process, are the most influential factor for realizing collaboration and interdependencies in project teams.
ideas.quote: the most influential theme that emerged was members' personality traits integrated into the BIM process, which aligns with most studies (Bond-Barnard et al. 2018; Ekung et al. 2015).

ideas.idea: Collaboration in construction contracts is achieved through mechanisms such as early involvement of key members, regular meetings, early warning systems, open dialogue, risk sharing, and pain share/gain share arrangements within long-term relationships.
ideas.quote: This is achieved by using the appropriate contract. As a result of regular meetings, early warning systems, open dialogue, and risk sharing, relationships are managed so that information is shared in a respectful atmosphere of mutual trust.

objectives: To examine six foundational supply chain management (SCM) perspectives (target project type, contract type, business strategy, production management, SCM practices, organizational culture) through observation of two California offsite construction companies, and to propose an outline for a supply chain integration theory tailored to offsite construction.
problem_statement: Offsite construction adds complexity to SCM due to the need to coordinate design, manufacturing, transport, and assembly, yet construction supply chains remain fragmented, relationships between contractors and suppliers are weak, and there is a lack of empirical studies on how companies integrate their supply chains for offsite construction, leaving no robust theoretical framework to guide firms.
methodology: An inductive, case-based theoretical study (Eisenhardt, 1989) using the Observation-Participation Method, involving direct observation, participation in supply chain integration processes, and informal interviews with project management teams at two California-based construction companies (Company A using a 'One Company Policy' portfolio/subcontracting model, Company B using internal vertical integration) that implement offsite prefabricated and modular construction across projects in the United States.
key_background_studies: Vrijhoef & Koskela (2000) - defined the four roles of SCM in construction and highlighted fragmentation/myopic decision-making issues
Christopher (2005) - defined supply chain as a network producing value for end-users, foundational SCM concept
Ballard & Howell (1998) - Last Planner System and lean construction principles related to workflow variation
Tommelein & Li (1999) - Value Stream Mapping enhancing JIT delivery for concrete components
Cossio & Cossio (2012) - JIT lean techniques for offsite facade delivery showing time/cost savings and stakeholder resistance
Lessing & Brege (2018) - Industrialized Construction requiring both internal and external supply chain integration
Prado (2022) - OM-based integration framework for OSC focusing on JIT delivery and interconnected production systems
Prado & Tommelein (2023) - linked production metrics to cost/schedule in offsite facade installation
Zhang & Fischer (2024) - optimized inventory via integrating fabrication and installation planning using Operations Science
Hall et al. (2022) - vertical integration as a business strategy enabling coordination of design, manufacturing, transport, assembly
Green et al. (2005) - slow SCM adoption in construction due to fragmentation
findings: Company A (project-centric, design-build with subcontracted offsite factory under 'One Company Policy') achieves project adaptability and early design input but suffers from separated profit centers, limited production visibility, and late design changes disrupting factory operations. Company B (product-centric, vertically integrated) achieves standardization, JIT delivery, and cost control but faces internal fragmentation between engineering/PM and manufacturing departments, and hard-bid contracts limiting flexibility. The study concludes that a hybrid business strategy balancing project-centric flexibility with product-centric standardization, integration of lean production and lean construction practices, and collaborative team structures are key insights for a proposed supply chain integration theory. Key enablers identified include collaborative contracting, digital integration, and cooperative organizational culture; traditional subcontracting models that shift risk to subcontractors hinder integration.

ideas.idea: Traditional subcontracting/lump-sum contract structures between main contractor and offsite factory create financial and operational separation that limits information transparency and hinders integration.
ideas.quote: Traditional subcontracting models shift risks to subcontractors, often hindering integration.

ideas.idea: Design-build contracts combined with early factory involvement in the proposal phase support earlier design input and better coordination, though production visibility remains limited.
ideas.quote: the contractor team engages in a design-build contract with the owner and a lump sum contract with the factory, reinforcing their financial and operational separation.

ideas.idea: Hard-bid contracts with vertically integrated firms can conflict with the need for design flexibility, as budget-driven changes reduce manufacturing repeatability and profitability.
ideas.quote: This situation can lead to reducing repeatability during manufacturing (the most expensive phase), therefore, reduce the profit of the job compared to most manufacturing-wise production.

ideas.idea: A flexible, collaborative contract framework is needed to align stakeholder incentives and enable transparency across the offsite supply chain.
ideas.quote: A transparent, collaboration-driven contract framework is essential to aligning stakeholder incentives across the supply chain.

ideas.idea: Lack of visibility into offsite production processes for clients/GCs, driven by subcontracting structures, can hinder collaboration and cause inefficiencies at the onsite-offsite interface.
ideas.quote: the client and the GC have limited visibility into the offsite production process during manufacturing, which can hinder collaboration and process integration.

ideas.idea: Vertical integration enables firms to control design, procurement, fabrication and installation, redefining traditional contractual/operational boundaries in offsite construction.
ideas.quote: By bringing in-house design, construction, and manufacturing, offsite construction firms redefine operational boundaries (Eldamnhoury & Hanna, 2020).

ideas.idea: Late design changes introduced by project teams due to insufficient communication with factories disrupt manufacturing operations and increase waste, pointing to contractual gaps in requiring production oversight.
ideas.quote: Due to minimal communication during manufacturing, project teams frequently introduce late changes to safeguard project profitability, leading to disruptions in factory operations.

ideas.idea: Integrated project delivery and performance-based contracting models are proposed as future research areas to address misalignment issues between offsite manufacturers and site teams.
ideas.quote: Research on collaborative contract models, such as Integrated Project Delivery and performance-based contracts, can address misalignment issues.

ideas.idea: Relational contracts are seen as a mechanism to foster collaboration and reduce adversarial dynamics compared to traditional subcontracting in offsite construction.
ideas.quote: Relational contracts foster collaboration, reducing adversarial dynamics in traditional subcontracting.

objectives: To investigate dispute causation in modular construction projects by (1) determining the most common causes leading to disputes, (2) categorizing these causes based on their interconnectivities, and (3) identifying and quantifying key associations between the various causes that trigger disputes among project stakeholders.
problem_statement: While modularization can mitigate industry challenges like poor productivity and safety, contractual risks and disputes remain a top factor affecting modular project performance. Existing dispute literature addresses construction disputes generally or in specific traditional contexts but fails to address the unique, complex sources of disputes associated with modularization, and there is limited work on the interconnectivities among dispute causal factors.
methodology: An integrated four-step analytical methodology was applied to 39 publicly available US legal cases of modular construction disputes (collected via Google Scholar search, screened using six selection criteria). Causal factors were manually coded into a binary reference matrix (40 causes x 39 cases). Social network analysis (SNA) was used to compute degree centrality and network density to identify common causes; spectral clustering (SC) grouped causes into four clusters based on interconnectivity strength (using silhouette score to determine optimal cluster number); association rule analysis (ARA) and the Apriori algorithm, filtered by support, confidence, lift thresholds and validated with Fisher's exact test, identified statistically significant associations of co-occurring causes within each cluster.
key_background_studies: Abdul Nabi and El-adaway (2021) - identified contractual risks and disputes as a top factor impacting cost and schedule performance of modular projects
Arashphour et al. (2017) - considered contractual problems and disputes as a challenge to integrating offsite technologies
Kumaraswamy (1997) - established the concept of proximate and root causes of construction disputes
Love et al. (2008) - argued effective dispute minimization requires examining complex associations among causal factors, not just identifying them
Woodley (2019) - stated disputes are caused by complex interplay among multiple factors, so simplistic avoidance approaches fail
Kumar Viswanathan et al. (2020) - highlighted poor communication as a key dispute factor and noted limited work on associations among causal factors
Wong et al. (2017) - highlighted need to address lead-time requirements for module delivery in contract conditions
O'Connor et al. (2014) - emphasized avoiding contractual transition disconnects between design phases in modular projects
Fateh et al. (2017) - identified lack of clear project standards, integration strategies, and customized standard contract forms for modular construction
Said (2015) - discussed labor union issues from dependency on offsite/out-of-state labor and higher cost implications of design/scope changes in modular projects
Choi and Song (2014) - noted modular construction requires higher design and engineering requirements than stick-built
Alwisy et al. (2012) - highlighted importance of accounting for onsite conditions early in design of modules
Duncheva and Bradley (2019) - linked unclear building codes/standards for modular products to rework and delays
Jaillon and Poon (2010) - emphasized early collaboration and coordination of participants in design/construction stages of modular projects
findings: The four most common causes of disputes in modular construction were payment holds/delays, lack of collaboration between trades, delay in project completion, and poor communication among participants. The dispute network showed high density (83.8%), indicating disputes are typically triggered by multiple co-occurring causes rather than a single cause. Forty causes were grouped into four clusters with significant associations: Cluster 1 (design errors, excessive design/scope changes, delays in design completion); Cluster 2 (time extensions, onsite delays, unforeseen site conditions, resource shortages, negligence); Cluster 3 (defective modules, misalignment with building codes/specifications, inadequate bidding, payment holds); Cluster 4 (starting construction with incomplete design and lack of collaboration among trades). These associations provide practitioners with early warning signs for dispute avoidance and highlight contractual aspects of modularization needing revision.

ideas.idea: Modular construction requires new or adapted contractual models compared to traditional construction because of its unique requirements.
ideas.quote: implementing the modular approach in construction projects necessitates the use of new contractual models and processes

ideas.idea: Contracts should explicitly address lead-time requirements for delivering modules.
ideas.quote: Wong et al. (2017) highlighted the need to address lead-time requirements associated with the delivery of the modules in the project contractual conditions.

ideas.idea: Contractual transitions between design phases (assessment, selection, basic design, detailed design) must be seamless to avoid problems in modular projects.
ideas.quote: the success of modular construction projects requires avoiding disconnects in any contractual transition existing between assessment, selection, basic design, or detailed design phases

ideas.idea: The absence of customized standard contract forms for modular construction is a key contractual/legal challenge leading to disputes.
ideas.quote: modular construction is associated with many contractual and legal challenges, including the lack of clear project standards and integration strategies as well as the lack of customized standard forms of contracts

ideas.idea: Labor union-related issues are a dispute cause unique to modular construction due to reliance on offsite or out-of-state labor.
ideas.quote: some of the causal factors are unique to modularization, particularly C22 (labor union–related issues), as it represents conflicts with labor unions due to the dependency on offsite or out-of-state labors

ideas.idea: Starting construction with incomplete design is a factor amplified in modular construction because it disrupts offsite manufacturing schedules.
ideas.quote: This factor may not be critical to traditional construction projects as compared to modular construction methods, where it is perceived to amplify delays and disruptions of the work in offsite manufacturing

ideas.idea: Interfacing defects between modules, and between modules and onsite components, are a distinct dispute cause in modular projects.
ideas.quote: C34 (interfacing defects), which represents defects associated with module-module as well as module-onsite component interfaces

ideas.idea: Excessive design/scope changes, defective design, and delayed design completion together form a key predictor of disputes, implying contracts should support early design freeze and adequate design lead time.
ideas.quote: early freeze of the design as well as appropriate allocation of design and engineering lead times are considered success factors for modular construction projects

ideas.idea: Late design or field changes are especially costly in modular projects compared to stick-built, underscoring the need for contractual mechanisms to manage change orders.
ideas.quote: higher cost implications are associated with design and scope of work changes in modular construction projects as compared to traditional stick-built methods

ideas.idea: Modular construction does not eliminate risks from unforeseen site conditions, and contracts should require contractor technical capability assessment and resource planning for both offsite and onsite work.
ideas.quote: the results show that the modular construction method does not completely eliminate the risks associated with unforeseen site conditions that can lead to disputes and conflicts among the project stakeholders

ideas.idea: Contract and bidding documents should clearly specify applicable building codes, regulations, and specifications to avoid misalignment issues with prefabricated modules.
ideas.quote: it is important to make sure that (1) the applicable regulatory, code, and specification requirements are clearly specified in the bidding and contract documents

ideas.idea: Successful modular delivery requires more collaborative contractual arrangements and early involvement of contractors/suppliers/manufacturers in design.
ideas.quote: the implementation of modular construction methods necessitates the use of more collaborative contractual agreements

ideas.idea: Improved coordination and synchronization between design team, offsite work, and onsite work is essential to avoid disputes stemming from incomplete design and lack of collaboration.
ideas.quote: it is crucial to ensure (1) early involvement of the contractor/supplier/manufacturer in the project; and (2) improved coordination and synchronization between the design team, onsite work, and offsite work

ideas.idea: Disputes in modular projects are generally the result of multiple interacting causes rather than a single isolated cause, suggesting contract risk allocation should address combinations of risks rather than singular provisions.
ideas.quote: modular construction disputes are mostly triggered by the occurrence of multiple causes rather than by just a single cause

objectives: To offer a better understanding of the key risks affecting cost and schedule performance of modular construction projects by (1) quantifying the characteristics of modular risk factors in terms of likelihood of occurrence and relative impacts on cost and schedule, (2) identifying the key risks affecting cost and schedule performance, and (3) examining how these risks are perceived by different project stakeholders.
problem_statement: Although modular construction offers documented advantages, the industry has not fully capitalized on its potential due to lack of understanding and proper management of unique modular risks. Prior research has largely focused on barriers and drivers of MMC adoption or on specific risk aspects (e.g., tolerances, supply chain), with no study providing an in-depth analysis of the key risks affecting cost and schedule performance of modular construction projects or examining stakeholder alignment on these risks.
methodology: A multistep quantitative survey-based methodology: (1) identification of 50 modular risk factors from a prior systematic literature review (Abdul Nabi and El-adaway 2020); (2) development and distribution of an online Qualtrics survey to 190 US construction professionals (owners, consultants, general contractors, subcontractors) rating likelihood of occurrence and cost/schedule impact of each risk on a 5-point CII Likert scale, yielding 48 valid responses (25.26% response rate); (3) Cronbach's alpha reliability testing; (4) calculation of risk ratings (likelihood x impact) for cost and schedule; (5) Kendall's concordance (chi-squared) analysis to assess within-group agreement; (6) Shapiro-Wilk, Levene's, one-way ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests to compare risk perceptions among stakeholder groups.
key_background_studies: Abdul Nabi and El-adaway (2020) - systematic literature review identifying the 50 modular risk factors used as the basis for the survey
Enshassi et al. (2019, 2020a, 2020b) - developed risk management frameworks for tolerance-related and geometric variability issues in modular construction
Luo et al. (2019) - used social network analysis to develop a risk network of offsite supply chain in Hong Kong
Arashpour et al. (2017) - conducted risk analysis of infrastructure/hybrid projects examining onsite, coordination and offsite risk dimensions
CII (2014) - identified critical success enablers for optimal use of modularization in industrialized projects
Abotaleb et al. (2019) - risk-based approach investigating causes of out-of-sequence work and owner/contractor alignment
Russell et al. (2013) - examined causes of time buffers and stakeholder perceptions, providing methodological template for this study
Haas et al. (2000) - defined modularization as preconstruction of a complete system in a controlled environment transported to site
Farnsworth (2014)/Dailey (2014) - B2 Tower case illustrating how mismanagement of tolerance-related modular risks caused cost/schedule inflation
findings: Eight risk factors were found to be common critical drivers of both cost and schedule underperformance in modular projects: shortage of skilled/experienced laborers, late design changes, poor site attributes and logistics, unsuitability of design for modularization, contractual risks and disputes, lack of adequate collaboration and coordination, challenges related to tolerances and interfaces, and poor construction activity sequencing/management. Environmental and safety risks were least critical. Kendall's concordance analysis showed significant agreement within each stakeholder group, but ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis tests revealed misalignment between stakeholder groups on 32% of cost risk ratings and 36% of schedule risk ratings, indicating different perceptions of risk criticality among owners, consultants, contractors, and subcontractors, particularly regarding transportation costs, activity sequencing, late design changes, site attributes/logistics, and labor shortage.

ideas.idea: Contractual risks and disputes are a top-ranked critical factor affecting both cost and schedule performance in modular construction, requiring special modular contractual terms.
ideas.quote: Contractual risks and disputes (R47) were perceived by the respondents to be highly critical to cost performance (ranked fifth) and schedule performance (ranked seventh) of modular construction projects.

ideas.idea: Contracts for modular projects need to incorporate special terms addressing lead-time requirements for module delivery and collaborative agreement structures for offsite construction.
ideas.quote: The contractual terms should take into consideration unique modularization characteristics such as those related to lead-time requirements associated with the delivery of the modules and the need for collaborative agreements in offsite construction (Wong et al. 2017; Nadim and Goulding 2011).

ideas.idea: Existing contractual models are insufficiently adapted to modular construction, amplifying the criticality of contractual disputes compared to traditional construction.
ideas.quote: However, the criticality of such factor is amplified when implementing modular construction methods due to the need for new processes and contractual models that meet the requirements of the construction method (Nadim and Goulding 2011).

ideas.idea: Late design changes are especially disruptive in modular projects because module manufacturing must begin early and modular designs are less flexible than traditional stick-built designs, making design freeze a critical success factor.
ideas.quote: inflexibility of modular design (Zhai et al. 2014) and the necessity for early initiation of modules manufacturing (Blismas and Wakefield 2009) hinders the ability to handle change orders and onsite modifications.

ideas.idea: Poor coordination/collaboration among stakeholders (design, procurement, logistics) is a major risk factor impeding modular project performance, underscoring the need for collaborative procurement and delivery arrangements.
ideas.quote: Collaboration and coordination among project stakeholders is documented to have a positive impact on modular construction projects by establishing a collaborative procurement method (Zhai et al. 2014), better coordinating shipments from subcontractor and/or contractor warehouses to the site, and improving the coordination of material inventory requirements (Said 2015).

ideas.idea: Choice or suitability of project delivery method itself is included among identified modular risk factors, signalling its relevance to contractual/delivery structuring for MMC.
ideas.quote: R48 Unsuitability of project delivery method

ideas.idea: Synchronizing offsite factory scheduling with onsite construction activities is essential; delays in either domain propagate schedule and cost overruns, implying contracts must address interface coordination between offsite and onsite work.
ideas.quote: Therefore, scheduling and planning of construction work at the factory (off site) and on site should be connected and synchronized in modular construction projects to avoid schedule delays and cost overruns (Taghaddos et al. 2014).

ideas.idea: Tolerance and interface management between modules and onsite elements is a distinct technical/contractual risk requiring predefined tolerance requirements and skilled manufacturers.
ideas.quote: it is important to mitigate such challenges by ensuring appropriate management of the interfaces between the different main components during the design phase, having a manufacturer that is skilled in tight-tolerance modular fabrications, and avoiding small modules with excessive interfaces (O’Connor et al. 2014; Isaac et al. 2016).

ideas.idea: Different project stakeholders (owners, contractors, consultants, subcontractors) perceive contractual and other modular risks differently, indicating a need for aligned risk allocation clauses in contracts.
ideas.quote: Only 3 of the 16 risk factors exhibiting statistical differences between stakeholders were among the top 10 critical risks affecting cost performance in modular construction projects: (1) increased transportation costs (R4), (2) poor activity sequencing/management (R12), and (3) late design changes (R41).

ideas.idea: Legal and regulatory challenges and permitting issues are recognized as distinct modular risk categories separate from general contractual risk, suggesting standard contracts may need explicit provisions for these.
ideas.quote: R49 Legal and regulatory challenges R50 Issues related to project permitting

objectives: To develop and validate an automated, decentralized blockchain-based smart contract framework for construction management by (1) using image-based deep learning to classify critical path activity images into blockchain-usable completion status data, (2) using simulation to derive optimal smart contract stipulations and risk mitigation strategies, and (3) building a web3.js-based decentralized application (dApp) to synchronize detection results and automatically execute smart contract terms (payments and penalties).
problem_statement: Smart contracts cannot inherently interact with real-world construction data, and current construction management practice relies on manual, centralized, time-consuming methods to document progress, plan production, and check contract compliance, leading to delays, distrust, and inefficiency. It is unclear how to represent as-built data in a blockchain, how to design governance mechanisms to minimize delay risk, and how to coordinate as-built data to decentralize smart contract execution—an area described as largely unexplored ('uncharted territory').
methodology: A case study of a 33-story high-rise building (EPC delivery method) was used. Unordered site images of critical path activities were collected (1,492 images), labeled, and augmented (7,210 training/1,492 testing) to train a convolutional neural network (deep learning classifier) to detect activity completion status; a Bayesian network refined predictions using schedule/prerequisite logic. A discrete-event simulation (ARENA) using fitted productivity distributions modeled 570 delay/workforce scenarios to derive optimal mitigation stipulations and risk categories (via Gaussian mixture model clustering). Smart contracts were coded in Solidity, compiled with Truffle, deployed on a Ganache Ethereum test blockchain, and a dApp front end (React/web3.js/IPFS/MetaMask) was built to synchronize image detection outputs with automatic contract execution (payments, penalties).
key_background_studies: Hamledari and Fischer (2021a,b,c) - explored blockchain/smart contracts for payment automation and information accuracy in construction, showing 200% improvement potential and highlighting governance barriers
Wang et al. (2020) - built blockchain-based information management framework for precast supply chain, showing cost reduction via real-time monitoring but lacking construction specifications
Tao et al. (2021) - proposed blockchain framework for collaborative BIM design to reduce cybersecurity risk, but blockchains unsuitable for large BIM files
Xue and Lu (2020) - introduced semantic differential approach to record BIM changes on blockchain, reducing storage needs
Ahmadisheykhsarmast and Sonmez (2020) - developed Microsoft Project add-on to condition smart contract payments using schedule/payment data, protecting against late payments
Elghaish et al. (2020) - developed blockchain framework for automatic financial transactions across the construction value chain, reducing reporting overhead and transferring risk
Hunhevicz et al. (2021) - identified challenge of smart contract inflexibility for unexpected cases due to lack of pre-built governance/adjustment mechanisms
Chen et al. (2022) and Li et al. (2023) - used simulation models to generate smart contract stipulations for dynamic construction scenarios, directly preceding this study's approach
Dimitrov and Golparvar-Fard (2014) - trained classifiers to identify surface materials from images under varying conditions for progress tracking
Kropp et al. (2018) - developed model to recognize construction activity states from as-built images matched to as-planned BIM
findings: The deep learning model achieved 96.31% accuracy/precision/recall/F1 in classifying activity completion status from images, improved to 98.93%/98.96%/98.93%/98.92% after Bayesian network refinement using schedule prerequisite logic. Simulation of 570 scenarios showed that delays in B1+B2 and CA1 could be recovered via additional workforce, but CA2 delays were often unrecoverable; ROI-optimal mitigation policies (e.g., specific numbers of added carpenters) were identified and coded into smart contract stipulations. The dApp prototype successfully synchronized image-based detection results with automatic smart contract execution, correctly triggering payments for on-time completion and automatically calculating and enforcing penalties plus workforce reallocation for delays (e.g., a 5-hour delay triggering addition of 4 carpenters and a $388 penalty). The framework demonstrates feasibility of using as-built images as blockchain oracles to decentralize and automate smart contract conditioning with minimal management effort, though private blockchain design was chosen over public due to labor-intensive industry knowledge requirements and data privacy concerns.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automatically assign payments and penalties based on detected real-world construction progress, reducing reliance on manual, ex-post checking of contract compliance.
ideas.quote: Smart contracts provide a reliable means of automating management stipulations based on certain detected events, such as assigning payments based on the progress of work

ideas.idea: A major barrier to smart contract adoption is their inability to interact with real-world data, requiring 'oracles' to bridge on-chain and off-chain information.
ideas.quote: a smart contract’s inability to interact with real-world data (Wu et al. 2022)

ideas.idea: Lack of a mature governance model specifying rights, obligations and sanctions for noncompliance is the primary barrier to smart contract deployment in construction.
ideas.quote: Lacking a mature and consistent governance model is the primary barrier impeding the deployment of smart contracts in the industry (Hamledari and Fischer 2021b).

ideas.idea: Smart contracts are inherently rigid and cannot be adjusted after deployment unless governance mechanisms for unexpected cases are built in beforehand, posing a challenge for handling contractual variations.
ideas.quote: it is impossible to patch ex-post when no governance mechanism for such adjustments is implemented beforehand in the smart contracts (Hunhevicz et al. 2021).

ideas.idea: Simulation-based analysis can generate 'what-if' smart contract stipulations that allow contracts to adapt dynamically to changing construction scenarios rather than relying on fixed static terms.
ideas.quote: Our previous work (Chen et al. 2022) proved the effectiveness of using simulation to analyze various “what-if” scenarios and establish situation-aware smart contracts to accommodate dynamic construction changes.

ideas.idea: Traditional penalty clauses for delay are typically enforced only near project completion, making it difficult to retroactively assign responsibility; blockchain/smart contracts enable real-time, traceable attribution of delay responsibility to specific subcontractors.
ideas.quote: In current construction practice, the penalty for delayed completion is usually not enforced until or near project completion... It is difficult for project managers to retrospectively check and identify who should be held responsible for the delays.

ideas.idea: Contracts should fulfill three fundamental functions—control, coordination, and adaptation—to manage risk, and smart contracts can be designed to operationalize these functions automatically.
ideas.quote: As mentioned by Yang et al. (2022), contracts should serve three fundamental functions—Control, Coordination, and Adaptation—to mitigate different risks.

ideas.idea: Embedding lean production principles of local responsibility into smart contracts allows automatic quantification of damages attributable to specific subcontractors for schedule deviations.
ideas.quote: The developed smart contracts integrate lean production management to focus on the ‘local’ responsibility of those to whom the various parts are assigned or contracted (Ballard 2000). The developed smart contract function clearly documents the reasons and quantifies the damages each contracted subcontractor should be responsible for

ideas.idea: Immutability of blockchain records, while providing tamper-proof documentation of progress and contractual triggers, also creates a governance challenge because erroneous data cannot be corrected once recorded, requiring more robust dispute-resolution mechanisms.
ideas.quote: the fact that the information contained in the blocks is inviolable also represents a major drawback, since this information cannot be changed when errors occur. This will increase the challenge of designing a more robust smart contract governance mechanism to ensure that all the self-executed stipulations are fair enough to eliminate potential disputes.

ideas.idea: Current smart contract stipulations focus on schedule/workforce but do not address quality compliance, indicating a need for more comprehensive contractual governance mechanisms covering multiple compliance dimensions.
ideas.quote: In reality, checking construction quality compliance is also crucial to ensuring the construction processes and products conform to regulations. Therefore, future research could explore a more comprehensive checking/governance mechanism to guarantee that all compliance regulations are unambiguously addressed in smart contracts.

ideas.idea: Private (permissioned) blockchains are more suitable than public blockchains for construction contractual applications due to the need for data privacy of business strategies and controlled participation by knowledgeable stakeholders.
ideas.quote: From a privacy perspective, successful construction businesses rely highly on their strategies, such as salary systems, lessons learned, and collaborative mode... This information is undoubtedly a top secret that businesses are unwilling to share.

objectives: To identify critical variation-related contract conditions across four international standard contract formats (FIDIC Silver Book, AIA A141, NEC4 ECC, PSSCOC), evaluate their importance and contractor favorability through expert survey, and propose a systematic risk evaluation process for variation management, illustrated through two case studies.
problem_statement: While prior studies have compared standard contract formats' variation/change clauses descriptively, there is a lack of research identifying and evaluating the actual risks these contractual differences pose to contractors, leaving practitioners without tools to assess variation-related contractual risk systematically.
methodology: A six-step comparative and empirical approach: (1) comparative analysis of variation clauses across FIDIC Silver Book, AIA A141, NEC4 ECC, and PSSCOC, classifying 30 key contract items into 6 groups; (2) development of a questionnaire using 5-point (importance) and 7-point (favorability) Likert scales; (3) survey distributed to 62 construction contract experts, 52 valid responses; (4) importance ranking analysis via mean scores; (5) Kruskal-Wallis H-test and Mann-Whitney U-test (with Bonferroni correction) to compare favorability across contracts; (6) two illustrative case studies (metro tunnel projects in Hong Kong and Singapore) applying the importance/favorability findings to actual contracts, validated through interviews with project variation management personnel.
key_background_studies: El-adaway et al. (2016) - comprehensively compared variation-related provisions across traditional standard contracts (1999 FIDIC edition), categorizing them into power/authority, execution/procedure, and price/time changes; foundational comparative framework this study builds on for 2017 FIDIC edition.
Syal and Bora (2016) - comparative review of Change Order clauses in US and Canadian standard contracts, focusing on procedural and cost aspects, but without risk evaluation.
Ibbs (2012) - quantitative literature review on impact, possibility and intensity of variations on productivity, establishing prevalence of variations (~40% of projects exceed 10% scope change).
Lee et al. (2020) - highlighted how employer modifications to standard contracts often shift risk to contractors by removing contractor-favorable clauses.
Abotaleb and El-adaway (2017) - compared payment contract conditions across FIDIC, AIA, and NEC.
McConnell and Clevenger (2018) - analyzed frequently disputed AIA A201 sections, highlighting Change Order clauses as recurring dispute sources.
Thompson et al. (2000) - found NEC improved contractual relationships and fairness in UK construction management practices.
Assaad et al. (2020) - explored differences in back-to-back provisions across US-based standard contracts (AIA, ConsensusDocs, EJCDC).
findings: Valuation method [C17], Variations by changes in law [C30], Extent of changes in law [C28], Sharing of benefit from value engineering [C11], and Limitation on variations [C2] were ranked as the top five most important variation-related contract conditions. Most contract clauses showed statistically significant favorability differences across the four standard formats, except Valuation method and Variations by default of contractor. Absence of change-in-law and value-engineering clauses (as in AIA and NEC) reduced contractor favorability; clear limitation-on-variations clauses increased favorability by protecting contractors from unreasonable scope expansion. Case studies of two metro tunnel projects confirmed that clauses identified as high-risk (e.g., absence of change-in-law provisions, unclear VE benefit-sharing, absent right to decline variations) corresponded to actual contractual disputes and management challenges experienced by contractors.

ideas.idea: Standard contracts are frequently modified by employers during tendering in ways that shift risk onto contractors by removing favorable clauses.
ideas.quote: these modifications tend to align with the employers’ interests and bring potential risks to contractors, often resulting in the removal or replacement of contractor-favorable clauses to unfavorable clauses

ideas.idea: A clearly defined valuation method for variations is the most critical contract condition because it directly affects cost compensation fairness and dispute minimization, though favorability does not differ significantly since all contracts allow negotiation.
ideas.quote: A clearly defined valuation method ensures fairness in cost compensation and contributes to minimizing unnecessary disputes.

ideas.idea: Absence of change-in-law clauses forces contractors to rely on claims rather than smoother variation procedures, increasing risk on long-term projects.
ideas.quote: the absence of a clause to manage changes in law through variations complicated project management for the contractor, who was forced to rely solely on claim procedures to address these issues.

ideas.idea: Value engineering clauses benefit contractors only when benefit-sharing terms are balanced; unilateral employer-favoring sharing terms are as unfavorable as having no VE clause at all.
ideas.quote: If the clauses governing the sharing of benefits from value engineering result in a disproportionate allocation of profit to the employer, contractors may be reluctant to initiate value engineering, potentially missing opportunities for improved project outcomes.

ideas.idea: Clear limitation-on-variations clauses protect contractors from unbounded scope changes and are viewed favorably compared to contracts lacking such restrictions.
ideas.quote: contracts that limit variations to the general and reasonable scope of the contract demonstrated a higher level of favorability compared to others, as they protect contractors from uncertain risks.

ideas.idea: Lack of a contractual right for contractors to decline variations creates practical risk, exemplified by forced acceptance of out-of-scope variations without adequate compensation for secondary impacts.
ideas.quote: The employer of Project B issued several variations for convenience, which were not within the general scope of the contract. Due to the lack of relevant clauses, the contractor was unable to decline these variations and was forced to undertake unexpected work.

ideas.idea: When contractors disagree with a variation valuation, contracts that leave final determination solely to the employer/engineer tend to favor employer interests, increasing contractor risk.
ideas.quote: when the contractor disagreed with the valuation assessment, the method for determining the final value was left to the employer’s sole discretion, which typically favored the employer’s interests.

ideas.idea: Standard contract formats differ fundamentally in terminology and procedural philosophy for variations (FIDIC's descriptive 'Variation', AIA's dual Change Order/Directive, NEC's Compensation Events), reflecting different legal and collaborative traditions relevant to how MMC/prefabrication-related scope changes would be managed.
ideas.quote: NEC contracts do not explicitly define specific terms for variations; instead, they address changes to the scope of work through Compensation Events... NEC emphasizes early notification of any Compensation Events by both the contractor and the client, fostering proactive management of variation.

ideas.idea: A systematic, quantifiable risk evaluation tool (combining importance weighting and favorability scoring) can help contractors proactively identify and prioritize contractual risks before and during project execution, which is broadly applicable to assessing novel delivery/contract provisions.
ideas.quote: The proposed process for evaluating potential contractual risks associated with variations offers contractors a systematic approach to identifying and addressing these risks within contract documents, facilitating the preparation of an effective risk management strategy.

objectives: To explore the critical cost influencing factors (CIFs) and critical stakeholders of prefabricated construction (PC) in China based on stakeholder theory and social network analysis, and to propose stakeholder-specific strategies to reduce PC capital cost.
problem_statement: High capital cost is one of the biggest obstacles to promoting PC in China, but existing studies have not adequately examined the complex interactions among cost influencing factors nor clarified the role and management focus of different stakeholders in PC cost control.
methodology: A hybrid qualitative-quantitative approach: literature review to build a preliminary list of CIFs; two rounds of expert interviews (17 experts from government, developer, designer, contractor and manufacturer stakeholder groups, using chain referral sampling) to establish stakeholder-associated CIFs and evaluate mutual influence via Likert-scale scoring with Rwg consistency testing; social network analysis (whole-network and ego-network analysis using NetMiner4.0) to identify critical CIFs, links, stakeholders and influence conduction paths; validation by removing critical nodes/links and recalculating network indicators.
key_background_studies: Mao et al. (2016) - analyzed nine cases showing lack of experience, skills and market demand increase PC cost
Hong et al. (2018) - compared eight projects across three regions to discuss basic PC cost composition and assembly rate correlation with cost
Qi et al. (2018) - identified incremental cost sources from interior wall components production and hoisting/grouting
Xue et al. (2017) - used mean analysis to study CIFs of PC and design accuracy/standardization importance
Wu et al. (2019b) - constructed transaction costs framework for PC supply chain using social network analysis
Xia et al. (2017, 2018) - integrated risk management and stakeholder management models for construction projects
Luo et al. (2019) - developed a risk network for PC supply chain in Hong Kong using SNA from stakeholder perspective
Lou et al. (2020) - used system dynamics to study CIFs interactions in PC
findings: The study identified 18 stakeholder-associated CIFs and 140 interaction relationships. Developer's cognition and attitude (F5) and transaction costs (F6) are the most critical CIFs, with government, developer and contractor being the most critical stakeholders. Relevant standards and codes, design accuracy/standardization, and application of information technology are also key. High transaction costs attract government attention prompting policy responses. Strategies proposed include: government improving standards/codes and mandatory assembly rate policies; developer reducing transaction costs and improving project definition; contractor increasing information technology application; and collaborative work between designer and manufacturer to reduce unnecessary costs. Manufacturer, contrary to expectation, was not identified as the most critical stakeholder despite influencing design standardization and production scale.

ideas.idea: Developer's low cognition and attitude toward PC leads to reluctance to adopt prefabrication, reinforcing traditional cast-in-place methods (technology lock-in) and hindering cost optimization.
ideas.quote: Developers have low enthusiasm to adopt PC due to their own reasons, such as insufficient cognition of PC, lack of PC cost control experience and other stakeholders' reasons

ideas.idea: Transaction costs are a significant but often overlooked hidden cost burden on developers arising from new technology and management processes required by PC.
ideas.quote: the developer pays additional hidden costs due to the adoption of PC

ideas.idea: Design changes are a major source of developer transaction costs and also damage developer reputation and willingness of other stakeholders to collaborate in future.
ideas.quote: design changes are considered to be the main source of developer's TCs... the hidden cost loss caused by design changes are mainly reflected in the decline in the reputation of developers and the reduced willingness of other stakeholders to cooperate with them subsequently

ideas.idea: Lack of comprehensive government standards and codes prevents effective supervision of PC construction activities and increases costs across design, production and construction phases.
ideas.quote: Lack comprehensive policies and specific standardized implementation measures... make the government unable to effectively supervise and regulate the construction activities of various stakeholders

ideas.idea: A high mandatory minimum assembly rate imposed by government can act as a market barrier discouraging developer entry into the PC market due to increased incremental costs.
ideas.quote: a high mandatory minimum assembly rate will hinder some developers from entering the PC market and form market barriers

ideas.idea: Contractor's application of integrated information technologies (BIM, RFID, GPS) acts as a bridge for information transfer and resource sharing among stakeholders, improving construction management efficiency and reducing cost.
ideas.quote: the integrated use of BIM, GPS, RFID and other information technology can monitor the construction process and improve management efficiency

ideas.idea: Design accuracy and standardization by designers positively impacts downstream production and construction, enabling economies of scale and reducing costs, and benefits from early manufacturer collaboration.
ideas.quote: the manufacturer can participate in the work of the designer in advance and propose optimization suggestions to facilitate the standardization of component design

ideas.idea: Incremental on-site construction costs are influenced by factors beyond the contractor's control, including design errors and delayed component delivery from other stakeholders.
ideas.quote: other parties' reasons (such as design errors, delayed delivery of components, etc.) will also cause the incremental cost of construction

ideas.idea: Collaborative work and coordination between developer and other parties (information interaction) positively affects cost management, highlighting the developer's coordinating role in PC delivery.
ideas.quote: The developer coordinates all parties involved and strengthens information interaction, which can positively impact the cost management

ideas.idea: Government economic incentive policies such as tax reductions and subsidies can alleviate enterprises' cost pressure in adopting PC.
ideas.quote: The government's economic incentive policies such as tax reductions and subsidies can alleviate the cost pressure of enterprises

ideas.idea: Standardization of design and production, as demonstrated in mature PC markets like Sweden, is a key strategy to achieve economies of scale and reduce cost, implying contract and process design should support standardized component approaches.
ideas.quote: standardization is regarded as the main strategy to promote prefabrication because it can achieve economies of scale

ideas.idea: Government demonstration projects and successful PC business models can be used to increase developer enthusiasm and acceptance, suggesting a role for procurement/contractual incentives in promoting MMC adoption.
ideas.quote: the government can actively assist the developer to develop and promote technology demonstration projects of PC and successful PC business models to increase the enthusiasm of the developer

objectives: To develop a literature-based analysis framework of contract sources of ambiguity; to evaluate causes of disputes by analyzing selected Canadian Superior court cases; and to analyze relevant terms from Canadian standard contracts (CCDC) that can address the significant causes of dispute found in the case analysis, comparing modular/offsite construction (MOC) and conventional on-site construction (COC).
problem_statement: There are no standard contracts for MOC in Canada, so MOC projects adopt and modify standard contracts designed for conventional construction, increasing the potential for contractual disputes. Prior research on contractual disputes has focused mainly on COC and has been largely qualitative/subjective, leaving a gap in systematic, quantified understanding of dispute causes specific to MOC projects.
methodology: A two-phase mixed methodology: Phase 1 used a qualitative literature review (105 articles: 57 COC, 48 MOC) to extract 396 sources of contractual ambiguity, which were clustered into a four-level hierarchical 'fishbone' framework (categories, subcategories, classes, subclasses) and weighted by frequency. Phase 2 involved collecting Canadian Superior Court construction dispute cases (2000-2019) from CanLII across four provinces (BC, ON, AB, QC), narrowing 4,708 cases to 178 contractual dispute cases (20 MOC, 158 COC), analyzing project characteristics, party typology, contract types, and applying the Phase 1 framework to classify and quantify causes of dispute (43 MOC causes, 463 COC causes), then comparing literature-based and case-based results and mapping causes to CCDC 2 and CCDC 14 general conditions.
key_background_studies: Arcadis [2] - reported rising disputes and dispute resolution times in North America, UK, Europe, Middle East over five years
Odeh and Battaineh [17] and other survey-based studies [5,14,16,19] - identified common causes of disputes via questionnaire surveys with construction professionals
Cakmak and Cakmak [8] - defined causes of conflicts/disputes from responsible parties' perspective through literature analysis
Studies [1,12] - identified causes of construction litigation through literature analysis, informing the need for a systematic framework
A previously developed conceptual framework [3] - provided the four-level hierarchy (categories, subcategories, classes, subclasses) structure adopted as the starting point for the fishbone model
[18] - noted MOC has different features from COC despite using the same standard codes and materials, and suggested CCDC 14 as most suitable for MOC
[9] CCDC 14 general conditions - source of specific payment clauses (5.2.3, 5.2.8) analyzed for suitability to MOC
[13] - cited regarding proportion of MOC work completed in factory (85-90%) versus on-site
findings: Ambiguity in contract terms is the most critical dispute cause in Canadian court cases for both MOC and COC projects (over 70% of frequency), followed by poor contract draftsmanship and lack of common-sense among contracting parties. At the class level, 'unclear payment terms' is the major issue for MOC cases while 'unclear terms for changes in work' dominates COC cases.
